Gameplay:
Playing alone, the game sucks. However, once you find a good clan with an active Teamspeak or Discord, the game becomes like 10x more fun. Having logged over 100 days in playtime, I'm not sure if I actually enjoy the game or if I have self-induced stockholmsyndrome, but I love the game none the less. The grind is there but is completely optional and will most times not stop your progress through the game at all. Please remeber though, this is a F2P game with MMORPG attributes, so there is some grinding that is required, but it's not that bad.
Economy:
Despite what the negative reviews say, this game is NOT pay-to-win. Paying offers you the ability to get some exclusives cosmetics and get platinum (the game's premium currency) fast. Platinum is used to buy weapons (that you can get through normal gameplay), buy a huge variety of cosmetics and utility items, rush the crafting process, and trade with players. The glory of it? You can get platinum without spending a dime! Warframe has a great, 100% player-run economy. Through sometimes fun, sometimes not fun grinding, you can earn lots of platinum completely free.
Devs:
The developers are just absolutely amazing people that listen to their community. If you want an example of this, go to [DE] Steve's twitter (@sj_sinclair) and look at all of his responses to fans talking about their ideas for mechanics or features in the game. Apart from that, they consistently host Dev Streams to show the player base what's coming to the game and where they are in the developement process. During these streams, they give away large platinum prizes to random viewers and take questions from the players. They are incredibly responsive on forums (as much as one human being mentioned hundreds of times a day can be) and are some of the kindest and funniest people you could have the pleasure of talking to. Not only that, but the customer support team is deserving of praise on their own. During their operation hours, my tickets hardly go an hour without a response at most. I could go on so much longer, but I think you get the idea.
Content Updates:
This is the only place I'm going to be even the slightest bit negative. Content updates do not come out incredibly often and they usually do not contain much in the way of adding more to the game. Major updates come out around twice to three times a year, that USUALLY just involve one 30 minute to an hour quest, some new weapons, and MAYBE a new game mechanic. They are also NOTORIOUS for delaying these updates, sometimes as much as several months. On the other hand, DE (the company behind Warframe) has showed us their newest W.I.P. that should be coming out soon(TM)., Plains of Eidolon. This is going to be the first true open-world experience for Warframe, with a 3km by 3km area to explore. Whenever I talk about Clicker Heroes with a friend of mine, I find myself having to put the word “game” in quotations. I just feel like it’s hard to call something a game if you’re not actually doing anything with it for roughly 95% of the time. This has become a running joke between us. Well, with thousands of hours poured into Clicker Heroes over the course of more than a year, I guess at this point, the joke is on me.
Clicker Heroes is what I would describe as a casual clicker and management game. You click enemies in order to damage and defeat them, and then they give you gold to power up your clicks or purchase heroes to click for you. Eventually you’ll get to a point where you just can’t progress any further and so you’ll have to ascend. Ascending does a sort of soft reset to your game, but it also gives you hero souls which can be used to upgrade your heroes. With your upgraded heroes, you’ll be able to progress further than you did the last time. You’ll repeat this process at least a dozen times until you find that once again you just can’t progress any further. Then you get to transcend. Transcending is much like ascending in that it will reset your game, but this time you will gain ancient souls. These, like hero souls, will boost your heroes even further.
This process will go on, and on, and on, and on…
I know this will not sound appealing to many, and admittedly I’ve started this review painting the game in a bad light, although not intentionally. It’s just that this is the elephant in the room that I must talk about; the repetitive/addicting nature of this game.
The reason I continue to play this game is because I’m a completionist. I have to get the last few achievements in this game. I just
to. I can’t explain it, it’s just who I am. If you’re anything like me, here is my warning to you; carefully consider if you want to start this game. It will take you thousands of hours to get all the achievements. Even if you’re not interested in getting all the achievements, you may find yourself wondering how much further you can push through the game only to realize that it was a few months ago when you first wondered that.
If the biggest negative aspect about this game is its repetitive/addictive nature, then the biggest positive about this game would be its depth. There are different paths that you can choose to go down, so to speak. You can be a clicker and do all the work yourself, you can be an idler and let your heroes do all the work, or you can do some kind of combination between the two. These paths will become more apparent in the way you spend your hero souls, and even more so later in the game when you earn your first ancient souls. Do you want to spend your points in ways that will boost idle bonuses, or would you rather focus on ways to improve your clicking power?
Along the way you’ll randomly receive relics to help boost your powers even further, earn gilds for your heroes every ten levels you complete that boost the damage of randomly selected heroes, and you have the option of creating or joining a clan in order to team up with others against a boss monster; a daily mini-game like challenge that rewards you in hero souls. The game has many small ways of helping you to progress, which brings me to micro-transactions.
Like most free-to-play games, this one contains optional micro-transactions. One concern many people have with micro-transactions in free-to-play games is that they will lead to a sort of pay-to-win scenario. Well let me put your mind at rest; that is not the case here. You can use real world money to buy the in-game currency (rubies), but the great thing is that you can also find rubies randomly through regular game play. As long as you check in on things every now and then, you will find enough to make the small purchases for things you need. I will eventually finish everything in this game, and have not purchased any rubies.
Although so many hours must be put into this game in order to make any real progress, this can be somewhat misleading. You see, Clicker Heroes doesn’t need your attention most of the time. Even if you go down a mostly clicker route, your heroes will still do a lot of the work. You see those hundreds, even thousands of hours that I and others have in this game? Well we didn’t actually sit in front of the computer and give this game our full attention for all that time. We just ran the game in the background for most of it and did other things. Once you know what you’re doing, things will be good to go for hours (although you’ll likely want to check in on it occasionally). I’ll often find myself playing another game while Clicker Heroes is running in the background, only to alt+tab to it every now and then to make sure everything is running smoothly. That’s how this review was written. If the time investment worries you or the repetitive nature is a large drawback to you, the fact that you don’t need to pay all that much attention to this game may grant you some kind of solace.
Once again, I know that the repetitive nature of this game is something that I and others will harp on, but there is a reason this game is voted so favourably. I believe the positives that I listed above outweigh the negatives. Clicker Heroes is genuinely a good game, and if you don’t mind sinking the time into it, then go ahead and give it a try.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare used to be a spectacular game and one of the top medieval, FPS, action game on the market... five years ago, but since then it's cancerous community, also refering to many of it's mod/staff who've ban me endlessly for sharing my opinion about the game. Great job, by the way. They called it hate speech and trolling. One of Steam's top most cancerous staff/fourm mods. Hell, for writing a review and giving them a thumbs down they might just ban me forever and I don't care anymore because this game isn't worth the money anymore. All that remains today is watered down gameplay.
I used to adore this game way back when people like myself were learning how to swing a sword into someone's face or crush their heads to dust with a maul. There was no better moment than being a King-loving blue knight with a longsword in one hand and a kite shield in the other, going up against one of those evil red knight that laughed as they carved their bloody way through your entire team. You know, back in the good ol' days when there were no pro level 60s blocking, parrying, and exploiting the hit-boxes to somehow delay or speed up their attack and still do full damage. You don't get moments like those anymore, it's all just cheap exploits now.
What really broke Chivalry for everyone was these hit-boxes exploits which scared away new players and made the combat trivial, broken, and boring. It's very sad.

Whenever I talk about Clicker Heroes with a friend of mine, I find myself having to put the word “game” in quotations. I just feel like it’s hard to call something a game if you’re not actually doing anything with it for roughly 95% of the time. This has become a running joke between us. Well, with thousands of hours poured into Clicker Heroes over the course of more than a year, I guess at this point, the joke is on me.
Clicker Heroes is what I would describe as a casual clicker and management game. You click enemies in order to damage and defeat them, and then they give you gold to power up your clicks or purchase heroes to click for you. Eventually you’ll get to a point where you just can’t progress any further and so you’ll have to ascend. Ascending does a sort of soft reset to your game, but it also gives you hero souls which can be used to upgrade your heroes. With your upgraded heroes, you’ll be able to progress further than you did the last time. You’ll repeat this process at least a dozen times until you find that once again you just can’t progress any further. Then you get to transcend. Transcending is much like ascending in that it will reset your game, but this time you will gain ancient souls. These, like hero souls, will boost your heroes even further.
This process will go on, and on, and on, and on…
I know this will not sound appealing to many, and admittedly I’ve started this review painting the game in a bad light, although not intentionally. It’s just that this is the elephant in the room that I must talk about; the repetitive/addicting nature of this game.
The reason I continue to play this game is because I’m a completionist. I have to get the last few achievements in this game. I just
to. I can’t explain it, it’s just who I am. If you’re anything like me, here is my warning to you; carefully consider if you want to start this game. It will take you thousands of hours to get all the achievements. Even if you’re not interested in getting all the achievements, you may find yourself wondering how much further you can push through the game only to realize that it was a few months ago when you first wondered that.
If the biggest negative aspect about this game is its repetitive/addictive nature, then the biggest positive about this game would be its depth. There are different paths that you can choose to go down, so to speak. You can be a clicker and do all the work yourself, you can be an idler and let your heroes do all the work, or you can do some kind of combination between the two. These paths will become more apparent in the way you spend your hero souls, and even more so later in the game when you earn your first ancient souls. Do you want to spend your points in ways that will boost idle bonuses, or would you rather focus on ways to improve your clicking power?
Along the way you’ll randomly receive relics to help boost your powers even further, earn gilds for your heroes every ten levels you complete that boost the damage of randomly selected heroes, and you have the option of creating or joining a clan in order to team up with others against a boss monster; a daily mini-game like challenge that rewards you in hero souls. The game has many small ways of helping you to progress, which brings me to micro-transactions.
Like most free-to-play games, this one contains optional micro-transactions. One concern many people have with micro-transactions in free-to-play games is that they will lead to a sort of pay-to-win scenario. Well let me put your mind at rest; that is not the case here. You can use real world money to buy the in-game currency (rubies), but the great thing is that you can also find rubies randomly through regular game play. As long as you check in on things every now and then, you will find enough to make the small purchases for things you need. I will eventually finish everything in this game, and have not purchased any rubies.
Although so many hours must be put into this game in order to make any real progress, this can be somewhat misleading. You see, Clicker Heroes doesn’t need your attention most of the time. Even if you go down a mostly clicker route, your heroes will still do a lot of the work. You see those hundreds, even thousands of hours that I and others have in this game? Well we didn’t actually sit in front of the computer and give this game our full attention for all that time. We just ran the game in the background for most of it and did other things. Once you know what you’re doing, things will be good to go for hours (although you’ll likely want to check in on it occasionally). I’ll often find myself playing another game while Clicker Heroes is running in the background, only to alt+tab to it every now and then to make sure everything is running smoothly. That’s how this review was written. If the time investment worries you or the repetitive nature is a large drawback to you, the fact that you don’t need to pay all that much attention to this game may grant you some kind of solace.
Once again, I know that the repetitive nature of this game is something that I and others will harp on, but there is a reason this game is voted so favourably. I believe the positives that I listed above outweigh the negatives. Clicker Heroes is genuinely a good game, and if you don’t mind sinking the time into it, then go ahead and give it a try.

Do you have a hankering to get RSI? Have I got a game for you!
Well I use the term "game" loosely…
Luckily I only sunk about 10-15 hours into this, the remainder of my logged hours were my machine chugging away with the “game” in the background.
“Game” Play: You click on enemies, each click deals a small amount of damage to said enemy, once enemy has succumb to the barrage of clicks the will die and spew forth coins. Once reaching certain amounts of coins you can hire a hero to click with you thus giving you more damage and quicker time to get to those sweet-sweet coins, then when you get more coins you can buy power-ups for yourself and your heroes providing even more damage. After a while once you have even more coins you can get one of your heroes to transcend moving you to a new world to click on more enemies and hire heroes again, and the cycle continues.
Basically this game is the perfect example of a Skinner box, if you don’t know what that is please lookup “extra credits Skinner box” on youtube for a very good video explanation.
It’s not the worst thing in the world, it’s not like its crack or anything, but your body will prefer it if you do not play. I mean seriously do you really want RSI from all that clicking?

Starting out the game, its a standard GTA-like story driven game. The "sand-box", or "free" style of gameplay however, is very lacking in comparison however. The game follows the career of a Detective, some "bad♥♥♥♥♥quot; veteran from WW2 and his hijinx. This game is VERY linear. there are "street crime" events that happen in the city, but you'll be doing the same thing for each - Chase, shoot, suspect dead, repeat. That said. > you could actually ask mostly wrong questions for all your suspects- then STILL manage to continue the story. - as punishment, solve street crimes- then carry on the story. pagnnhn!
Conclusion > I actually had a good time for the first hour or two. I mean, the story isn't bad, but it's vastly inferior to anything that GTA gave out. Graphics? They're OK. Game-play? Not too good- not going to touch this for a LONG time. Instead of a detective game like I wanted, it was more like a Japanese style graphic novel where you just watch.

DIRECTIONS

L.A. Noire, why are you so entertaining and so disappointing at the same time?
L.A. Noire is mostly the story of Cole Phelps, a former-marine-now-policeman working in the Angels' city. As such, he will have to work his way up the food chain, starting in patrol, soon to be promoted to trafic, homicide and what not.
The game is a mix and match of several genres: it's a bit of a point n' click, but with third-person shooting and driving around, in a beautifully recreated L.A. Mostly, you'll be collecting clues on crime scenes, and interviewing suspects, while a partner lets you do all the work and comments on your action.
Those parts are great. Thanks to some fancy facial-capture technology and the help of professional actors, the characters of L.A. Noire feel alive, and real. You can see their expression on their faces, notice when they tell the truth or when they lie (in which case you gotta shove a clue you collected into their face). Coles Phelps yells, gets mad, doubts... In a very convincing way. The cast includes many well-know series actors, from Madmen, Breaking Bad or Twin Peaks.
What's more, the shooting parts (relatively frequent) aren't that bad, for an investigation game.
But L.A. Noire's greatest success is its wonderful film noire atmosphere. Secret loves, murders, illegal gamblings, corrupted politicians and cops, jazz, femmes fatales... Everything is right here, in a post-WW2 US. A country that feels invincible, but whose confidence hides nasty stories.
Great, heh?
Yeah, except that L.A. Noire also disappoints. If you don't stick to the cases you're supposed to be solving, you quickly find out its greatest weakness: Los Angeles has no soul. The city is beautiful, mind you. But nothing happens. Car drives around, people walk. There are a few scripted events. But that's about it. You can't drive around and tail someone just because he looks weird. The game has to tell you to do it. You can't get into a restaurant a get yourself a coffee and read the news. You can't discuss with people. The city feels like a beautiful, but empty playground.
If you're expecting a game that looks and plays like Gran Theft Auto, let's say you might be turned off by L.A. Noire. The game has little in common with Rockstar' behemoth. But if you like the film noire genre, and are willing to put up with sometimes clunky or repetitive gameplay, then you ought to try L.A. Noire. I personnally see the game as an interactive story (a bit like The Walking Dead), taking place in an open world where you can drive fancy old cars. Too bad the game could have been so much more.
DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME!

To start off, I'd like to say that this is a game for someone with patience and an open mind. You may or may not encounter bugs, and official servers do have their own problems. Overall, my review is an 8 of 10 for Ark despite any issues it may have. It's fun, it's challenging, and it's different. You may only hear about the issues but, in my opinion, the good outweighs the bad. Whether or not the game is worth $60 is up to you. Everyone has a different experience and don't always value games in the same way. Honestly, I'd dare say Ark is better than a lot of AAA titles.
There is something to be said about the graphics and performance of Ark. I don't know what others are playing on, but my friend has a mid-tier PC. That said, he can run the game on high settings. The point I'm trying to get across is that you should run Ark fine on high if you have a mid-tier PC. Lower mid-tier PCs may struggle a bit on high, but medium should be fine. I honestly don't see how others are having issues unless they're trying to render in 10,000 dinosaurs at once (which isn't a good idea in the first place).
Aside from that, it is clear that Ark has beautiful graphics. Small details such as the moon are high resolution rather than just a ball of silver in the sky. My only problem lies with the fog, which looks like someone had a bit too much fun with an airbrush tool. The fog makes vision almost impossible at times and you have another thing coming if you think you can escape it by going underwater. Other than that, Ark is gorgeous.
Ark does have it's bugs but I have yet to encounter any that are problematic enough to make me set this to not recommended. There are some that may be a bit frustrating at first but all that I have encountered are bugs that you can reverse. If you have patience, you will be able to enjoy yourself even with these bugs. You just need to take on the mindset of "things happen." Stuck inside your dinosaurs somehow or your dinosaurs are stuck in each other? Wistle them to a new spot. Baby fall through a floor? Pick up the floor (or check the next floor down if you have multiple levels). Dinosaur stuck floating midair on top of another? Punch it. Dinosaur appearing where it isn't (only happens with specific creatures such as Kaprosuchus where putting them in pens may cause them to sink to ground level when they aren't actually that low)? Whistle it to follow and it'll fix itself. Aside from that, there's the issue of ragdoll glitches. Still, this can be fixed by harvesting the body, though sometimes it will go flying away (namely fish; for some reason they have learned to ascend post-death but it's only some of them). It's generally only an issue with smaller creatures, however.
You will encounter hitbox issues. If you've played the game long enough to know what dinosaurs actually have these issues the most, you will know how to counter it. It isn't hard and only requires a bit of reorganization on your part. Don't want to be smacked off an edge by tails? Put your dinosaurs further away. You know this happens, so move them. Sometimes this issue is actually amusing. Imagine swinging back and forth on the tip of a Diplodocus tail (which is so thin you shouldn't be able to stand on it). It's great.
If you enjoy a singleplayer sandbox experience, you will absolutely adore this game. It is a lot of fun and, with mods and maps, it is endless fun. Don't like player made mods but want to mess with rates? You can. Ark is completely modifiable even in singleplayer. Just make sure you know what the values do (some aren't self-explanatory if you don't know much on the game) or you may have quite an interesting experience to say the least.
I, personally, do not usually play official servers. With that in mind, I can't say much aside from what I have heard of them. You can find good PvP servers, though they are few and far between. Most have alpha tribes that more or less run the server and, honestly, I'm not a big fan of occasional server wipes unless it is really needed. For those servers it is quite possible it is needed but, as I run my own server, I am aware that there are servers that can run much more smoothly for longer periods of time without being wiped at all. In any case, that much is up to you. A lot of people enjoy the official PvE servers, so I think that says enough about those. Other than that, I've heard that official servers are very laggy. Personally, I have played on only three and do agree that has been a trend among them even with a low population. It's very frustrating, honestly.
Overall, I recommend playing on unofficial servers. There are some that run vanilla settings, though some are a bit modified. They range from different levels of modification as well, so you can have something completely broken in the name of fun or something entirely balanced. These are your best bet if you want fully moderated and balanced PvP. Most of these little server communities are also very relaxed and fun. I've seen a lot of really awesome people come and go on servers like these. If you really like interaction, these are the way to go. They give you the best chance to build yourself up before you get raided (and often have offline raid protection, which protects everything you own). For example, I once had a friend lose an Argentavis on a PvP server to a player. The player didn't want any hostility between them and brought back a higher level Wyvern instead.

I’m almost ashamed to say that I have more hours invested into
than any other game. As far as first-person, multiplayer-only medieval games go, this is the best there is. Considering how often this goes on sale, you’d be doing yourself a disservice by not buying it.
Let’s skip straight to the gameplay, because there certainly isn’t really any story to speak of. The game is traditionally played in first person mode, although some servers allow you to switch to third person. You control movement with WASD and use the mouse to control attacks and blocks. There are three basic attacks – the horizontal swing (left mouse button), the overhead (mousewheel backwards) and the stab (mousewheel forwards). Right click functions as your parry. Each player has a health bar, which gets depleted as you get hit, and a stamina bar which drains when you attack, jump, block or feint an attack.
You play as one of four classes - the knight, vanguard, man-at-arms or archer. The knight is the tankiest of the four, having the most health but also moving the slowest. The vanguard is somewhat more nimble, at the cost of a lower health bar. Man-at-arms is a fast but fragile little thing with the ability to dodge (by double-tapping a direction, much like
). Finally, there’s the archer, who can shoot arrows and is hated by everyone in the game. Each class has a distinct set of weapons to choose from, each with different amounts of damage, speed and range, allowing for a variety of playstyles.
The game offers several game modes. If you’re in the mood for an objective-based game, pick the Team Objective mode, where you and your team might be tasked with defending several catapults or even the King’s royal family. Are you in more of a cluster ♥♥♥♥ mood? Pick free-for-all. Do you fancy yourself the best melee combatant in Chivalry? Prove it in a duel server. Given the Steam Workshop integration, there are now more game modes than ever to try out.
Most importantly, regardless of what mode you play, killing an enemy in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing satisfying, especially if you’re able to take out multiple enemies by yourself in what looked like unsurmountable odds.
A warning to the new: It’s one of those games that starts off a bit difficult. Although the game does feature a tutorial, walking into a multiplayer game for the first time might feel dreadful. Experienced players will be able to exploit all your bad habits and there are times you’ll feel helpless. I admit that it’s easy to get discouraged. Despite how simple the game looks on the surface, there is some amount of skill involved, and I’d recommend you either ask a friendly player or look at some guides or tutorial videos online for a bit of help before you give up on the game.
The game is commonly criticised for lacking depth, particularly from new players. When two new players duel, you’ll often find that one player attacks and the other one defends, then the same thing happens in reverse and keeps going back and forth without anyone gaining ground. The issue is that the game contains many advanced techniques that make use of the game mechanics that aren’t really explained in the tutorial or a manual, such as dragging, look-downs, matrixing and reverse-hitting, all of which will vary the timing of your attack or counter-attack and make battles far more interesting.
The graphics are… well heck, it’s an indie game. It’s definitely not mind-blowing, but it could be far worse. One thing they did nail really well was the amount of gore in the game. Apparently, medieval warfare isn’t pretty, and people do bleed and have their limbs and head cut off, and the game manages to capture that in a somewhat comical but effective way. Whilst games like Call of Duty allow you to teabag an enemy upon killing them, Chivalry allows you to walk up to your dead opponent and chop their head clean off if you so desire. It’s wonderful.
The only other notably thing about the presentation is that the game contains some of the most comically-hilarious voiceovers ever. It definitely doesn’t take itself too seriously.
is an absolutely hilarious game that has offered me countless hours of fun. It’s also a game that gets considerably more enjoyable as you get better at the game. I’ve yet to play another game that’s made killing an enemy this damn satisfying. The numerous different game modes on offer also help to prevent the game from becoming stagnant. This is an awesome game that’s going to last you a long time if you’re willing to put the time and effort into getting better. Just don’t be discouraged when you first start out – we all started somewhere.

Well, there is a lot to be said about Chivalry: Medieval Warfare.  It's a real love-hate relationship; sometimes leaving you with that feeling like your newly transplanted kidney just got prison chiv'd.  It has had more "updates" than any other game I can think of, for better or worse, always requiring you to rebind your keys.  Some of the ingame taunts like "Your brain is as dry as a biscut after a long voyage" or "Your stupidity is no accident, it is your birthright!" accurately portrails a fair portion of the Chivalry: Medieval Warfare community.
The Cons:
-  Still uses dx9 (Can't utilize 64bit OS)
-  Updates sometimes make optimization worse
-  Limited online servers
-  Location restictive servers (80+ ping = poor performance)
-  Buggy textures or landscape that causes characters to get stuck
-  Steep learning curve, requires many gameplay hours
-  No shortage of trolls, emotional vampires, and snake oil merchants
The Pros:
-  Ingame voting option (Next map/kick abusive player)
-  On sale often; lots of fresh meat
-  Active community with new maps/skins.
-  Active game updates
-  Exciting melee combat
-  Teamwork potential
-  High replay vaule
-  Endless comic scenarios
-  Ingame taunts
This game is certainly unique, providing you a comical medieval experience and thrilling melee combat.  Even for those who are unable to dedicate many gameplay hours, there are low ranking servers with many different gametypes.  I highly recommend playing with friends or seek out a clan to bring out the best in the game's potential.  Even with all the frustrations this game can throw at you, it has provided some of the most fun of any game I've ever played with friends.
Final Verdict:  Medieval times awaits you now!

However, finding a nice quiet corner far away from resources and having to run to get what you need to scrape out a meager hut and start building up, only to have an admin strafe you with infinite rockets while flying just really puts a sour taste in your mouth.  You could just start your own server I guess, but then you run the risk of staring too long into the abyss.
So, with all of these complaints, why do I recommend the game?  Because I genuinely enjoy single player.  The "game" aspect of it is actually a lot of fun.  I love exploring, running through a jungle and then smack into a raptor that is level one million, then having to try and get away from that sucker as he eats your face off is both exciting and hilarious.  Mods also improve the building and taming aspects of the game, you can have a whole dino community and none of them will knock you out and cage you up, filling your inventory with their poop and watching you starve to death.  I have no problems with PvP games at all, I just hate when one group gets so established that new players are unable to ever get into the game.  If they designed AI players that would build bases and raid, not just you, but each other, I would consider this game the perfect solo game and totally ignore the multiplayer aspect.  I want to fight people, but when I'm done playing for the evening I don't want everything destoryed and have to start from scratch the next day.
So, get it if you like single player exploration and crafting games, or... if you're an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and everything that I said above made you chortle so hard your mountain dew came spewing out your nose and dripped down your cheeto dust covered neckbeard.
But even then, wait until it's on sale.

Welcome to Chivalry: Medieval Screamfare!
Let me start off with the fact that team kills happen often, with "often" being an understatement. If that type of thing pisses you off, you should probably already start looking elsewhere. The team killing is managable, especially if one learns how to defend themself properly, but it'll still happen regardless of how well someone trains, so don't expect to avoid it completely. However, if you like grown men screaming in their armor and swinging all types weapons at each other, this game is completely up your alley.
So what makes the Chivalry good? Looking at it first glance, Chivalry is rather clunky, and there are many times someone may put the mechanics into question. An example of this is, "What? How did an archer block a ♥♥♥♥ING WARHAMMER with their butter knife? Let alone decapitate someone in full plate armor?" Luckily, this game has a few major benefits. At it's core, Chivalry is all about timing and playing mind games with your opponent. Feint an attack to make someone attempt a block too early, or begin fleeing from your enemy, only to turn around and jab at them while they run right into your weapon. Weapons work the way they're designed to work; I advise against attempting to slash someone with a spear, or use a hammer for jabbing. You'll only make yourself look silly. Use weapons for their real purpose, and you'll see better results. In accordance, body and weapon positioning actually behave correctly. Crouch and face downward, and you'll doge a horizontal swing. Crouch and turn left or right of your foe while sidestepping, and you'll dodge an overhead swing or thrust. Combine this with your weapon mastery, and you'll be virtually unstoppable.
You can be your own medieval Neo. How cool is that?

Pros:
This game is solid and was the game that War of the Roses tried to be but failed miserably at: the quintessential medieval  multiplayer game. The controls are fluid, the classes make sense, the servers are stable and flowing with players, and there's lots of servers in regions unaccounted for in other games, like Australia. It's forgiving for new players thanks to low rank servers and a HELPFUL tutorial, something that games lack. Game has a lot of depth for something that's simple on the surface (like Pokemon and Counter Strike: Global Offensive) so veteran players always have room to improve. Can't win a 6v1 so teamwork is important. Team kills and friendly fire balances the game so that weapons like Zwei or Messer aren't the only viable weapon 100% of the time. People can kick others if they grief or hog a spot with high ping/long idle times.
Cons:
While there's a lot of players in servers, you will often encounter a server list with either 24/24 or 32/32 OR 0/24 (and 0/32), so basically half the time the servers are full or completely empty. You can often get into what appear to be full games sometimes, but other times you'll be spamming "Connect" for a few minutes hoping to get in. While the game is balanced, things like Archer daggers blocking Maul and Messer weapons, Vanguard Claymore/Zwei charge One-Hit Kill attacks, and broadsword (not sure if right weapon, but one weapon does) having an impossible to predict riposte and feint are clearly overpowered, and weapons like the Flail and Warhammer are ridiculously underpowered (and in Flail's case, just poorly designed). Sometimes characters bug out and parries don't work/reach of weapon is longer or shorter than it should be which leads to undeserved deaths. People can be griefers and team kill with no consequence to them if the enemy team refuses to kick them.
The cons aren't game breaking most of the time, and are mostly inconsequential, and don't impact the game as negatively as they might sound. I think this game deserves an 8.5/10 for being one of the best multiplayer experiences out there.

An excellent open world, crime drama. You play Cole Phelps, who starts as a beat cop on the L.A.P.D. and you work your way up through different "desks" as a detective investigating traffic, homocide, vice, and arson cases.
The Combat (hand to hand, and shooting) is about average, but isn't especially frequent either. The game really shines when it comes to the interrogations, where you must ask questions, use collected evidance, and read the faces of those you are interrogating to decide who is guilty and who is innocent.
Speaking of reading faces, the faceial capture and acting are top notch and help set this game apart. Everyone on screen (for the most part, you'll get what I mean) has had their faces captured while they deliver their lines, (and as a result, the characters look like their actors, those familiar with "Fringe" or "Dark Matters" will recognize John Noble in a later part of the story).
Highly reccomended for fans of Film Noir featuring hard boiled detectives like Sam Spade or Phillip Marlowe, or even modern crime dramas like CSI or NCIS.

My rating: 6/10
It's such a shame to see a game that does so many things right essentially ruined by getting so many things wrong.  I finally finished the game after starting it over 1 year ago - I started playing but quickly got so frustrated with its faults that I gave up on it and moved on to other things.  I really hate wasting money, though, so unless a game is abysmally bad (like, say, Assassin's Creed 1), I will generally force myself through to completion just to feel like I got my money's worth.  The thing about LA Noire is that it isn't abysmally bad, in fact there are a lot of things about the game that are outstanding, and I really wanted to like the game and finish it; it's just that the bad parts of the game are so bad that it took me a year before I could dredge it up again.  To clarify, let's first look at the things the game does right:
- Top-notch acting from every character, particularly the many well-known faces who populate the game
- Amazingly impressive motion capture of the characters' faces
- Great attention to detail regarding the world of 1940's LA - the look and feel were spot-on
- Outstanding soundtrack
- The devs realizing how horrible the "action" sequences were and providing the opportunity to skip them
All these things were done so well that it would normally be easy to overlook a few faults and love the game.  The graphics weren't exactly photorealistic, but the motion capture was so great that when coupled with the excellent camera work and soundtrack, the game felt more like an interactive movie than many other games I've played.  Unfortunately the game doesn't suffer from a few faults, and those faults are hardly minor:
- First and foremost, the "interrogation" system - it's horrible, it doesn't work, and it's incredibly frustrating.  This is obviously a problem because it's the primary point of the game - to gather evidence, then interrogate suspects and ferret out the guilty.  It's really the main reason why I quit the game the first time around, because half the time it's a complete guessing game.  You basically have a list of pre-generated questions, and based on the suspect's answer you have to determine whether they're telling the truth or lying, and if they're lying you have to decide if you doubt their answer - meaning you know they're lying but can't prove it - or whether they're actually lying - meaning you have evidence to prove their lie.  Seems simple enough, right?  If only.  There are supposed to be visual queues to when they're lying or not - if they stare straight at you confidently and calmly, they're supposed to be telling the truth.  If they fidget, smirk, blink excessively, or refuse to look you in the eye, then they're supposed to be lying.  This works great until the game devs decide to break their own rules, as happened to me several times when a suspect was staring straight ahead and not fidgeting at all, but it turned out they were lying.  It happened the other direction, as well - not very often, but just a few times was enough to constantly make me second-guess myself.  Then there were the times when a suspect was clearly lying and I had to pick out the precise piece of evidence the devs were looking for, which wasn't necessarily the most obvious piece of evidence I had.  A good case in point was the pregnant girlfriend of a car thief I was searching for.  I asked her if she knew what her boyfriend had been up to, and she clearly lied to me.  Now I had a piece of evidence - a diplomatic flag, taken from the stolen car, sticking out of a coffee mug that was sitting 5 feet away from the girlfriend, so I accused her of lying and pointed out the flag.  Nope! Despite evidence of the theft being mere feet away from her and her obvious lying, the devs had decided the correct answer should be "doubt", so that's what I had to choose in order to get it correct.  There are countless examples of this in the game, many being even more egregious than this, so that every interrogation question ended up making me feel like that college kid at the beginning of Ghostbusters sitting across from Bill Murray, who had his hand on the electric shock button, just waiting for the kid to answer wrong.  No interrogation in the game was a fun, sensible or even consistent experience.
Even worse was how pointless the interrogations ended up being,
- The driving - very few games get driving right, and this game isn't one of them.  It wouldn't have been a problem if the game didn't require so much of it, or at least didn't punish you for any damage you inflict while trying to get around.  Kudos, though, to the devs recognizing this and allowing you to skip most driving sequences and just fast travel to your destination.
- The shooting - not the worst part of the game, but the cover system is terribly implemented, and the shooting itself is just boring and uninspired.  Unfortunately, there's a lot of it.
- The story - it started out well enough, if a little too much like LA Confidential (which clearly inspired many of the game's elements and characters), but by the end made almost no sense at all, and ended with you gunning down innocent MPs and burning dozens of fellow LA police officers alive.  Though it was fun to watch the story unfold, it ultimately ended in a totally confusing and unsatisfying way.
Overall, the game simply isn't nearly worth full price, or even a moderate discount.  It's probably good enough at 75% or 80%, if you're a big fan of James Ellroy or movies like LA Confidential, but if not then you'll probably do best to stay away.

1,755 hours doesn't lie, I've practically wasted my life on this game, I love it to death to the point where I've gotten multiple friends and my girlfriend into it. There's a very slight learning curve when you first start, but just remember, mobility is key. Once you get the movement down, everything else will be a cake walk.
Playing solo is fairly fun as is, but I would definitely recomend grabbing a group of friends and having a damn good time on it, that is definitely where the game shines. A close second is the community, sure with the massive player base, you got a few stinkers here and there, but I've met some genuinely amazing and kind hearted players on pub matches, especially when I was first srtating out.
The devs are incredibly dedicated to this game, and it really shows. There's frequent updates inbetween larger content drops, that fix up little things here and there to make sure everyone can enjoy the game. Warframe is trully a labor of love.
Moving on from that, let's get into the core aspects- the graphics are pretty damn nice, even on lower settings. Sure, it's not the best, but I'd give em a 7-8/10. Gameplay, as stated earlier, is really fast paced, mobility is key, though if you want to play a bit slower- don't worry, that's definitely acceptable, just know how to dodge and you'll be set. There's a large stash of content, from the games warframes, to a vast stock of varied and unique weapons, and we definitely can't forget cosmetics, with more added extremely frequently. Each month you can expect to see at least 2 or more new weapons or cosmetics.
The warframes are all unique and each have different playstyles, and with more of those added every so often, I guarentee there will be one that you wil fall in love with. Like a warframes playstyle but don't like how it looks? Don't worry buddy, the steam community is here to help with a vast array of community created skins and helms to give your warframe a special flair, not to mention delux skins added in every so often by the devs.
Now as this is a free to play game, you can spend money on it, that's a given. Personally for me, I really never saw myself spending money on it in the beginning, but as I spent more and more time on the game and kept having more and more fun, I wasn't all too unhappy to toss some money towards it, however, you don't have to. There's a trade economy where I've heard people being able to buy all the frames in the game without having to drop a single real world penny, it's all up to you. Just know that this game isn't pay-to-win. you can buy a good frame, and a good weapon, sure, but not only do you have to level them yourself, but all mods you have to find, collect, and level up as well. You have to put in the work or you're not going anywhere, no matter how good you think a frame is.
Hopefully this helped a little, I think I touched on most of the key points. The game is extremely fun, but it's not for everyone, just give it a try and you might be surprised.

It's a game you must try at least once because there is nothing else like it.  If you like watching detective shows like CSI then you will instantly fall in love with it.  It's a unique experience I've never really had in a game like it before or since.  It's a detective game in every sense of the word.  You get a case, you find clues, interrogate witnesses, deduce the culprit, arrest the culprit, and then go out for donuts.  There's chase scenes and shooting sections for the more action-y crowd but these sections have the option to be skipped which is great for people who aren't really good at those or just hate doing them.  There are detective games with crimes to solve but none have the depth of L. A. Noire as far as quantity, quality, and continuity between cases.
Each mission takes less than an hour to start and solve depending on how determined you are to find every clue so no case will have you stuck forever.  There's also the option to just drive around and solve street crimes for you more free-roaming mission grabbing junkies.  There is no failure for messing up an interrogation because there will always be a way that leads to the right convition so you don't have to look up walk-throughs for exactly what to say and find unless of course you want a perfect score.
The real satisfaction comes the very first time you nail an interrogation on the first try and slap someone behind bars.  Your boss tell you "good work Phelps" and your partner says "nice job rookie" but it feels like they are saying it to you and you feel like you accomplished something on your own.  One case down, 41 to go.

Story - I should start off this review by saying I am totally biased in favor of this game and it is my favorite game in my library at the time of writing.  I love the setting of the 1940's and especially the noir and detective aspects.  This game is the closest you will get to playing L.A. Confidential: The Video Game.  I found the story and even the individual cases to be very engrossing and they feel like actual crimes that could have been committed.  I love a video game with a great story above all else and this one totally delivers on that.  All of the characters feel very real and have more depth than in other Rockstar games.  Cole Phelps, the protagonist, at first seems like a squeaky clean detective, but as the story goes on, that changes and you become very engrossed in him as a character.  When you add a deep and perplexing murder myster to that, I was hooked.  There are even real historical characters (gangsters like Bugsy Siegel) in the game and scientology makes an appearance (in an interesting way) too.
Gameplay - You assume the role of Detective Cole Phelps and investigate crimes, interrogate suspects, tail suspects, and sometimes get in shoot outs and fist fights.  I really like the way L.A. Noire handles investigations.  You have to find clues at the crime scenes by picking up and examining objects.  When you find suspects, you can interview them and respond in three ways (truth, doubt, or lying) depending on what they say.  This is probably the most challenging part of the game because unless you're very good, it can be hard to know whether to doubt or call the suspect a liar.  You can and will arrest the wrong person if you get too many questions wrong or don't find all the evidence.  Fortunately, there are plenty of guides out there to help you if you are worried about getting it wrong.  In total, the game has somewhere between 20-30 cases and it took me around 30 hours to get through them all.  I never got tired of playing L.A. Noire and would have played many more cases if I could.
A lot of the other game play is really similar to Grand Theft Auto.  Driving is arcadey in a good way and shooting is cover based and pretty fun too.  While you spend more time investigating in missions than doing shooting and car chases, the game also offers street crimes which are often foot or car chases with a shoot out or a fist fight thrown in.  These aren't necessary to beat the game but they are fun and were a nice addition.
Presentation (Graphics and Sound) - The graphics in L.A. Noire are both dated and incredibly impressive at the same time.  I'm pretty sure this game uses a version of the Grand Theft Auto 4 engine and while the graphics are solid, they do look like a PS3 game and if you have a good gaming pc, you can certainly find games that look better.  What makes this game great though is the acting and animation of the characters.  L.A. Noire uses a newer animation system that captured the way the voice actors looked and acted when delivering the lines.  This makes it possible to see when someone is lying and it also makes the characters look really distinct and believable.  I hope we'll see more games use this technology in the future.  In addition, the makers of this game put an incredible amount of detail into replicating the Los Angeles of the 1940's.  The city looks and feels real.  There is so much detail and nothing feels recycled when you drive around.
The sound is excellent from the voice acting to the authentic music on your car radio when you drive around.  I love the theme song for this game and think it sets the mood for the game better than almost any other I've seen.
Overall - As I said at the beginning, I truly love this game.  From the story to the realism to the satisfying game play, I think L.A. Noire has it all.  If you don't care about these things, especially a great story then it is very possible you will like this game a lot less than I do or lose interest in it before beating it.  I've certainly heard people say that they felt this way and I think this is just one of those games that some people will really love and others will just find to be pretty good.  However, if my review sounds appealing to you, this game is one of Rockstar's best and that is really saying something.
As far as achievements go, this game is very easy to get a high percentage on by playing through the game once and trying to grab achievements as you go.  You will want to find a good guide for getting five stars on every case and for making sure to use all the weapons in the game or you will have to repeat parts of the game.  The one that kept me from trying to get them all is an achievement that makes you drive every car in the game.  There isn't an easy to find all of these cars and you almost need some luck to get them all.  That one is a bit of a bummer but I would still say that compared to other games, L.A. Noire has more reasonable achievements, especially if you can live with getting 90% or so of them.

This is the movie-game David Cage would never have the talent to pull off. Remarkable characters, impecable acting, engaging plot, a stylish sense of time and place, and good old linear narrative. I have my problems with the gameplay though. The inconsistent nature of interrogations gets pretty confusing, as you never know what Truth/Doubt/Lie actually translate to in each situation. And the slow, realistic handling of everything in the game can get inconvenient at times. Also unskippable dialog.
At it's core what matters here are the characters, though, and both writing and acting are exceptional. The face-technology thing is awesome too.

When you think of F2P games, you always think of games like tiny tower, Roblox, in general lower quality games. Games that sometimes are very simple, or in Roblox's case, kinda broken. When you think of a F2P you don't usually imagine a game running in 1080p, 60FPS, triple A title. Welcome to Warframe.
First, I'd like to address the first question people will obviously have about the game.
"Does it have paywalls?"
No.
In Warframe there's no paywall in any shape or form at all. Anything you see in the game you can do/get completely free. Granted, it might take longer to get there without paying, but it's possible. The only things you can't get without paying are some cosmetics, which are of course cosmetic and not necessary. In Warframe, you don't actually buy weapons or characters (warframes), rather you craft them.
In order to get a new frame or weapon, you need to get the blueprint, and whatever else the blueprint calls for in order to be completed. Sometimes this is the barrel, receiver, and stock of a weapon, or some simple parts you collect on missions. An alternate way to get new frames or weapons, would be to buy them with platinum, or plat for short.
To get plat, you can do one of two things: A, use money from your steam wallet/credit card, or the free and better method, B, trading. In Warframe the best way to get plat is simply to go into trade chat and try to sell your rare weapon or frame parts to someone who will pay in plat. A lot of people are willing to trade, so this is the best way to get plat. This is why there's no paywall in the game, because you can trade to get plat completely free.
So you're probably wondering, "if there's no paywall, what does plat do?". When you craft something, it takes IRL time to be done. For example, it takes 3 days IRL for a frame to finish, but that can be rushed with plat. Or, you could buy a frame outright with plat. In laymens terms, Warframe is a P2P, not pay to play, but pay to progress. If you put in plat, you can buy weapon parts, rush weapons, ect.
But now let's move on to some negatives about the game. My biggest issues with the game is the grinding, and the devs.
In Warframe, the only way to get the parts for weapons/frames, ect, is to just grind it out. This week I was trying to get a Rhino Prime Blueprint. I kid you not, I had been playing literally all week, and all day, since I have nothing else to do. In order to get the blueprint, I need relics which contain the blueprint. Basically, I need to grind for a chance to get the relics, then grind again to open the relics and HOPE they contain what I want. In the end, I never did get the blueprint, I just traded things for plat, then bought the blueprint off of someone who was selling it.
If you don't like grinding, Warframe probably isn't for you. If you don't mind it, however, it may be a game you like. Also note, me taking an entire week to get rhino prime is extremely rare and just very bad luck, and I should've traded for it sooner.
However, grinding isn't the only issue....
The developers, Digital Extremes, can be rather shady. I've heard several cases where they have banned someone for talking bad about the game. Not trolling, but geniunely giving thoughtful, negative feedback. DE tried to take legal action  against a data leaker, who leaked things like what the percentages of getting a certain item is, where it's found, what rotation a defense mission is, ect. We pretty much HAVE to have this data in order to play the game properly, and DE doesn't give it to us for whatever reason.

Hello fellow gamer! :) I wanted to do a review on this game for so long for the simple fact that i have loved it for so long and it has provided me so much fun, and as such i find this as my way to say thank you but also as a way to maybe convince at least some of you out there to give it the chance that it TRULY deserves.
Let me start with the game's economy, because in a lot of free to play games it becomes our primary concern. Is this another pay-to-win game? The answer is "not by any chance". Digital Extremes has done a phenomenal job of actually keeping this game in the most pure form of free to play. You are able to trade the in game stuff you find in missions (e.g. part of a weapon) with other players for Platinum, the currency that is obtainable with real money. So everyone has access in the shop currency without the need to spend real money. Farming items to trade for this currency isn't hard either, it usually comes down to clever negotiation, or just spending a bit more time farming than others are willing to.
Now when it comes to gameplay, we are talking about a fast paced, action packed 3rd person game, where you can kill different types of enemies in MANY, MANY, MANY different ways! :3 Do you want to kill everything with a bow with explosive arrows? A shotgun? A rifle? A ballista? A pistol? A hammer? A katana? Dual wield knives? Oh btw, all these categories and many more not mentioned have many different actual weapons that you can craft, with different stats and types of damage.
I know what you are thinking:
"Ok man, you can kill stuff with different weapons.. big news, it's 2K17, we 've seen it elsewhere..."
Just keep on reading. :)
As the player you get to control warframes, battle suits that each have different abillities covering different types of roles in a mission. Then you select a primary, a secondary and a melee weapon and along with other friends (co-op PvE) you jump into a mission, of which there are several types (e.g. capture, survival, exterminate, defend, rescue etc.)
All of your warframes and weapons are modified through mods, which you find as drops from enemies you kill during missions. These mods give you extra stats or modify completely the way you would use this specific weapon or warframe. There are countless cool builds and countless mods available that you can use and experiment with on all the different weapons, allowing you to make your own gameplay style.
Have i talked about how cool this game looks? O.O Well, you can see gameplay videos for that, you don't need me! ^^ What i can tell you though is that this game is really well optimized, making it a lot easier to play even with older, lower on specs pcs.
It actually has an interesting story to follow which is brought to you with the form of quests that have really well done cinematics but also SUCH good music! You are greatly rewarded by following them with good rewards at the end of those missions and new mechanics or abillities unlocked for you!
For our PvP friends out there, there is the conclave, the place where you battle against other warframes, using PvP specific mods, in stages designed for PvP. There are different modes (1v1, 4v4 etc) but there is also a sports PvP where you actually play a form of team based ninja - handball/basketball called Lunaro.
Game rewards you for playing with alerts that have cool rewards, events that happen quite often and with the Developers being actually close to the community. It is one of the few games where I have seen such a nice and close relationship between the Devs and the player base, with mutual respect towards each other, pushing the game to be the best that it can be.
All this said, there is nothing perfect in this world, as such i have to honestly lay out a couple issues that you might find on your journey. One of those unfortunately, is the start. The game doesn't do a great job of allowing new players to get quickly into the game. At first you might feel kinda lost, not knowing what you should next, what to farm, where to go. That's where the community has stepped up immensely and helps as much as they can in game each other, but still the start is just a rough one. My best advice would be, follow up the linear progression on the planets, try out all the types of missions and try out different weapons, at first just enjoy the ride without worries of where it leads. Then try and join a clan with helpfull people, become an active part of the community and there will be for sure players to help you out on the further steps of your journey, since it's actually one of the friendliest communities i 've had the pleasure to be a part of!
Also, a loooong way after the rough beggining, comes a rough "late game" point. You 've spent lots and lots of hours, you 've farmed and ranked up so many weapons, warframes and mods. You might feel a bit burnt out from the grind / repeated nature of the farm. Eventually you just might want to drop the game for some months, let it bring new challenges and stuff for you to have to have to grind anew.
All i can say for sure is that it's a trip that is SURELY worth it! :) Thank you all very much for your time, i hope to see you all in Warframe! Have fun! ^^
P.S. I am really sorry for any mistakes in advance, english is not my native language so please forgive any small mistake here and there. :)

This is yet another masterpiece of a game delivered by Rockstar. The addition of 'real' facial expressions may seem a bit gimmicky but is essential when questioning suspects. It is up to the game player to determine whether suspects are telling the truth or lying, and this can be done by carefully watching facial expressions. However, if you accuse a suspect of lying you will need to have some kind of proof to back it up. Graphically, the developers has done an amazing job - there does not seem to be a noticable repetition of buildings within the map. Vehicles are rendered beautifully and appear to be fairly faithful to the real things. It is a shame that the game is limited to 30fps on the PC but it is a solid 30fps (played with Fraps running to check). The XBox 360 version has moments where the FPS drops well below 30. Sound is used very well, using a dramatic score when something important is happening in the game. Music is also used during the searching of clues and helps the game player stay within the 'search area'. NPCs have dialogue but it can be quite repetitive. Sound effects are spot on, even down to the sound of aircraft flying high up overhead and chirping birds, etc.
L.A. Noire will appeal to gamers who like to think and solves clues. It may appear to be similar to the GTA series but the missions are in no way similar. If you are an arcade game fan this game will not appeal as it is very difficult to pick it up for a quick blast.

There are only a few medievil-themed FPS games out there, but I would recommend any of the other ones above this one.  This has to be one of the most laughably-bad games I have ever played.  I have a good ping, my net connection might not always be the most STABLE mind you, but when it's up it is SOLID.  Yet it doesn't really matter in this game, as often when I join a server, even those listed as East Coast Official servers, my ping is the only one below a 100, and most are well above that.  I joined a US server once where everyone had a 200 or higher.  I think by now everyone knows WHY this is bad for a competitive online multiplayer game, but in Chivalry it gets even worse...even with zero latency issues between you and your opponent, aim and where the weapon will strike have very little to do with one another.  I've played War of the Roses pretty extensively, so I had an inkling of how the combat in this game would pan out, but NOTHING I aimed ever hit where it was supposed to.   I often just swung randomly out of frustration, and ironically this is where I got most of my kills.   There were also several players I met, all wearing custom skins, who just seemed absolutely unkillable.  They would obliterate you with 1 hit blocking or not, yet any counter-attack on your part was shrugged aside, and didn't even break their swing, and as with WotR 2-handed swords are definitely the be-all, end-all of this game, unless you are a ping exploiter and prefer the fast-swinging hammers that often kill you in a fit of lag and leave you staring at a red screen going 'wha?'.  More than once I was killed by someone I had swung at before they even reacted to me, only to instead be killed by them as they phased through me and attacked my shadow.
All in all, the hit-detection and serious, SERIOUS latency issues, both of the game and the player-base, make this a joke of a game at-best to me.   The best thing I can say about it is that a game hasn't made me laugh this hard in a LONG time.
Which is unfortunate, as I'm pretty sure that is not the intent of Chivalry: Medieval Warfare.

Pros:
- Every Warframe, every weapon, every quest is completely free. Every new non cosmetic content is free.
Cons:
- Repetitive. You are doing the same missions over and over and over again. Same missions, different rewards.
- You as a player are completely overpowered. Most of your time you are playing against lvl 10-40 enemies who you can one shot. And even the hardest content in the game is too easy. It's almost impossible to fail a mission.
- Because you are overpowered most bosses have invulnerability phases (very bad design).
- There is no challenge whatsoever.
- Progression aka Mastery Rank is completely meaningless. It only shows that you leveled up a bunch of items. That's it.
- Endgame? Is non-existent.
- PvP aka Conclave is abysmal. And almost noone is playing it (1% of the playerbase plays PVP).
- Every new content gets 1-2 months of attention and then the developers abandon it.
- Most of the new content are reskinned weapons.
- Every new content has many bugs (up to 3 hotfixes sometimes even more in the first 2 days after new content release).
- No auction house in game so the only way to find stuff that you want to buy or sell from/to other players is through Trade Chat. That means you have to sit there and look at the chat for hours instead of playing the game if you want to buy or sell items. Developers are not interested in adding an auction house.
- Many things are poorly explained.
- You can't kick anyone from your squad (Leechers and AFKers love that).
- Some items/resources are only available from random generated alerts. That means if you really need one specific item or resource you sometimes have to wait for months until there is an alert that has the reward you need. And then you also have to be at home and ready to play this alert cause it only lasts for 1 hour.
- After 4 years the developers still pretend that this game is in open beta.
Would i recommend this game? Only to people who can't pay or don't want to pay for video games.

L.A. Noire has to be one of the most over-rated games I've ever played. First of all, this game is sold as an open-world game. Well, you don’t get to do anything but going to the locations you need to investigate, so if you can call that open world, then I’d rather play non-open-world games. But this isn’t the main problem with the game, in fact, the game has a lot of problems. One of the most annoying problems is that it is a terrible, unoptimized mod locked at 30 fps. You can bypass this with apps like Widescreen Fixer, but still, the game runs terrible, you can be facing a wall and getting 22 fps or looking at the city and getting 60. They are jumping all the time, making it really annoying to play. Fortunately, this game is more of free-roam point-and-click game rather than the action game they try to sell us here.
Another problem is the linear and extremely repetitive gameplay. You will end up waiting for the clue sound, realizing that you won’t find anything in bodies unless they’ve been strangled, had a ring or a watch, or a document in one of the pockets – so don’t look at the corpses’ hands or heads unless any of this conditions apply. The “distractors” are sometimes so random they don’t even make sense. There’s this mission where a card has been crashed near a sign and this dead woman with a blunt force trauma injury to the head. I found a golf club outside the perimeter, but Phelps said “this doesn’t pertain to the case”; well, why do we need CSI if we have Phelp’s magnificent nose! On another crime scene I remember finding a knife, seriously, a knife!, which of course was “circumstantial”.
Then we have the acting. So many popular actors, and such a terrible acting. Phelps sounds like a cyclothymic freak who has just escaped some mental asylum, dressed as a cop and started questioning everyone. Seriously, he’s mood is so borderline he can go from being the good cope to a maniac in no time. I’m sure this doesn’t have to do with the actors, but with poor scripting and the editors joining the audio with the scenes in a not realistic way.
The interrogation in the game usually makes no sense. Either the suspects make some very obvious lying expressions, or they don’t. And some times, they look like they are obviously lying but you get it wrong. This doesn’t affect your progress except in one case, so who cares? Phelps will be accusing everyone of lying anyway.
Finally, the action scenes… they are pathetic, so say the least. The shooting is so stiff and boring you just can wait with your gun out and shoot everyone with one clip. And the driving/chasing scenarios are god-awful. Usually, the car you are pursuing will accelerate breaking physics laws and making turns so robotically you will end up crashing against a corner most of the times, not to mention than driving is so irritating you will be asking your partner to drive to most locations just to avoid it. There’s also one of the last sections in the game where you have to escort a car and some police cars are trying to take it out, and by just bumping into one of these cars they immediately dismantle – it’s hilarious!. It’s a good thing they added the option of skipping this stupid parts of the game after you fail them twice.
One thing I did like of the game was the face animations… that I will be missing in probably all non-AAA games, but that doesn’t compensate for this mediocre, over-rated piece of crap.
Seriously, avoid this game. Or borrow it from a friend, or even use steam family share. But please, save some bucks and don’t buy it even if it is on sale like I did.

This game ticked all the boxes in what I wanted in a survival game. It's much like Terraria in a sense that there is always something to do and you can always build towards it. I purchase this game on my Xbox One and recently got the PC version which is 10x better. Here are my pros and cons.
Pros
>Variety of Bosses
>Good RPG Elements
>Quick start which is rare in survival games
>Custom taylor your world the way you see fit
>A mod for almost all your needs with easy workshop access in game
>Tons of other creatures you can play around with and even tame to ride or provide other uses
>Playing with your friends makes the quick start even quicker and provides a hilarious time
>Many different types of biomes
>Very easy crafting system
>Frequent updates to fix game issues
>Useful in game commands
>Very VERY distracting. I have played several times before I was supposed to do something and ended up burning so much time. It’s not a game you play right before you have to do something.
Cons
>So many collision problems. They aren’t as bad as the pre release days but I still had my fair share of being stuck in a rock underwater. Sometime Dinos will get stuck inside trees, rocks and other objects. Sometime while running with them they get stuck on the object. It’s even worse when big animals like Titanosaurs get stuck on puny rocks or it gets slowed down by trees it should easily effortlessly stomp right over. Collision is probably the biggest con on this list, it’s that bad. Although it does make for some very funny moments.
>Lighting is kinda choppy even when running it on decent specs.
>Game randomly hangs for seemingly no reason.
>All the others are just random nit picks that don’t harm the experience in anyway.

I was bored of games being all about action and not about characters and story. I had over 200 games on steam and I was still bored out of my mind. I figured it was about time I tried L.A. Noire, figuring it's GTA with a proper story in the 1950's but I was pleasantly surprised. The game is all about solving murders, the action is rare but when it happens it feels out of place. I guess Rockstar was afraid to make a game with the bare minimum of action so they made some random shootouts which suck me out of the game. The same with driving around, I would be happier if the game was more like a TellTale game where it's more like an interactive movie because now you speed through the city, crash every now and then because the car you drive is fairly fast, this GTA style of driving doesn't fit in this game.
The facial animation is the best I've ever seen, the dialogues feel genuine and the player and NPCs feel and look like real people. The interrogations are challenging but it gets really hard to see who's lying or not after a while.
All in all, this game is perfect if you want something with a story and real characters instead of "Shooty action fun time 7".

Warframe is like Destiny, in that it's game that can only really be enjoyed in a specific mindset, that mindset being wanting to smash through ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s like the badass space ninja you are.  If you can get into that mindset and deal with all the annoying stuff that comes with it; the long wait to getting all the completely necessary mods, the fact that the game is for the most part an endless grind, the irritating crafting times, and the occasional bugginess of a game that apparently is still in beta despite being released to the public for almost 5 years;, this will be a game you'll love forever.  That may seem like a lot to look past, but the core gameplay is just so amazing and the world is just so interesting that it's totally worth it.

For what it's worth, it's a great game. Let me just say whats wrong with it:
Little to no replayability - what I mean by this is that once you beat the game, it's done, you have to make a new game to play the whole story over again
Not much "open worldness" - it's a big map, when I say big I mean that it will take 15-20 minutes to go from the northern most point to the southern most point, but you have no time to explore it, it's just case after case. (You can go exploring but you may forget things from the case which changes things in game)
Frame rate lock - frames lock at 30fps in game, but when at the loading screen, you can pull off 60-70fps.
Not too great on PC - you can tell that they made it for xbox and playstation and just threw the game together for PC without real attention to it, as if they said "Hurry up Jim, we need this out yesterday! Don't worry about what PC's have to offer, just get it done by the end of the day with only the necessities!"
Now for the good:
Amazing looking game - the technology used for this game is spectacular. No other game looked this good.
Story is very good - it does get boring, but some how, some way it keeps bringing you back like that ex you had in high school
Good character development - this is something I look for in games (and movies), characters make the game, you need to know who they are
The good, to me, outweighs the bad. Get this game and you won't be sorry.
