This is a game for those who are in love with the film noir genre. The game is not spectacular as a game, having many shortcommings, but for for those Sam Spade and Philip Marlowe fan, it's exactly the detective work dose they need. The game has spectacular graphics, not to mention the face animations, which are not really animated as much as they are motion captured. The city map is huge and it realistically copies Los Angeles of the 40's. The drivable cars are also awesome and there are about 95 cars in the game to collect, which is awesome. The bad part is  that the city doesn't present many activities and those which exist are rather repetitive, though always entertaining. (Spoilers from here on) The cases are very entertaing and each one represents the exact amount of noir a person needs for a day, in the sense that each case lasts about 1-1,5 hours which is about a noir movie so that's a good thing. Also the noir fans will recognize many references to noir movies( either in main cases or sidequests). Now the bad parts. The cases are entertaining at first and in the end. I don't know why they left the middle ones, more exatcly the ones in Homicide to be so repetitive, except the last one. And also in these cases, many times i observed that i got the wrong guy and it was clearly obvious, yet i couldn't do anythong about it because the game is very liniar. I knew that a guy or another wasn't guilty but i couldn't  change mi options and the acussed ones didn't cooperate even when the game obliged me to book them, although they were inocent. Then, when Cole is kicked out by his wife, i didn't feel anything because we never see her or his kids before it's convenient for the intrigue.
Another big problem is the fact that the character you play like the last 3 or 4 cases is more likeble and more a noir hero than the character with which you played 3 quarters of the game. Also you invest time and interest in Cole Phelps, the main character, just so you can play the final mission with another character, which is an insult for me as a gamer.
Also the game's core mechanics are more or less rubbish, that is until you get acustomed with them. What i'm refering to are the interogation mechanics. They are flawed in the sense that at first they are unclear and many times i picked the wrong answer because, the game made What the character was about to say unclear. An improvement would have been if in interogations next to the captions of truth, lie, and doubth, the dialog of my character for each choice would be shown(like in mass effect, for example).
My final verdict would be an 8-8.3 for this game, and i clearly recomended for everyone, not only noir fans, because it's badass in spite of its flaws and a type of game that i would like to see and play again in the future, with the condition that it's perfectioned. It manages to create and convey an atmosphere so authenthic that you will either stop and ask yourself if you are watching a noir movie or you will take a brake to fill your glass with scotch and light a new cigarette. The only major question to ask yourself before buying this game must be, " Can i and do i  like playing slow moving games that concentrate on story and revolutionary motion capture and lying detection techniques rather than non-stop action and a multitude of sidequests and activities?"
P.S. If you want to buy the game buy the complete edition, it's the only one that's really worth it because you have about 8 more cases that in the simple edition and  those cases make the experience more complete.

Warframe is a game that seems decent at a casual glance but has numerious serious problems that ensure I could NEVER give this game a positive review score. Playing money to support this games ensures its poor and sloppy design decisions and greedy monetization will be copied by many new games to come.
Very unfun and unfriendly decisions are completely motivated by monetization. There are tons of free to play games out there that don't heavily compromise game design, and focus on selling cosmetics. This game shamelessly lets you buy a massive number of powerful items.
"Orokin Reactor" and "Orokin Catalyst" are two items you can buy for premium currency that DOUBLE the mod slots on your warframes or weapons. Mod slots are the primary method of gaining survivability or damage in the game. The way that mods are poorly balanced in this game has resulted in making many mods can stack damage multiplicatively. The end result is having one of these makes you not 2x stronger but often 4x or 6x more powerful! If you are a free to play player, good luck even getting one of these for your main weapon early on, since they are tied to random timed events and can't easily be farmed. If you pay a decent chunk of real money, you get a free reactor or catalyst for every purchased item. If this isn't pay to win, I don't know what the heck is.
Player progression is tied to rank, which increases by leveling up weapons and frames. Each weapon has a relatively low max level so you need to grind LOTS of weapons to progress. You can directly buy weapons and frames with premium currency crippling progression for those that don't pay.
Inventory space is EXTREMELY LIMITED. You only have space for 2 frames and 6 weapons! Each loadout incudes a 3 weapons, so that is just enough space for 2 sets of weapons with no space for spares. Digital Extremes actually DECREASED inventory space in an update to increase "monetization pressure" on the player. I personally had items DELETED from my inventory when this happened and support refused to acknowledge it. Inventory slots can be expanded with premium currency only, so if you don't pay, you'll have to constantly discard levelled up frames and weapons. Also the level of weapons is tied to the weapon, so if you re-buy the weapon later it is reset to level 0! Expect to have a very unfun time deciding which weapons and frames to lose if you don't pay. Oh, but don't worry, purchased items come with a "free" inventory slot.
I hope you like Wikis, because this game does not explain it's mechanics well. Examples: Orange Crits, Elemental Procs, Crafting material locations.
Disrespects player's time. Login streaks. 24 hour rank up timers that block access to missions and main story progression. First wait 12 hours, login to click something, then 72 hours to build frames. They employ every method you would expect from player behaviour training garbage chinese mmos. If you like to play in short bursts, this game is not for you.
Now what about the actual gameplay? It is actually a kindof basic shooter. If you've played any Unreal Engine 3 shooter game, you have played this more or less. You would think having a variety of frames would really mix up gameplay, but it does not all that much, especially since they all use the same set of weapons. Shooting things is generally fun, and this game relies heavily on that to keep the grindfest from being boring. The abilities are and weapons aren't all that different compared to what you have seen in other games. The only thing that will keep you playing this game is pure addiction --- the need to get loot drops and more gear, not the strength of the gameplay.
I am very sad that this game has been financially sucessful, because there is a strictly better version of this game with better balance that was made for player enjoyment instead of monetization that could have existed. Tolerating this game only pushes pc gaming in the direction of the mobile market.

I play a lot of incremental games, while rendering videos in the background or, when feeling down. They help pass the time in fun ways.
Clicker Heroes is probably the most satisfying incremental game on all of Steam as far as I'm concerned at the time of writing this review. According to Steam I've played the game for 1819 hours right now, which of course is mostly just idling, and less time actually playing (Leveling stuff), but still. What this shows is, that I keep coming back to it no matter what.
A few points about the game:
*
The monster design in this game is unique and memorable. I will always know, where these monsters came from, if I ever see something similar elsewhere. Same can be said about a lot of the characters.
*
The game's UI looks pretty good and does the job. When mentioning actual UI use, however, there is one problem for me personally, which is just a nitpick in the grand scheme of things: Relic leveling could be made more convinient.
*
I have found no visible issues in game balance. The progression was nice even back in 0.26, but now since the Transcendence update I feel like the content is more meaningful than ever. I don't know, how many Clicker Hero players like starting from Level 1 every time, but I personally like this newer style more than the Ancient Iris (Iris was an ancient, who increased your starting level back, when Transcendence didn't exist yet)
*
Graphically the game looks nice and colorful. The artstyle is consistent throughout the entire game as far as I can tell, and pleasing to the eye.
Conclusion:
Clicker Heroes is an incremental game with the most replayability I've seen to date, its content is satisfying to go through and the artstyle together with the monster design is memorable and pleasing to the eye. It's the best incremental game available at the time of writing this little summary in my personal opinion.

I've had really fun times, and really bad times on this game.  Some offers for how to improve it:  Make dino ranching and raising way easier.  Seriously, if you're trying to raise a dino yourself, the little bugger will literally keel over and die if you're not constantly attending to him for HOURS!  That's not really what I'm here to do, and the littlge guy has parents!  Why should he die if I'm not constnatly supervising him?  Don't they care for him at all?  Also, the kibble system is way too overdone.  Kibble is super-good dino food you use to help you tame dinos.  Problem, to make kibble you need specific dino eggs for EVERY species!  Why the hell do I need so many different kinds?  Can't there just be a few different sorts of kibble that I can make with a broad variety of eggs?  Why should I spend so long ranching up every species of dino just so I can get the eggs and make every kibble?  Combined with how incredibly buggy it is, like how your dinos keep escaping by snapping through your fences, or their precious eggs just fall through the planet denying you the entire reason you herded the damn things, why even bother with this entire part of the game?  Oh....because you NEED high level bred dinos to fight the bosses, or even just survive the incredibly toxic community.  Seriously, when you log on to a public server, you'll probably find the entire start zone built over so heavily, that your computer begins to lag.   So what can you do?  You could start in a higher level zone, if you don't mind getting killed over and over by the more dangerous creatures.  Oh, but you'll place a harmless hermit living in a shack in a worthless area where nobody could possible want to harm you?  Nope.  You'll log on to find that even your humble thatch hut hidden among the trees near nothing of value has been burned to the ground by a guy riding a gigasaur in tek armor.
Seriously, for best experience, just get your own server and only play with your friends, if you don't mind the horrendously glitchy, unoptimized, and poorly designed elements of the game.  I now I sound negative, and rightly so.  But it's also true that this game feels good in ways.  It can be a thrill to trek the jungles with your friends, hunting for resources or certain dinos, not knowing where danger may come from at any moment.  I really enjoyed going on expeditions and working with my tribesmen.  But for all there is to enjoy, there's things to frustrate you, and not good challenge based frustration, just crumby badly designed buggy frustrating.
And sadly, at this point in development, I think it's unlikely that these things will get fixed.  More bugs might be fixed, some more optimizations may occur, but the basic design flaws are here to stay.  End of the day, I would not pay full price for this title.  I picked it up when the whole package with Scorched Earth DLC was $20.  That I'm fine with.  But the combined $80 that they ask now...not worth it, and I doubt it will be.  Maybe grab if you see it the game with Scorched Earth DLC for around $30 if you're interested.

Okey, first of all a bit of backstory:
I played the game a long time ago during a free weekend, hopped onto a server and hated it. I could say with 110% sincerity that I would NEVER play Ark ever again...
But, then I got it on a 50% sale and a friend of mine wanted me to get it and I got peer pressured into getting it and oh my god... mixed feelings up the kazoo!
The UI is quite strange, the way that singleplayer content is handled is bizarre to say the least, ancient ideas about one-save systems are common as all balls and yet...
I can now recommend the game.
Why? Because of two things:
1. The oceanfloor is BRIMMING with life!
Usually in games such as ARK and other survivial games, any ocean or water is usually an after thought or used to limit a player. See any game that has an open world of any kind and you see that the Ocean is usually the least developed area. In ARK it's different tho'... you have underwater exploration and I have just started and I can already say that with this much life under the water and how stunning it is on my OLD computer running on at most MEDIUM... its still stunning!
Its not perfect, its no Subnautica but its certainly a pleasant and quite terrifying place to explore as opposed to an underdeveloped art asset telling the player 'please stay away from me, I got nothing to show you'.
2. It invoked a memory that I had 10 years ago from World of Warcraft
During The Burning Crusade, World of Warcraft's second expansion, flying was introduced into the game. It amazed people with its stunning visuals and amazing landscapes that just lay before you!
Ark invoked that EXACT same feeling when I first got to fly on a dinosaur and just... the world opened up in a totally breathtaking way. The same way of having an entire world to explore right beneath your neat and all you needed to do to see it all was to take flight and... look.
There are flaws with the game, no doubt about that and the multiplayer should be avoided unless you are willing to pay for a dedicated server or want to run it on your own with your friends. However... I can thoroughly recommend the game even with all of these flaws and I didn't buy the game at full price but you can betcha' I am gonna get EVERYTHING this game has to offer!
I want to see MORE of ARK: Survival Evolved, I want to see more maps, I want to see folks making their own content, I want to go to lengths above and beyond with this game!
Buy it all full price because I certainly would've if I had known about even HALF of all of these things I do now!

At first Chivalry reminded me of 'No Room Left in Hell' because of it's clunky melee nature. I still look at Mount & Blade as a great example of how to make a smooth-feeling sword-swinging game (plus it had great mounted combat) and am not sure why it's apparently so hard to get right. Example: I was spectating after my traditional early death in a round when I saw the last remaining red managed to take out about four blues one after another in impressive fashion. Then he squared off against the last blue from across a log laid over a waterfall. The two bowed- because of course they did- and then charged at one another and met in the middle of the log. And then the blue one unceremoniously kicked the red hero in the shin, sending him toppling to his death. The whole server had to pause to try and stop laughing.

Note that I'm not saying this is cheating, but they are stupid 'gamey' issues that should be patched out but aren't- they're leading to ridiculous outcomes. Archers are also too overpowered overall in that a reasonably experienced archer is very powerful in 1 on 1 melee (they can stab, block and move so quickly they can be the equal of other classes). It's absolutely stupid that a tiny archer's dagger can block a broadsword, axe, or MAUL. While this sort of thing is done for 'balance' it is in fact unbalancing, as archers have the complete advantage at range (including a 'zoom cam' which just makes me shake my head).

This is not so much a review but a bit about how Clicker Heroes affected me personally.
See I live with debilitating migraines & headaches.
Headaches every day. Migraines 1-2 times per fortnight.
Lots of people think a migraine is simply a bad headache, but that is not the case. I regularly have severe headaches but they are nothing compared to a full blown migraine.
I juggle full-time work in a demanding job, often working extra hours with no overtime pay just to do the best job I can so I can to support my wife and 3 kids. Wouldn't have it any other way, though the headaches could ease up every so often. Would make my life MUCH easier.
And when all is said and done I like to game. I mean I just really love it. I am sure you can understand.
I also collect games (sometimes too many games) and don't really have enough time to finish them all.
But my real issue here is that I don't always get to play some of the games I want to, when I want to.
Skyrim - had it for years, never completed it
FO3/New Vegas/4 - made a good start, but not finished any of them
Deus Ex games, Borderlands (pre-sequel), Divinity:OS, Pillars of Eternity, Metro, Total War: Warhemmer....the list goes on.
Why? The headaches. I just get so tired after working and looking after the family all whilst battling a headache I just don't have any energy to commit to playing the types of games that require a decent time commitment to progress.
Now it is not all bad. Sometimes I do have a period of mild headaches and can get some decent play in, but what about the other times?
That's where Clicker Heroes comes in. Sometimes I want to just sit there, zone out (especially after taking prescription painkillers...those things will mess you up) and mindlessly play a game, or just take it at my own pace. Single player of course as I sometimes need to step away for the kids etc. With Clicker Heroes I can do this anytime I want.
After almost 900 hours of Clicker Heroes I am still enjoying the game and regular updates such as the Outsiders keep it fresh.
And best of all - it is free!
So do I recommend it? Absolutely!
Clicker Heroes has given me the pleasure of being able to continue to game when life presents me with its challenges and tribulations.
Thankyou Playsaurus - keep up the good work! :)
*Edit* and can't wait for Clicker Heroes 2!

ARK has been a very interesting experience for me. I get on, play for a while, and think to myself "Hey, this isn't too bad. Maybe I'll actually have fun this time." Suddenly.....All hell breaks loose. While i'm peacefully putting my own♥♥♥♥♥♥in a box for later use, Suddenly, and without warning, I'm dead. What killed me? Probably a raptor, because they are all♥♥♥♥♥holes, but there are also hundreds of other horrible creatures that wander suddenly into my vicinity, and end my life without question. After dying about 20 more times from ridiculously overpowered creatures, I think to myself, "Oh yeah, this is why I quit this game." This is all on my own private server I play on with my friend. I haven't even tried an online server, but have heard they are even worse.
ARK has so much potential, and has lots of good things to it, and even more bad. While ARK has a lot of content, it is difficult to reach any of it. Story progression requires exploration, and exploration requires weapons, armor, and tools, and weapons, armor, and tools require resources. This, all in all, is not a bad progression. It gives a goal, and a way to achieve it. The underlying problem with ARK's progression however, is the resource gathering (which is a big part of ARK). Some items require a realistic amount of resources, but most require a very unrealistic amount. For example, let's take the Metal Pick and the pistol silencer. To make the Metal Pick, you use 1 Metal Ingot, 1 Wood, and 10 Hide. This Pick has realistic resource units. Then there is the Silencer. To make the Silencer, one must collect 50 metal Ingots, 5 Oil, 20 Chitin, and 10 Hide. The unrealistic amount of required resources is rediculously unrealistic, specifically when compared to the pick, which is actually a bigger item.
Now, I understand why the developers went for this. They needed progression, and they needed the silencer to be more difficult to make than the pick. However, there are much better ways of going about doing this, and I think it is required to make this game both work better, be less tedious, and therefore much more enjoyable.
To Conclude, I don't completely dislike ARK. It has some entertaining elements, and a lot of potential, but it hasn't even nearly reached that potential. The Developers greed asside, the things that need to change the most, are required resource amounts for most items, and the difficulty of creatures around the world.
PS I think the developers of ARK need to take a peek at the crafting system of Witcher 3. While it isn't a survival sandbox game like ARK, it has one of the best crafting systems i've ever encountered, while still taking in account acurate resource units.

Final Verdict- 8/10
L.A. Noire is different. It's not like most video games developed by Rockstar. You don't play the outlaw running wild, free to kill, steal, and cause destruction. You're a cop. A good cop at that, determined to restore order to the violent streets of 1940s Los Angeles.
L.A. Noire's not like most games. Sure, there are car chases, gunfights, and a point-tally to judge the quality of your police justice, but it's a slow-paced, meditative experience. The focus isn't on how good you are at scoring headshots with a pistol but instead your ability to read a suspect's face and determine if he or she is telling the truth, holding something back, or flat out lying
You're a detective, so you're going to scour crime scenes searching for clues. And when you question witnesses, you have to think less like a gamer and more like a sleuth. It's not easy. In fact, it's often a real challenge to judge the trustworthiness of a witness' statement. The line between "doubt" and "lie" is very narrow. Though L.A. Noire's hero, Cole Phelps, is regarded as one of the best case men ever, I still managed to falsely accuse dozens of suspects, doubt witnesses who were actually forthcoming, and use the wrong clues to try and catch killers in lies.
After every question, selected from Phelps' trusty notebook, you get a response from the suspect. Then you must choose to believe, doubt, or accuse them of lying. Get it right and you can open them up and get more clues. Get it wrong, and they offer less. The better you do over the course of a case, the more you'll understand the suspect's motivations. The worse you do, the tougher it is to get at the truth, but there's no possibility of failure in any conversation. L.A. Noire won't abruptly end if you fail to catch a killer's lie or miss an important clue. The bad guy only gets away if it's pre-determined in the story. The only game over screen comes from dying or allowing a fleeing suspect to escape. This makes you less of a real detective and more of a page turner, destined to always reach the next chapter so long as you make a choice -- any choice.
L.A. Noire isn't all about badgering people, though. This is still an open-world game. You're free to deviate from a case, explore faithfully recreated 1947 Los Angeles, and tackle more action-oriented missions. No, you can't run wild like in Grand Theft Auto (you're a cop, accept it), but there are some other things to do. Forty "unassigned cases" come in as calls on the radio. These aren't random; they're single-scene missions where you'll stop a bank robbery, chase down a bat-wielding lunatic, or shadow a crook to his hideout.
A few other distractions can be had -- finding all of the famous L.A. locations and discovering more than a dozen hidden cars -- which earn you points towards leveling up your rank. New ranks mean new clothes, hidden car locations, and intuition points (which can be spent to reveal clues and narrow choices when interrogating a suspect). This is the "game" portion of L.A. Noire, the part built for those who aren't ready to release their old needs as gamers. And maybe Rockstar is struggling to release that same hold. I like going about town, but L.A. Noire would have been stronger with greater focus on the experience and less concern for including traditional game elements.

Based on my personal experience with Chivalry, I'd say that, in spite of its popularity, it's just not very good at what it does. The game's entirety is built around first-person melee combat. Sure, there are objective modes in addition to standard deathmatches, but even those still revolve around combat being necessary in order to achieve the given objective. In my opinion, said melee combat has to be among the least functional and least enjoyable that I've experienced to date. When it's not just plain dull and unsatisfying, it's an infuriating, unresponsive, clunky mess.
Getting down to the nitty-gritty of what made me stop playing after less than three matches, the combat designed around the kind of precision that would normally be associated with a shooter. Strikes need to be carefully aimed and timed to exploit gaps in your opponent's defenses, and successful blocks require following the tip of your opponent's weapon. This could have made for a good game, but Chivalry comes with numerous design flaws that constantly conspire to make things as frustrating as possible. First, the controls are horrendously unresponsive. Pressing a button or rolling the mouse wheel (yes, rolling the mouse wheel is the default input for thrusts and overhead strikes) seems to make the player character begin winding up his mighty strike between an eighth and a quarter of a second afterwards. The slow windup is an obvious attempt at making the weapons feel weighty, but it feels artificial and arbitrary, and creates an obnoxiously long delay between player input and on-screen action, additionally compounded by the aforementioned delayed response.
To illustrate another problem with the unresponsiveness, this issue also comes into play when attempting double strikes, consisting of a standard horizintal swing (normally executed with a press of the left mouse button) followed by another horizontal swing in the opposite direction. One would think that pulling off this maneuver would involve simply pressing the "horizontal slice" button again during the first swing. Instead, Chivalry demands two immediatley consecutive presses of the "horizontal slice" button, often quickly enough for both presses to occur before the first swing is even initiated. In other words, double-striking requires you to tell the game that you want to do so before you even begin telling it to start the first swing, and leaving you unable to do anything else until the full double-strike animation is done. And don't even think about cancels, as they require incredibly acute timing, made all the more impractical by the absence of decent responsiveness.
Whereas the unresponsiveness impedes the player's timing, their aim is impeded by the horrendous camera. Every swing, block, and hit taken causes the camera to drunkenly toss about. If it isn't inducing nausea or headaches, it's creating a scenario in which strikes are monitor-smashingly difficult to place. Not helping is the lag inherent in the game's multiplayer nature, as even a slight misrepresentation of any given player's positon completely throws off the precision that a successful hit or block demands.
Moving on, consider how, in many first-person games, the weapon model seems to exist on a separate plane of reality from the environment, as it remains held in front of the player character even as they attempt to french kiss a wall. Chivalry has this same fault, but it wouldn't be such a problem if it didn't make it nearly impossible to judge exactly how far away from oneself a weapon's strike actually reaches in comparison to weapons with different values for their reach statistic.
In the miraculous event of a weapon actually connecting with an opponent and dealing damage, the game does a remarkably poor job of communicating the impact to the player. In other words, it's very hard to tell if you're actually hitting your opponent or not, leaving the desire for a cathartically damaging hit usually unsatiated. Instead, it typically lacks any sense of something being sliced/bashed/stabbed. The result is a combat experience that's cruelly boring when it's not causing aneurisms from the barely playable controls.
Let it also be mentioned that the player characters all move agonizingly slowly. Even the man-at-arms, the fastest class, can barely sprint faster than a sumo wrestler in cement shoes. It makes the game feel generally sluggish, even when the controls aren't the culprit. It also aggravates the frustration of battling the movement speed all the way from a spawn point to where the action is, only to be killed instantly by someone outside your field of vision.
The tutorial is the rotten cherry on top of this sewage sundae. It obsessively holds the player's hand throughout, forcing you to complete each and every maneuver several times before moving onto the next. Each lesson is separated by unskippable, torturously cheesy, Renaissance-fair voice acting as it over-explains every single facet of the game. The game includes no information on these facets outside of the tutorial, so forgetting something means either exiting the game and doing research, or slogging through the tutorial again.
In summary, Chivalry is a game that consists of dreadful medieval combat and nothing else. I'm utterly mysitfied at how people can bash Skyrim for its lackluster combat, yet turn around and praise this dreck. I do not recommend Chivalry to anyone. Two and a half matches was all it took for me to decide that I couldn't take any more. How this game is even remotely popular is beyond my understanding. If you are interested in trying this for yourself, find someone who owns it and play it on their system. Don't waste your money on this putrid offal.

**EDIT: after quizzing friends that have played this for a long time, and personal experience, changing things a lil bit.  Mainly taking out the gripe about in-game lore as a seperate strike and lumping it into the category of lack of info.
Keep in mind that this is all my own personal opinion...  I see this game as a "love/hate" relationship.
This can be a beautiful game that runs well.  Lots of action.  But for me, this game promises huge potential and delivers very little on it.  The game relies FAR too much on grind and farming for my tastes.  Most items must be crafted using a system that requires TONS of materials and not in a realistic fashion either.  I purchased a blueprint for some kunai that were usable by my "mastery" level, and it cost me most of my credits, but I was fine.  "Space ninja uses Kunai" sounds cool.  But when I go to build it, it costs alot of materials I don't have.  4k more salvage than I had at the time plus 2 sets of materials that weren't available on any of the planets available to me.  And even after that, it'll take 24 hours to craft.
Several hours later, I'm still in the same spot: no dent on salvage amount and still haven't reached a planet with the required materials... Oh, but it's available to me IF I SPEND REAL LIFE CASH.
Pro's ( + ) and Con's ( - ) (combined, cause... you'll see.  Prepare for QQ...):
+ + + + + Still actively supported by the devs with new content all the time.
- - - - - - - - - - - Tons of info, some of it being vitally important info needed to play the game, is never given to you or is given in a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥manner.  Example: Mission info is given on the map as a short tool tip showing location name, mission type and Expected enemy level ( not suggested player level.  Will it be sparse population or will you be swarmed the entire mission?  Enter to find out. ).  Not terrible until you encounter the road block system put into place where you have to complete multiple objectives in this planet or across multiple planets just to unlock the FIGHT that unlocks the next planet.  Want lore?  Normally, games make you collect it.  Warframe does this as well but neglects to tell you that you need to buy a pack of scanners from the cash shop in order to collect the nodes needed to get the lore... Seriously devs, hire someone that knows how to make a "How-to ---".  This is my BIGGEST gripe against the game.
+ - The aforementioned scanners can be bought rather cheaply in a pack of 25 for a measly 500 credits (in-game currency). Why make it so they can only be bought in a pack of 25?  Why not just a single purchase of a reusable blueprint?  Or maybe just give it to us automatically.  Considering how much scanning is in the game, for the sake of lore and a few crafting materials we can otherwise pick up, you've needlessly complicated this.
+ + Supports control pads...
- - - - ...but acts like it doesn't WANT to.  The only game of its kind that I have played that supports control pads but refuses to tell you how to play using the control pad's input.  You have to drastically slow down and go from game to options menu to decifer what does what in translation between keyboard and controller.  This should not be an issue for a game this old, especially when it's on TWO consoles AND PC.
- - - - - - Returning to the game?  I can't speak for the current tutorial of the game cause the only tutorials available to me now are moving screenshots that are not showing what the tutorial is about while text is on screen showing me keyboard and mouse inputs when the game knows I'm using a controller.  That or, in the case of "Mods", a small box on teh side of the screen that displays text paragraphs at random for a few seconds at a time.
+ + Character/ship/weapon Customization
- Almost all of it, even color palettes, are locked behind a pay wall.
+ Supposedly, you can earn cash shop muns in game
- I have yet to see this.
+ Lots of players
+ Fast paced action
- So fast that if you are new and team up in a PuG, prepare to be left in the dust while the bigger boys thrash everything in sight.  People don't like to slow down for *anything.*  Some players will even yell at you in chat to go faster.
- - - Typical F2P model: Sure, you can play the game, but it'll be a struggling and grueling grind to get anything good (albeit, WORSE in this game, cause you have to grind to unlock the grind to do things).  Conversly, look at how much FUN you can have if you just spend money cause you can get so much good stuff NOW!
+ Can swap Warframes on the fly while aboard your ship which effectively changes your class...
- - - - - ...Gender locked classes.  ( I HATE this!!)  Apparently you are a genderless and amorphous blob within your Warframe cause some of the frames are very clearly female while others are clearly male.  And the game clearly treats you as a person/entity wearing a suit!
- Female Tenno have potato butts, apparently  :(  (A closer look shows it's just very poor modeling / IK rigging.  Don't believe me?  Pick a warframe that shows the hips well and then do the "Meditation" emote.  Look closely at the crumpled scrunching pinch of your hip joints...)
- - - - Effort it takes to craft an item to free you from the parasitic mind control of an undead cyborg enemy: 30 seconds crafting time and uses very few materials, all of which are common and easy to obtain.   Effort it takes to craft a decent set of throwing daggers: over 5k salvage, some common items, and nearly 1000 rare items only found on the opposite side of the solar system (or in your convenient cash shop), requiring you to fight your way back and forth across the planets and then 24 hours of actual crafting time.
+ If it makes you feel better, the aforementioned throwing knives have a pretty ribbon on them.  And are better than a semi-automatic pistol.
- - - Can't trust the stats given.  Stats are very mutable in this game due to the "mod" items you can equip to practically everything.  But also, item performance itself weighs heavily.  Example: the aforementioned daggers.  Accuracy rating: 100.  The pistol I'm replacing with them: 18.2.
Using them while carrying something else forces you to wield them one handed.  There's a bit of a throw curve to them, but it can be compensated for and you can still reliably hit targets.  Not carrying anything else makes you to dual wield them.  Every throw alternates hands.  But there is now an offset to the offhand.  The 2nd dagger will land well below your targeting reticle.  And the offset/offhand throw stays for a good while if you just throw one with the main hand and decide to wait for a minute.  The 2nd throw will always be that offset.  This is not 100 accuracy.
So many people hail this game as something new and innovative, but I'm honestly seeing something done before in many other mmos... but with space ninjas thrown in.  It's just interesting eye candy to me without proper knowledge on how to play or knowledge of what to do.
I shouldn't be forced to go to youtube, a website or beg people to explain things to me.  Thing that really upsets me here is that another game that I enjoyed more, Firefall, did almost everything this game does and failed.
The game design as a whole just seems very clunky and broken to me, despite the game having alot of elegance and polish in some areas and showing lots of promise.

There is a workaround but it's not a problem-free fix (I played the game without the fix, but it's still very much playable). The gameplay can become repetitive at some points, and how game deals with some case scores that I don't agree with. Despite these problems, I still recommend this game because of story, characters, and overall experience.

L.A. Noire is a game focuses more on story-telling and characters. There are also actions involving cop chases and gun fights (both main and side missions). Crime solving is the backbone of the game, but for me the over-arching story piques my interest more than the technical side of individual case solving, as looking for clues and picking up objects one by can become somewhat repetitive. The strong point of the game is its interrogation process. The game used advanced capture technique at the time to capture minute and accurate facial expressions.

If you want to know a thought-provoking story not only ties to the era but even true today, realistic characters with ideal and frailty, and if you like driving classic cars roaming the streets in a vibrant, virual parts of historical L.A., then you should give L.A. Noire a try.
Pros:
+ Story
+ Character acting and facial animation
+ Nice replicate of sight and sound of post-war L.A.
Cons:
- Frame rate locks at 30 FPS
- Gameplay can become repetitive at one point or another
- Questionable game design decision — what is politically correct in the era should be separated from what player expects as correct based on evidence when dealing with out of game scores.
Personal score: 3.8/5

The easiest description of L.A. Noire would be a cross between L.A. Confidential: The Videogame and Grand Theft Auto 1940's for Snobs. This doesn't do it justice, though, nor does it communicate the appreciation I have for the game. First and foremost, it's a great litmus test for movie and television fans to convince themselves whether or not games can reach the point of art and/or work as alternative ways to tell a good story, even allowing you the audience to impact its outcome somewhat. The case-chapter structure here is great for both hardcore and casual gamers—actions scenes, for instance, can be skipped if that's really not your thing. Although the plot here is pretty linear—and there is only one "right" way to follow it if you keep score—it's still fun to replay levels and see how different decisions you take are handled to bring you to the same conclusion. On the other hand, if you're more of an action buff or just like eye candy, you'll enjoy driving around the beautifully rendered streets of 1940's Los Angeles and taking on the side missions. Also there is plenty to love for fans of Mad Men, with mo-capped cameo appearances by series regulars like Michael Gladis, Rich Sommer, Myra Turley, Andy Umberger, Kate Norby, Patrick Fischler, Vincent Kartheiser and of course, game star Aaron Stanton, a.k.a. Ken Cosgrove, my favorite Mary Sue character ever. Other film and T.V. buffs will also get a kick from appearances by character actors like Greg Grunberg, John Noble, Ned Vaughn, Brian Krause, Keith Szarabajka and Hal Landon Jr., among others. It may have been better, for instance, with more of a Half-Life "show, don't tell" approach, sure, but regardless L.A. Noire is an undeniably good genre game. You owe yourself a look-see.

I will start with giving this game a thumbs up, simply because If I didn't I'd be a hypocrite.
Having said that, Ark is an experience that is extremely hard to describe.
When it comes to graphical fidelity, sound and immersion in general It is undoubtedly the best experience I've had so far in a survival game. And survival is something Ark, indeed does extremely well.
But when we take a step further and see the systems that sum this game together, It can be a total nightmare to behold. Past the honeymoon phase where you experience things for the first time and stand in awe at the sheer complexity that exists within the game, patterns emerge; The grind is real and so are the plethora of bugs. But most importantly and the major offender that would justify anyone giving the game a thumbs down: The community. Ark has one of the worst online communities I've experienced in my life and as much as I'd like to deny it, it is the systems within the game that allow, or to an extend promote extremely toxic and unhealthy behaviors. New players will find little to no sympathy when they join an official server to find themselves almost instantly griefed to the point of quitting. Make no mistake; Another player can capture you and keep you alive just to torture you and there's nothing to do unless you start a new character. That is, If you can even survive the lag/unrestorable character losses and exploits that are simply of no end on official servers.
So, in order to enjoy the game you may play single player mode, join an unofficial server, or rent one yourself and either play alone, or have a group of friends to play with. And if you're the Admin, prepare yourself to go through  entire of pages of different settings, so that you tailor the server to your demands (If you even know what they are). If you aren't the admin, then lay at the mercy of whoever is moderating the server and what cheats they could use...
All my good experiences are from playing solo on an unofficial server that I've rented. Problem is, that after countless restarts on multiple maps and nearly 400 hours I have absolutely nothing to show for it.
But I do have those rare moments of thrill and excitement and this is why I'm giving Ark a thumbs up, which yes, I know has to be the most inconclusive thumbs up I've ever given...

Having played 16 hours now, I will review. Chivalry is a pretty cool game but it has its ups and downs. Having unlocked nearly all of the weapons in 16 hrs of game play I am pretty much bored and done with it for now. So here are some pros/cons/and suggestions for future games of this type.
Pros:
- The concept is amazing.
-The team objective  modes are the best part of this game and the only reason I keep playing.  It is super fun and brilliant. Could be expanded upon more though.
- The way the weapon system works and unlocking of weapons is smart and a good way to keep people playing and motivated to get better at the game.
-War cry button = awesome
-team damage counter and ability to kick out people that keep team killing is a good feature
- good diversity of class/weapon types
Cons:
-No female characters.
-Limited costume options.
-maps and characters limited to medieval Europe.
- armor difference between vanguard and the knight isn't significantly noticeable.
- Some melee weapon ranges are off. Have received damage from weapons that havent actual come in contact with my character.
-lastly, and simply from the perspective of someone who makes historical recreations of medieval plate armor in steel... some of the costumes are not really very historically accurate. But you can see where some, even small degree, of effort was applied here and that is commendable.
Suggestions:
- Add more than just medieval Europe. This creates more diversity of character/weapon types and maps. Middle eastern fighters, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, etc. All of these areas where in some degree of contact at the time and would add a great deal of diversity to game play.
- My last suggestion would be to strive for more historical accuracy, especially in a game that seems to be trying to avoid being a fantasy game. The more realistic you can make such a thing the more truly amazing it will be. The only counter suggestion to this is adding female characters. There are a large number of female gamers and they need to be included. I have tried to get a few of my female gamer friends to play with me and they have refused because there is not character to represent them in the game.
All and all, awesome work! Make another one :)

This is a hidden gem of a game. Not only are the facial expressions amazing, but the storyline, and sequences as you advance the game, very well put together. As always, there are things that can be improved, but this did not diminish my enjoyment and suspense. You play a rookie cop that moves along the ranks and various divisions of the police force, as you begin to solve (perfectly and sometimes not so perfectly) crimes of varying degrees. The music adds suspense, tension and lends atmosphere to dramatic scenes. There is a certain realistic feel to the characters and animation, as well as the layout of the game. The controls for the most part are simple and easy to learn. The use of an accessible notebook adds flavour and is really helpful in remembering clues. The puzzles range from easy to pay-close-attention, but generally don't distract from the flow of the story. Depending on your system, the graphics are decent and flow well. My wow-factor is in the facial contorsions and mannerisms, which capture the moods of characters quite well. It is unfortunate that a sequel or a continuation of the genre won't be possible, given that the studio that started this is, as far as I know, now gone, but I recommend this game to those who enjoy noir detective films and books. It still has the feeling of a game, not a novel, but in this one you get to take part and your actions will have consequences. I will certainly recommend it if it is on sale and it should make a nice gift if your intended victim enjoys games with detective storylines.

I've put a lot of hours into ARK, over a year on the public servers and several months on private servers.
CONS:
Game is buggy, I can still drown in rocks.
Specifically on the public servers - Good luck starting the game. Pve means the land is claimed and good luck finding a spot to build, and pvp means that dinosaurs aren't the problem, the arrow in your head is. Par for the course on survival games I know, but I can't imagine the frustration of starting fresh now.
Anything and everything takes a LONG time. Taming a bronto can take up to almost nine hours, breeding and birthing one can take up to four real life days.
Game is buggy, guys, I've drowned in metal, falling through a mountain, into water and then drowned in a second set of rocks.
If you're on a public server, sufficient progress requires you get on everyday just for upkeep. 30 minutes a day, it became a chore. Feed the herbivores, poop the dinos, fertilize the plants, reload turrets, hunt, feed the carnivores, repair the walls. Toss out anything with a disease that came up overnight. Collect oil, make gasoline, refill generators. Deal with drama and land disputes on a pve server, deal with your base suddenly not being there on the pvp server.
Running a private server and quickening all of the sliders makes this game playable now for me.
Game is buggy, buggy as the day it went into early release, there's just more dinosaurs to glitch now
There's no way to run a server and play without third party support.
The game at 20$ was steep. The game at 60$ is ridiculous when I can still die running into a rock and drowning in the ground.
I've lost several dinos to suddenly and violently being underground.
PROS:
Otters man, how can you not love their smiles?
This game teaches you loss. It's become a zen experience taming a bird for hours of my day only to lose it the second it's awake to ants. You learn to understand loss. All dinosaurs are impermanent. All things are impermanent. We are impermanent. The only thing that persists is your knowledge of the past and the rock that drowned you.
New dinosaurs come out practically every other day. Not literally, but the game updates a lot. If only some fixes could be made.
In conclusion, the uphill battle with the game isn't worth it. You will lose and a lot of times the thing that kills you is going to be a glitch. It was ok at $20 in early release. It's trash at $60.

To start it off, i'm a big fan of dc cinematic universe, and the year 2016, hadn't been a good year for me and the other fans. Even though, i'll state myself optimistic, since actually, all my hopes and expectation fall into this movie instead.
OK, Let's start with the strong aspects of the movie; performances and characters. well, i actually think this is what the director want to top off and show to the audience, thus forgetting the plot, which we will get into later. but the characters and the performances are well-performed- Margot Robbie as Harley Quinn really tops off my expectation. i'm a fan of harley quinn character, and she actually brought me the harley quinn i'm expected for- sexy, beautiful, it girl of joker's. while watching the movie, and whenever i'm feeling bored, harley quinn is there to make the scene fresh. and i think all audience, including audiences who didn't know her will love her and feel sympathetic to her. Will smith as deadshot actually didn't deserve much of my appreciation. i mean even though he's one of the great and strong aspect in the movie, i just thought i don't see will smith even trying to act, which weirdly works. watching Will smith here is just watching him using a kickass suit. Jared Leto as The Joker, is actually isn't the worst part of the movie (unlike what people might have said) i think that Jared Leto pull of a great effort into his character, and some scene of him showing up gave me goosebumps and own joys. but, maybe how little the scene for him is, or his character is pretty under-developed that just doesn't fit the puzzle in the movie. Viola Davis as Amanda Waller also brought up my her characther pretty well, as she played the cold-hearted leader Amanda Waller. other performances are great, like Joel Kinnaman, Jai Courtney, Jay Hernandez, Karen Fukuhara, and Cara Delevigne.
The chemistry between the characters are great, as well as the development between their relationship. in my opinion, one of the strongest chemistry is Harley Quinn and Deadshot. Their chemistry is electric, funny, and watching them teasing, and slowly started to care about each other, is entertaining, and make me ship them together. even, i have a relationship that had a weak chemistry, that is Rick Flagg and June Moore's relationship which is bland, forced, and unnecessary.
Now, parts that i think is the weak part of the movie, I think the plot is the main reason. The plot is lazy-written and under-developed,and at some point is pretty ridiculous. i don't want to get into it too much, since it will spoil some things, and i need you to watch the movie without spoilers, yet. even, i could tell you that the CGI is pretty cringy and sometimes, so does the visual effect between the scenes. the ending is actually rushed, predictable, and i think they could do better after building up the story of the fight scene.
At the end, everything has its bad and has its good, what i really suggest for you to do is just lower your expectation, yet don't miss it either. it may not lift the hype as in the greatness in the trailer, but i think it's still a great fun must see summer movie , and you should enjoy it without all the overly negative critics.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a very linear game where it takes place in the medieval era in which you fight with swords, cannons, and etc. It includes no campaign but does include a tutorial for new players to learn at the game mechanics. However the game mechanics can be easily manipulated by certain high skilled players. Take a look at the pro's and cons.
Pros
+Pro: The graphics aren't that bad for the Unreal Engine
+Pro: It a Includes level editor which means you can download workshop maps
+Pro: Good optimization
+Pro: It has Trading Cards!
Neutral
= The game provides a 0 - 15 skill level
= The voice acting is meh..
Con's
- As soon as you play the game you will notice the extremely bugged out game mechanics when you hit a weird spot when swinging your sword.
- There are high skilled players who completley dominate you and you're forced to learn the extremely unrealistic game mechanics
- Sometimes there are really big physic glitches that are really stupid and bad
- The characters cant keep up with the extremely bad game mechanics so when you loose a limb really fast your character will end up looking like a distorted alien
- And I have read other reviews and apparently there are bugs and glitches since the start of the game and were never fixed!
- Developers have basically abandoned this game because all they do is add new weapon skins and cosmetics and no actual game fixes
Overall: 4/10

This game is a good time waster as it basically never ends. For a free game you get a lot of content. It's an idle game in which you kill monsters for gold. That gold is used to level up heroes, unlock hero skills and player skills. The game is actually quite complex so I won't get into it here, but you can check out the Clicker Heroes subreddit for more info.
The monetization strategy revolves around using actual money to circumvent the time required to grind certain resources to unlock things. Those resources can be gained without paying but can take a long time, so it's not mandatory.
In short - click or don't. Get money and level up heroes to do stupid damage.
There aren't many cons to this game seeing as it's free, but one thing that annoyed me was how the new "auto clicker" is described in-game. I'll copy it verbatim - "Auto clickers can be used to automatically level
, activate skills and click monsters for you."
The above emphasis is mine since that's the reason why I spent $9.99 on the rubies required to unlock it. I don't use the skills much or click since I've opted for a maximum idle-damage build. What I was really interested in was the fact that it said heroes. Plural. I figured an autoclicker will automatically apply levels to EVERY hero whenever it can, but that is not the case. Instead, for $9.99 I got something that clicked one single hero level up button 10 times a second.
There are 44 heroes. I'd need to purchase 44 auto clickers in order to get the functionality I believed I was getting. Also, the autoclickers get more expensive after each purchase. The first was 100 rubies. Now it's 150. That will probably keep going up.
I don't believe that the description is intentionally misleading but I think it is vague enough to warrant a change. Instead it should say that the autoclicker only levels ONE hero at a time instead of saying heroes plural.
Conclusion - I know I just wrote twice as much complaining about the one and only time I spent real money on this game, but I will give it a pass for now since $9.99 is still a steal for 100 hours of gameplay. Just be warned that the autoclicker doesn't do what it says on the tin.

However, this game isn't necessarily bad, it just takes a very high capacity for stress to continue playing for prolonged periods. The combat is excellently done, this not being a "spam LMB to win" game.

L.A Noire is a highly underrated game, emerging from an unusual meeting between open world action game, point-and-click adventure and a 1940' or 50' film Noire.
The game places us in the role of Cole Phelps, veteran of the sixth marines, former war-hero from Okinawa who, after coming back to L.A. in 1947, takes up a job in LAPD. Through the course of the game we assist Cole in solving various cases grouped into four desks - traffic, homicide, vice and arson.
Each case is diferent, and may require different aproach, but the general tools we use over the course of the game remains the same - we need to gater as much relewant evidence as we can, and later, eventualy use them to prove our point during many witnes questioning parts of the game. To nawigate through this piling mountain of names, locations and objects we get a cool interface feature resembling LAPD detective notebook, that alows us to track case progress anytime we need to.
The strongest point of the game is definitely it's plot, settled in an alomost perfectly recreated 40's L.A. Cole's tale, as he rapidly advances through LAPD desk offices and departments perfectly catches specyfic atmosphere of Noire movies from mentioned times, with all it's moral ambiguity and dillemas. Above that every single case tells a story of it's own, often re-telling some well known crime-stories like 'Black Daliah' case, or creating a longer plotline connecting some seemingly unrelated cases.
I'd strongly recomment L.A. Noire to any fan of Noire movies, and good thriller or crime stories. The game itself is quite specyfic and to be frank, due to the nature of it, the replayability of this title is very low (what point in solving a case, if You already know the culprit ?), but nevertheless it's still worth playing !
- Amazing storyline based on 40's and 50' film Noires.
- Game with one of the most convincing characters in history of VG.
- Engine simulating real facial expresions and body language.
- Story set in almost perfectly recrated L.A. from around mid 40's.
- more than 90 historicaly correct car models to drive !
- Extremely low replayability (due to the nature of the game)
- Huge amount of cinematic breaks and introductions slowing the pace of action.
- Controls may feel somewhat curde

I must say this is the most unique and engrossing games I have played in quite some time. The game forces you to slow down and look for clues in order to solve the array of mysteries that you undertake. Having a keen eye and a good memory is imperative to cracking the case. The interrogations are truly the most gripping part of the game; nothing is more exciting than getting a confession after spending hours unearthing clues, following leads, interviewing witnesses and chasing suspects.
Team Bondi has changed the face of video games with L.A. Noire. The facial expressions in this game are unrivaled by anything currently out there, and they're not just used during cut-scenes, it's in effect at all time during the game; a level of dedication most becoming of a Rockstar Game. They're so good in fact that you're left wanting the rest of the world to be on par. I'm not saying that it looks bad but it is missing minor polish seen in other Rockstar games (I understand it's a Bondi game...) like limited damage on the cars, bullet holes are missing when a car or person is shot... and that's it. That's all the nitpicking I can pull off.
Gunplay isn't as sharp as Grand Theft Auto and takes a little getting used to but it feels right for this type of game and works just fine. The focus isn't wholesale gunfights, rather poignant, key engagements that mean something; you are an officer of the law after all.
Give this game a shot if you like cop dramas, film noires, GTA, tacos, fresh and unique gaming experiences.

I have slightly mixed feelings about Warframe, but the good parts of the game like the combat, visuals, and worldbuilding outweighs the neccesary "evil" that is the buisiness model of a free to play game. That being said, just about everything in the game aside from cosmetics can be obtained without buying the in game Platinum. Gameplay wise, this is the closest thing to Destiny you will find on Steam (and when Destiny 2 comes out in September you'll have to play it on the Blizzard app). You're meant to play the same environments multiple times with different objectives, and each environment is designed as modular tilesets so despite the repetitive design it still feels fresh. You are a Tenno, a soldier that utilizes different Warframes to combat warring factions. These Warframes are all different, each possesing different looks and abilities that fit different play styles and needs. They are very satisfying to play and are complimented well with the massive armory you kill hordes of enemies with. As a Tenno, your agility lets you traverse the game levels with great speed and elegance. Not only is it fun to use, but the controls are easy to make you feel like a parkour god. The varying Warframes, interesting guns, and enhanced mobility makes controlling your character extremely fun. It's always a bonus too when the game is optimized good enough to enjoy at 60fps. I can manage max settings on my slightly outdated machine!
So the business models for free to play games usually lock people who don't pay out of most of the fun, but Warframe's "Platinum" is closer to letting you buy in to things earlier. The only parts the game locks off with Platinum is cosmetics for Warframes like skins, cape-like Syandanas, and colors to customize item appearances. The cost for these things is moderate, color palletes for example are 75 Plat, which is around eight dollars. Warframe limits the amount of important items you can have like slots for your suits and weapons. You can expand these for Plat as well, and they are vastly cheaper than cosmetics. You can buy two slots for weapons for a meager 12 Plat. The lowest priced bundle will give you plenty of Platinum to increase the amount of things you can use. Despite all that you don't always have to shell out for the goods. Platinum is tradeable among players. There's a possibility to get a very rare blueprint or item to offer to players for their Plat. You can also get some in the daily login reward or giveaways by the devs.
My original account was created during the beta, and have seen nothing but amazing changes to this game.

A lot of haters out there who will complain about this game and frankly I just don't get it.  It's free.  You don't HAVE to pay for any aspect of it to enjoy it.  It's a fun shooter that has very unique elements that people either seem to fall in love with or hate.  Best part about it though is that it is completely 100% free to play so you can try it before you decide if you want to spend any money on it.  I thought it was fairly stupid at first, but I fell in love with it as time went on and have enjoyed the time I have spent playing the game.  There are always new updates and added content, all free and it looks like the game is even further evolving.
Give the game about 3-5 hours and you will know if you are a fan or not.  If you are on the fence still by that time, give it another 3 -5 hours and I am confident you will be hooked.  Upgrading weapons, improving your abilities and finding the right combo of Mods to optimize kicking the crap out of your enemies  seems like a daunting experience at first, but there are helpful tutorials all over the place and it is actually all very simple.
The people who are overly complaining about the game are either:
A) Trolls, people who have nothing better to do than hate on things that they don't fully understand. Remember, if you're having fun, they are not.
B)  Pathetic souls who are too wrapped up in the game and are unhappy with changes made because they think they know the "Best" way the game can be played. It's a game, not a job. If you stop enjoying it, stop playing. No one is holding you hostage or forcing you to invest your time in it.
C) Communists. People who don't understand that, while the game is free-to-play, the developers made the game to make money. It wasn't developed out of some altruistic desire to make gamers happy.  It was developed to offer fun content that would entice players to pay money for things in game.
Is the game less fun if you don't spend money? No, not at all. Does spending money on the game make it more fun? Depends, the small amount of money I have spent on the game I personally feel has enhanced my experience while playing and thus made it more enjoyable. Was it necessary? NOT AT ALL.  There has been no point where I have felt that I was required to pay anything in the game. You have the choice to do so if you'd like and frankly I expect that if you enjoy the game enough, you will wind up spending a little cash on it too. I could understand if people made these complaints about a game which you had to purchase first, but again, this is free-to-play so you are not out any money except for the electricity it costs to run your PC.

A game where you are the main detective. Follow the main character as he evolves through the ranks, and slowly gets deeper into a great mystery plaguing L.A.
What is great about this game:
Atmosphere, art, sound, music, details, story. Music is fantastic. It looks great. Great voice acting, and acting. Motion face capture is a great concept, and adds another depth to game play. Many talented actors in this production. High production value.
What is not so great about this game:
It is a bad port, and frame rate is slow on even a great PC. Game is slow, sometimes tedious and repetitive. Many sections/ideas feel like an afterthought and not even necessary. Game feels too long. (It should have been a shorter movie instead without all the game stuff) Game plays better with a controller, but is ok with a keyboard and mouse. The actual gameplay is not that great. The ending was just a lack luster, and a disappointment after all this work to get there.
Well, this is without a doubt a great game, and I am happy it was made.  My review will seem somewhat negative, because I think those points are important to bring up. But this is still a very great game that you should try.
I think I can understand what the developers were after - Let's create a noire movie where you are the investigator. Let's make the game world really immersive like you are back in the 40-50s, let's make the inhabitants look and feel real. Let's make a game where you can read peoples' reaction just like you would in real life, in order to crack the case.
Well, the motion capture is a great idea. I hope this develops and that more games can use it to make characters in games less robot like. I loved this idea in this game. The actors' face expression are captured really well, and it makes the game much more alive when interacting with other people. It is fun to deduct if people are lying or not.
But I felt there were too many cases in the end, and I just wanted to get on with the story.
I know it sounds weird that I think the game was too long; that should be a good thing, right? But it takes so long to get on with the story. I think you can finish this game much faster than I did. I replayed many episodes, but then realized that is not really necessary, as the progression is the same no matter how good or bad you do.
Driving around in the city, even though beautiful, and apparantely historically acurate, is not necessary at all. It just becomes tedious after a while. You can skip all those sections, but then you wonder what the point is in the end. The driving is ok, but nothing to write home about.
There is some "cover shooting" in the game. It is ok, but also nothing really special. Some sections felt tense and exciting, but you die many times because of bad controls.
The replayability consists of bettering the score for a particular case, but replaying a case isn't that great when you already know everything that is going to happen, and it feels more frustrating to have to go through everything just to better a few questions at the end for example.
You can also finish a bunch of achievements, but in this game, I just did not see the point. This game is supposed to be immersive, like a noire movie. That gets slightly spoiled by gamey achievents, and none of them are too satiesfying anyway.
I loved this game because of the style and the music. The motion capture is fun too. It has the right atmosphere and is a great experience. Too bad the game sections are not that great. Good, but not great.

I've lost nearly tamed dinos, i've lost powerful tamed dinos because i forgot my Whistle hotkeys, i've also paniced and sent my weak dinos against strong dinos.
This one time on a private server (My first private server) with a friend, we'd put work in, now this was when you could ONLY harvest fiber with your hand, by picking it, slowly, painfully. We had a ncie base going, no increased rates of any kind, no super tranq rifle. Our first tame was a Stego, it was pure stress. It was hellish. Picking berries as you go, worrying about the narcotics, etc, its really not that bad but your FIRST yeah its a thing. So we get him and suddenly berries for days, fast tracks us, we can start killing bigger things cause we have a dino, get Raptors, a Carno, we're doing great. I saw this bronto not too far from base "Hey i bet i can kill that and get all the hide and meat!" well friends, thats when i learned, DO NOT MESS WITH BRONTOS! He wrecked me on my Raptor, i ran back to base with it almost dead. It chased me the whole way. It started tail swiping EVERYTHING, SWOOP! Chests destroyed, SWOOP! Walls GONE! SWOOP! Dinos Dying left and right. I ran my raptor away, my friend is yelling in my ear asking "WHAT HAVE YOU DONE!" we start going at it with spears, not wanting to risk our raptors, We are dying left and right but have plenty of beds near by (You learn to have plenty of beds pretty quick) we finnaly down the Bugger. So, Much, Hide, and meat! Worth? Nope, nope not at all. Only have two raptors left (easy to tame really) all our Herbivores are dead (berries suck) and our base is half wrecked. We salvaged most of it, and rebuilt and most importantly learned a lesson, i don't regret a thing. We still laugh about it and every time we play with someone new i tell them "DONT Mess with brontos!"
Have i had bad times in this game? Sure, i guess, i mean can you have good with out bad and vice versa? Would/could i recommend a public server? Nope, didn't waste my time with it. Loaded in to a couple, one was PVE ENTIRELY WALLED OFF! EVERYWHERE! I had good luck on PvP servers, YEAH i got wrecked a couple times but PvP is what it is, thats the players not the game. Would i recomend this game? Hell yes. Words don't do it justice, its the reason i upgrade my PC, am i actively playing? Nope, waiting for Abberation, just finished a full play through of Annunaki Genesis, taking a break while wating. Will i play again? Hell yes. Will it be on a private server? Yep.
TL;DR The game is good, PLay on a private server, ignore anyone who says the game is unfinished, the amount and quality of whats there is astounding. It is a good game. Hell its a great game.

Preface: It's alright but there's plenty of better games you could look into first, but if you can catch it on sale, it'd be worth a purchase. All things considered, most of the DLC cases aren't the strongest, however. If you're willing to pay the extra money for them feel free to do so though.
There's a lot to this game, both in variety and amount of content. I'm going to just bullet-point everything.
*Story: The overarching plot is mostly put on the backburner throughout, it comes up from time to time especially at the last desk but there's no real "climax" to the overall story as a result. Case-by-case, it's hit or miss. Some of the cases are really good; the entire vice desk especially is a blast to play through. Some of them are pretty bad though; the homicide cases become a blur due to their sameness and the arson cases are generally disappointing.
*Investigating: It depends on how easy orr hard you want to make it; I had audio cues but no visual cues, which basically still makes it a joke anyways. With no cues on though I don't know how you'd find some of the important things, it's never obvious what you can look at or not and some things don't make much sense.
*Interrogating: It's generally really easy to see when someone is telling the truth; however determing between "doubt" and "lie" can be a pain, especially when the evidence you have to use is not immediately obvious. Some of the acting is also incredibly over-the-top, but on the other hand a few people are just too subtle to the point of it coming down to their words alone whether or not you believe them.
*Driving: I don't enjoy driving, but even I can tell that the controls here are, well, not that great. Very floaty, it took me a long time to get used to them and even then I let my partner drive any time I could. Some of the car chases also have some pretty unrealistic expectations of the player, though thankfully those are in sidequests.
*Shooting: I can't subjectively judge this one, but it seems fine enough to me. Though Cole Phelps sure can tank a lot of bullet wounds...
*Side-quests: Lame. Most of the street crimes are chases (car or foot) or shoot-outs, two of the aspects I enjoy less about the game, so yeah. The rest are just a collection-fest. Getting all the gold film reels is as hard as you want to make it, it'd be near impossible to do without any outside resources, but the official site has a map providing the general area that I consider "not cheating" so. Getting all the cars is a lot harder and basically required abusing a glitch for me :B

How? I will tell you.
I played Warframe since the beggining, no Vor's Prize as intro or 4 revives per mission (more like 4 revives per day) the grind was just as bad as it is now, this is a free 2 play game expect some type of grind, but I liked the gameplay so I stuck around for more, they developed more content pretty fast, so I kept coming back, the community grew, I lurked like a lurker and watched as the lore grew and evolved.
2 or 3 years of that and then the Second Dream quest came around...
I've kept this in mind It's a F2P game, it does not have to be a rich game, hell even HOTS said "You shouldn't think too hard about these things"
So yeah space magical ninjas! go and have fun!
But Second Dream came they have made a storyline. A good and compelling storyline and it's still being developed with more content every year.
I came for the ninjas but stayed because this is a game that care about being more than a bunch of mechanics tied together by gameplay and aestetics.
This would be seen in full price release, but it's a F2P with no pay wall (except if your want to do fashionframe as color schemes are behind a pay wall etc...).
Long story short ninjas play free.

Some people report technical issues but I can assure you that I haven't encountered any. If your pc is good enough to run it on maximum; then you're in for a treat. The world is very detailled and realistic. When driving around you have the feeling that you're actually living in Los Angeles. The interior locations are detailled as well.
But driving around isn't the main part of the game. That's investigating cases and interrogating witnesses and possible suspects. That interrogating is based on your prior investigations. The more evidence you collect; the more easier it gets to solve a case correctely. When a person answers your question you can react in three different ways; you think he speaks the truth, hides something or is lying. The way to determine that is to carefully examine the evidences and/or carefully watching the body language of the suspect. In the beginning it can be quite difficult to determine the right reaction but once you'll get the hang of it it's not that hard.
And that brings me to another great part of the game; the acting. Team Bondi has used a very advanced style of motion capturing to capture every tiny bit of detail from the actors and that really shows ingame. Aaron Staton plays a really good role and if you're fan of the TV series Mad Men, you'll be pleasantely surprised to see some other actors of the series as well.
The story mode is good and offers some nice plot twists. When you've completed it, you can enter some kind of free roam mode to explore Los Angeles and to collect unique cars, film reels, landmarks,...
Because of the uniqueness of the story there isn't really very much replay value. I mean, sure you can replay every case until you get a five star rating on every case but that's about it. You can naturally start the storyline again from the beginning, but it's just that because of the story being so closely interwoven with the game, a second playthrough takes away much of the excitement.
All by all you'll spend at least 50 hours to complete everything. I've really enjoyed this game and I'd recommend it. Getting the DLC is recommended as well as it adds some great cases
