Wow I am 100 hours in already. I guess it is time for a review.
Warframe has grown exponentially from it's years. I say it has grown but not fully developed yet.
The level progression as it stands is extremely slow and tedious but the visuals, controls, and quests are quite good.
It is easy to get started as they start you on a quick tuturial and helpful hints guide you a bit more throughout the game without being intruisive and forceful. You are free to pick up side quests as well as your main quest as well as venture into all regions that are close to your level. If you are invited by your friends and they are higher level than you are, you can join their current quests as well.
I am a big fan of the drop-in and out feature of this so others can randomly help you as you are exploring. It used to be better in previous versions of the game but the current set-up is not too bad either.
I do not reccomend this game if all you want to do is level.
I do however reccomend this game if you like something different in MMOs.

As the name suggests, Chivalry is about medieval warfare. You are playing a foot-soldier from 4 classes of your chosing : archer, man-at-arms, vanguard and knight, EACH with unique weapons and pros/ cons. There are many game modes, classic team deathmatch, free-for-all, capture the flag, horde (zombie) mode, duels. My favourite is team objective, where each team competes for a series of map objectives (like raiding villages, conquering castles, assaulting forts and defending kings etc).
Chivalry will offer you a very satisfying time fighting with lots of weapons (swords /axes/ maces/ spears/ polearms/ bows/ crossbows, and many others) in 1st person or 3rd camera. 1st person camera feels like playing Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, for those of you who know the game.
You can use different atack moves to kill your enemy, each with advantages and disadvantages. This game also features lots of gore, which is to my liking :warcry:, and you can also chop members off and decapitate enemies in killing-blow.
Graphics are quite demanding, but offers a nice degree of quality, even for 2016. The sound ambience and music is great, with voice acting even greater, and weapon sounds and clashes even much MORE greater ! You can also taunt and mock your enemies (which is a common thing in Chivalry and fun to do) and complement them via "radio messages"
Combat, I would describe it as, straight from Dark Messiah, and even enhanced. Very pleasant to learn special moves and tactics like dragging etc.
Game is easy to play, hard to master ; it's easy swinging swords left and right, but to become a true sword-master ? Hah this takes time and thinking. But once you do become a veteran of this game, you will discover an immense pleasure in dueling with other high-level player and beat the challenge.
I am a true fan of this game, even before, I played a lot of Age of Chivalry, it's predecessor as HL2 mod. It's much more challenging and fun to play than other PvP games like Dark Souls or Mount and Blade.
So, get this game and meet the real men on the battlefield ! *what is it ?* Oh my grand mace says he wants to give you a kiss !

Chivalry Medieval Warfare is an excellent and technically sound game.
Chivalry is a unique fighting game - it's action packed, intense and realistic.
The fighting system is based around real time strikes and blocks. So you need to aim and direct where you attack and block. This makes for an intense are real experience, where timing and being technical can mean life and death.
A summary of the action - it's bloody and graffic, with decapitations and limb lopping fun!
Chivalry sets the bar for real time stikes and every other fighting game has begun to follow by it's example.
There are a huge arsenal of weapons you can unlock from playing and you always have the option to change between different character classes: knight, vanguard, man at arms, or archer.
Each class is unique and has it's own style as well as weapons. Each weapon has pros and cons, meaning certain styles of playing work better or worse with it.
Chivarly also allows your character to call out and say things, from insults, to respectful congratulations, warnings and even team objective reminders.
It makes it a more social game and adds an extra bit of fun to the experience.
You can also switch between 1st and 3rd person, anytime during the game. So everyone is happy.
The levels are well set up and work well for the different game modes. from the mateship of team objective and team deahtmatch, the chaos of free for all and the techical battles of duel.
I strongly reccomend this game for anyone who likes playing online games and has interest in fighting games. You will not be disappointed.

It's like an RPG grind without the hassle. Just click the enemies until you buy yourself some heroes with in-game currency (NOT real money) and let them do the clicking for you, while you just sit back and enjoy the massacre. It couldn't be simpler! So there are a million different things in addition to clicking the enemies, but those little things will come naturally over time. What really matters are the basics: Click the enemies!
I have nothing else to say, and frankly I don't think there's any need to say anything else. It's a free game! You've got nothing to lose, so try it out! I certainly like it for what it's worth!

Warframe is an awesome game in the beginning, but gradually looses its appeal as you get to higher content.
But for the first 50-100 hours, fun and challenging.
What I like:
- Progressing through planets and missions and being locked out till you finish. This can give a little frustration but the reward is great feeling of accomplishment, a very much missed thing in modern games; I love how Warframe makes this bold move in a world on instant gratification gaming.
- Player skill matters, and so does gear .. in a good balance (at least till higher content). It is a great feeling to see you get better at the game as you learn small tricks and gain knowledge.
- Extremely good random map generator. It really feels like maps are handcrafted while they are actually random generated chunks.
- Feels damn good to be a space ninja. It is one of those things you can't explain, the game just clicks gameplay wise.
- Farming for materials to build stuff.. you actually need to earn your gear (disregarding you have no idea what gear you want or need whatsoever as only the wiki gives you clues there)
- There is really no warframe that is better than the other, it is all about how you play it and your upgrades. You could argue there is no p2w as "everything" in theory can be farmed and you can max a (one) warframe to the same degree as a paying player. Pretty fair monetization model, and that is a rare thing these days.
What I dislike:
- It is impossible to play this game without extensive reading about various mechanics on wiki, forums etc. Learning these things by trial and error or otherwise observing in game is not possible, as it is so complicated.
- Many missions and story progression are impossible to figure out on your own. Watching youtube, wiki, forums etc is the ONLY way to solve these complex mysteries, there are no pointers or help in the game or the missions. Some missions require special gear types (that require farming other stuff, that require completing other missions); this is not a problem in itself as it add challenge, the problem is you cannot figure this out ingame, you have to read the wiki.
- When playing most mission types with others, it is just a race to finish.. You will probably find yourself struggling just to keep up with the frontrunners, hardly doing anything useful for the mission.
- The freespace missions/maps are annoying.. nothing more to say, simply not fun.

For starters, I would highly recommend this game. As far as idle/incremental games it's one of the better ones I've seen. The devs interact with players, updates are done relatively frequently, and the game is very bright and cheerful. It even has some (minor) lore aspects, a bit of story is told, though if you're looking for a game centered around story, this is probably not it.
Recently, patch 1.0 came out bringing Clicker Heroes into its first full version. There's been a lot of knee-jerk reactions with a new system (transcendence) that came out with 1.0, in which you trade in most of what you have for some mechanics that greatly speed up your game. Because the very first run after this "transcending" is very slow, there has been some negative reactions towards the game. Most people who have spent the couple hours that it takes to get back into the soul gain levels have found the update very enjoyable, whereas those who quit tend to not spend those couple hours. Please take those reviews with a grain of salt! The game does have its problems, but transcendence is not one of them.
Edit: For anyone wondering, I have a large amount of time spent on this game because it's an idle game. I leave it open full time to idle through it.
Edit 2: A few updates have come out since my review. Primarily, "offline" (as in, when the game is closed) progression was added, which makes it much easier to play this game casually.

A good game for a fair price.
It's a First and Third Person medieval shooter/fighter. Most of the time you can choose which camera you prefer, some servers may restrict it to a single camera angle/point of view.
Game core mechanics are around learning each weapon’s reach and speed and exploiting it to its max potential. Game shop is merely cosmetic, so it isn't pay to win. Currently there is a single glitche that ruins the game:
Drag => It's an exploit that Devs made legit. Example of drag: With melee weapon you have basically three options when attacking: Horizontal swing, Vertical Overhead and Thrust. While a single click of the left mouse button will trigger a counter clockwise swing attack, you can speed up (make it reach you opponent faster) your attack by turning your mouse (and consequently your facing) into the same direction - which I think is fair. Although you may also 'drag' your facing clockwise while doing the same attack, which will make you hit your enemy while he cannot defend himself (whenever you fail to parry, there is a cooldown of about one second before you can try to parry again). In my opinion, drags are huge immersion breakers for this game. I'd suggest you to search for videos with the subject 'Chivalry dragging' before buying the game.
I'd recommend it if you like First & Third Person medium-to-low paced combat. Or if you ever wanted to try a medieval FPS.

When I first started playing this game, I thought it was OK. I joined a clan eventuallly, but that aspect wasn't what really interested me. It's basically your standard clicker game. You either actively click to advance in level or you create an idle build. Gradually I made it (the other day) to level 3,600, which for some time was considered a bit of a benchmark in the game. It even has a Steam Achievement.
However, recently a new patch was added, usually reffered to as the "Transcendence" patch. Now, supposedly you can "choose" whether to play the old school CH or the Transcendence version. This is not entirely true as the patch fundamentally changed the original version by some serious nerfing of Ancients, which are an integral part of the game. Those changes apparently effect both versions of CH. It is a serious blow to people that want to stay with the older system, and honestly feels contrived to force gamers into the new system. It also effects people that purchased gems to a certain degree, especially if you Transcend.
It doesn't help that some of the forum staff and the game's fanboys are calling people names (i.e. fools) who disagree with the patch. Not the best customer service/PR decision one could have taken with the patch.
I'll prob still piddle with CH a bit, but I woud rec that if you are looking for a clicker style game to play, shop around. There are prob better ones out there. But with hundreds of hours in, well you know how it is.

I've been burned out on MMOs for a few years now, even after trying WoW for the first time only a few months back. And so, for years, I've been stipulating the kinda things MMOs need to change the formulae and come back on top. After a sudden surge of the ARPG I thought this was the way forward. Combat is fundamental in maintaining gamer's attention and overal meat of the game. ARPGs have a knack for making enemies a physical construct (that you don't just tab target to) and so the feeling of attacking NPCs becomes more real. But little did I know this could still be done in 3rd person.
Warframe contains within it at least most of the things I want MMOs changed to. It encorportes two essential games into one, IMO, which are Borderlands and Prototype; both of which were games known for their fun gameplay. To encorporate high level design, for parkour, loot scavanging and creative exploration is not an easy feat especially fitting it into a sub MMO. I say sub because it's two multiplayer varients; 4 player co op for all missions and actual mass multiplayer for Hub areas; for trade. It's easy to see why they did this, we all know how belittling it is to be part of vast groups online where you hardly feel any impact coming from your own actions. Warframe counters this pathetically ancient trend, the holy trinity, by making all classes self sufficent by allowing you to change how they work through mods (roughly translated as armour upgrades and skills all in one).
The only drawback I've found is, as mentioned earlier, a distinct lack of mass multiplayer due to 4 player co op system. There are emotes put into the game your character performs in a familiar mmo archetype but this is evidently inconsequential given the lack of social mechanics beyond trade and guild hub interactions. Arguably this applies to most MMOs as well, as we expect to bump into other players during escapades and come together naturally, achieving common goals. The lack of a holy trinity system, limited players per match and lack of interactable non-combat related mechanics beyond trade is the only reason a Warframe player will seek additional content in other MMOs. However this is certainly not something that can easily draw players away. When I think about the social interaction, yes it is vitial to the genre but, it's being away from the rest of what Warframe does right that ultimately negates bothering with another MMO again. I will miss being self sufficient, powerful from the start, high & layered level design, solid phyiscal models for NPCS and simplicity of crafting and progression. All of which is offered at no cost to the player to play. I can only hope ARPG MMOs will lean towards these single-player influences mechanics as it still remains the fate of MMO genres depend on their success.

Warframe is a F2P, third person shooter that revolves around getting gear and using it to kill enemies and complete a variety of missions. It sounds simple, but trust me, the game is actually very complex, which is both a good and bad thing.
Pros:
-Warframe features very fast gameplay with a robust parkour system. You will be running around on walls and flying through the air while also using powers and using your guns once you get the hang of it.
-There are a variety of guns and characters (warframes) to choose from with over 30 warframes and well over 200 weapons. Frames (warframes, think of them like characters) range from support frames like trinity to damage frames like ember to crowd control frames like vauban to tank frames like chroma. Meanwhile, weapons are equally varied. Sure, you have your normal automatic and semi-auto assault rifles and pistols, but you also have thing like the javlok, which is a spear that you can either throw for high damage (but you have to pick it up) or can shoot fireballs for less damage.
-The progression system is good. Early on, your main objective will be to get through the star chart by doing a series of missions on planets (and moons!) throughout the solar system. These will be delineated by a clearly defined path on the navigation console. Progressing to unlock the next planet requires you to beat bosses at the required junctions. Once you clear the star chart, you will next embark on the quest of obtaining gear and gaining mastery rank. This system is great because you will want to get lots of gear anyways, but the mastery rank system rewards you for building more with a variety of bonuses like: more possible trades per day, higher void trace storage, etc.
-The game is beautiful. It's easily one of the best looking free to play games ever, and it is incredibly well-optimized for a variety of options for both high-spec machines and potatoes.
-The game is NOT pay to win. What I mean by this is that in your typical P2W F2P game, the game will  require you to grind for literally hundreds of hours for even basic gear. That is not the case here. Sure, there are some weapons that will require a significant amount of grind, but you can obtain most weapons (especially basic ones, you know... the ones YOU will be starting out with) fairly easily. However, basically everything in this game has a crafting time. Weapons are relatively short: either 12 or 24 hours while frames are longer: 24 hours for each component plus 72 hours for the frame itself. You get used to these crafting times pretty quickly though. It's as simple as grinding for a little while and simply returning from work/school the next day and POOF! your weapon is done!
Cons:
-The game is INCREDIBLY grindy. If you want the good gear here but don't want to pay for it, you can expect to play mission and after mission looking for the part you need to make the frame/weapon you are looking for. That said, the core gameplay is very fun, so it's a lot of work, but you should enjoy yourself at the same time.
-End/late game (what you do once you have all the gear you could ever want) is kind of lacking. You don't notice this problem at first (it only appears in high-level areas), but time to kill for both enemies and players is incredibly low in this game. Essentially what this means is that end-game is kind of cheesy in that players rely a lot on either CC or insane tankiness, and a lot of the core aspects of the gameplay kind of fall apart. A lot of the end game content isn't very rewarding or fulfilling as it takes hours in a survival to reach high-level enemies and then you are met with cheesy gameplay and the same rewards you've already been getting.
-For a new player, the game is VERY hard to understand. This is probably what the game does worst is telling new players what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on in the game. There are so many complex systems like modding, fusion, void fissures... with nothing but a little 2 sentence explanation buried away in the codex about what they are. If you don't want to feel lost, join a clan where there will likely be people willing and able to help you (the community is largely very nice and helpful in this game)
Overall, I am recommending the game because it's not P2W and it has great combat. For sure, it is flawed in many ways, but you can easily get hundreds of hours out of a FREE game before you notice any of these flaws. I have well over a thousand hours, and even I still have fun when I pick up this game, which says something I think.

I put it away until release, watching from afar the news of controversial paid DLC and complaints of features being added before old ones were fixed. Now that Ark has “released” I find it to be in much of the same state as when I first played it. The UI is still a few generations behind, there is a lack of a unified aesthetic beyond “realistic”, and the new user experience is awful. Even the most basic information on how to play had to be obtained through youtube videos.
Ark looks like fun, and a lot of the fun is where you make it – especially if you bring friends. Honestly, it’s hard for me to get those who even own the game to dedicate a significant amount of time to it. I can see the fun that can be had, but it doesn’t feel like it’s worth it. I don’t recommend this game for both the controversial paid DLC on an already insanely popular early access game and the issues that have been ignored to stuff in more content.

Ark. I have sunk a fair few hours into this game and first things first:
Graphics.
The trailers and other images you've probably seen make it look as it's the best looking game you've seen since minecraft. In all seriousness, good luck running it at that level of graphics without a top-end PC. Like... SUPER top-end. I can run Battlefield 1, one of the best regarded games graphics wise, at Ultra while getting 60fps.. I can't run this game at medium getting over 20 FPS.
This game is horribly optimised and seriously needs some more work before demanding 60 bucks.
Second, gameplay.
Ark is SUPER fun to play, apart from the fact that it's boring as bat♥♥♥♥♥♥on your own, vanilla rates are slower than a human catepillar getting poles shoved up it's numerous asses, so unless you like grinding, have fun playing on the official servers.
PvP is just stupid. Alpha Tribes rule all servers and demolish anyone who doesn't have 10+ people to back them up. Bases are gone within 2+ hours of you logging out to offline-raiders and starting a freshly wiped server is just horrible. When you're starting alone, getting the basic tools and run along a beach to find a 20+ man clan setting up their metal bases with their turrets on a spawn point, not very inviting.
Taming, I love the creatures in ARK as they are modelled beautifully and most have their own unique ability worth taming just for that. But the times... do you want to sit there for 2 hours taming a level 12 pteranodon? If so, have fun! But if you just want to drop in, even on a PvP server for an hour or so, you might be able to get a Dilo. The taming is so utterly slow I remember seeing a mate of mine tame a high level T-Rex which took him 5 hours or so.
The starting point, it just takes forever. Once you've played a few wipes and have started over a few times like I said, unless you have friends it's just boring. Hit a tree, craft basic tools, and just attempt to level up for hours until you can actually start delving into some of the deeper aspects of the game, it seems alot of the main gameplay elements in ARK are for much higher level players with alot more friends to help them.
I'm also pretty sure I recall the developers saying that their DLC will not cost any money, and would all be free. They held true to that promise when they released the Primitive Total Conversion, but as soon as they realised they weren't making enough money from their hugely popular game they released Scorched Earth for 20 USD, and soon Abberation will be coming out for ANOTHER 20 USD making the total price of this game, along with all the extra content that should be included in the base game 100 bucks. Also don't be fooled by the trailers of this DLC, as interesting and exciting as it is, they are just as boring and stupidly grindy as the main game.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for 60 bucks, if they lowered the price back down to what it was, I might have but the gameplay for this price is just ridiculous.

Ark. I have sunk a fair few hours into this game and first things first:
Graphics.
The trailers and other images you've probably seen make it look as it's the best looking game you've seen since minecraft. In all seriousness, good luck running it at that level of graphics without a top-end PC. Like... SUPER top-end. I can run Battlefield 1, one of the best regarded games graphics wise, at Ultra while getting 60fps.. I can't run this game at medium getting over 20 FPS.
This game is horribly optimised and seriously needs some more work before demanding 60 bucks.
Second, gameplay.
Ark is SUPER fun to play, apart from the fact that it's boring as bat♥♥♥♥♥♥on your own, vanilla rates are slower than a human catepillar getting poles shoved up it's numerous asses, so unless you like grinding, have fun playing on the official servers.
PvP is just stupid. Alpha Tribes rule all servers and demolish anyone who doesn't have 10+ people to back them up. Bases are gone within 2+ hours of you logging out to offline-raiders and starting a freshly wiped server is just horrible. When you're starting alone, getting the basic tools and run along a beach to find a 20+ man clan setting up their metal bases with their turrets on a spawn point, not very inviting.
Taming, I love the creatures in ARK as they are modelled beautifully and most have their own unique ability worth taming just for that. But the times... do you want to sit there for 2 hours taming a level 12 pteranodon? If so, have fun! But if you just want to drop in, even on a PvP server for an hour or so, you might be able to get a Dilo. The taming is so utterly slow I remember seeing a mate of mine tame a high level T-Rex which took him 5 hours or so.
The starting point, it just takes forever. Once you've played a few wipes and have started over a few times like I said, unless you have friends it's just boring. Hit a tree, craft basic tools, and just attempt to level up for hours until you can actually start delving into some of the deeper aspects of the game, it seems alot of the main gameplay elements in ARK are for much higher level players with alot more friends to help them.
I'm also pretty sure I recall the developers saying that their DLC will not cost any money, and would all be free. They held true to that promise when they released the Primitive Total Conversion, but as soon as they realised they weren't making enough money from their hugely popular game they released Scorched Earth for 20 USD, and soon Abberation will be coming out for ANOTHER 20 USD making the total price of this game, along with all the extra content that should be included in the base game 100 bucks. Also don't be fooled by the trailers of this DLC, as interesting and exciting as it is, they are just as boring and stupidly grindy as the main game.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game for 60 bucks, if they lowered the price back down to what it was, I might have but the gameplay for this price is just ridiculous.

This game is fantastic, don't let these hours fool you. I started on xbox one with roughly 2300 hours in game. If you enjoy grinding, gathering weapons and different warframes (characters), trying to see how long you can stay in a mission, then Warframe is the game for you. Early levels are very grind heavy, while you're trying to build your arsenal so you can increase your level to obtain the higher end/end game weapons and warframes. Mid game is whatever the hell you want it to be, grinding more levels to make it to the top, making platinum (in game purchasable currency), do raids or head right on to end game. End game is either fashion frame where you try youre best to make your warframes look the best they could possibly look, raids to obtain arcanes to enhance your warframes capabilities or just to make platinum and lastly endurance runs, endurance runs are when you spend 4-5 hours just slaying enemies to see how far you can get and how skilled you really are. This is how I spent most of my time, leveling up and modding all of my characters to get the most out of them so me and my freinds can go sit in a mission for 5-6 hours maybe even longer sometimes. DE constantly updates the games with special events to get special weapons, they update the game frequently providing new warframes/or fixes to warframes, new and unique weapons, and new mods. This game is fantastic, the only gripe I have with it is that DE doesn't have the end game player base in mind to much. They focus more on the grindy aspect which is kind of a bummer but hey I got 2300 hours in it, I can't complain to much.

This was supposed to be the game for all dinosaur-lovers, a dream come true... it became a disappointment instead.
It started as an interesting project. During Early access, it was playable: no fps drop while being able to have all settings maxed out for example, and things had logic behind them.
Bugs were always looked at with "it will be fixed" eyes, just like with all the other mistakes in this game.
Developers focused more on content instead of developing a solid base for their game and work from there, instead of focusing on stability and performance like any decent team should.
So I can't, in good conscience, recommend this game to anyone. Much less now when it costs the outrageous price of 60 eur.
60 eur for WHAT exactly?
For a game that only rich people with the best computers can play?
Full of creatures that aren't even remotely decently modelled, which animations are so bad and clunky?
Far from any realistic concepts?
A game that isn't even finished yet?
Yeah it's literally the only game that lets you tame like 200 different creatures more or less, so? that's the only positive thing about it, that and that it's a sandbox and you can build a fort. What does all that matter when you can't even RUN the game? And even when people can, what do they find? That unless they "cheat" in the game or tweak the server properties it will be unplayable.
Or people just likes to waste their time like trying to tame a creature for 10 hours and then notice it was for nothing when that creature dies to the first battle :awkward: I wouldn't be surprised if this was the case of many after seeing the shenanigans in The Isle... which by the way is a better choice if you value graphics, animation and sound quality, aswell as environment quality and details (things which by the way are, again, a huge disappointmend in ARK).
Honestly, after being here since almost the very start, I just feel immensly disappointed at how this project turned into one big, sad, money grab.
People raging about it's price now? Everyone had the chance to get it when the game was worth something.
Wasting 60 eur on this game isn't really a smart decision, so if anyone really wants to experience the disappointment themselves I suggest they get it on sale ^^, trust me, you'll feel less bad about your decision.

This was supposed to be the game for all dinosaur-lovers, a dream come true... it became a disappointment instead.
It started as an interesting project. During Early access, it was playable: no fps drop while being able to have all settings maxed out for example, and things had logic behind them.
Bugs were always looked at with "it will be fixed" eyes, just like with all the other mistakes in this game.
Developers focused more on content instead of developing a solid base for their game and work from there, instead of focusing on stability and performance like any decent team should.
So I can't, in good conscience, recommend this game to anyone. Much less now when it costs the outrageous price of 60 eur.
60 eur for WHAT exactly?
For a game that only rich people with the best computers can play?
Full of creatures that aren't even remotely decently modelled, which animations are so bad and clunky?
Far from any realistic concepts?
A game that isn't even finished yet?
Yeah it's literally the only game that lets you tame like 200 different creatures more or less, so? that's the only positive thing about it, that and that it's a sandbox and you can build a fort. What does all that matter when you can't even RUN the game? And even when people can, what do they find? That unless they "cheat" in the game or tweak the server properties it will be unplayable.
Or people just likes to waste their time like trying to tame a creature for 10 hours and then notice it was for nothing when that creature dies to the first battle :awkward: I wouldn't be surprised if this was the case of many after seeing the shenanigans in The Isle... which by the way is a better choice if you value graphics, animation and sound quality, aswell as environment quality and details (things which by the way are, again, a huge disappointmend in ARK).
Honestly, after being here since almost the very start, I just feel immensly disappointed at how this project turned into one big, sad, money grab.
People raging about it's price now? Everyone had the chance to get it when the game was worth something.
Wasting 60 eur on this game isn't really a smart decision, so if anyone really wants to experience the disappointment themselves I suggest they get it on sale ^^, trust me, you'll feel less bad about your decision.

This is the one game in existence that keeps sucking me in, but it has it's flaws.
Warframe has a LOT of info you have to absorb, and it doesn't really explain it too well.  It's honestly intimidating to work through it yourself, so if you're just starting out then ask for help, A LOT.
Warframe has a lot of content, and a good number of quests, but the quests only constitute maybe 10% of the game.  The rest is building, modding, and leveling.  This game defines the word "grind".  Once you reach the endgame content, and have finished all the available quests, all that's left is grinding.  Grinding for mastery points, grinding for relics, grinding for mods, grinding for prime pieces....
I keep coming back because acquiring new Warframes means a new type of gameplay, and more mod setups to play with.  I love that they keep adding new stuff, new things to acquire and play with.  Even if the actual levels and enemies don't change a whole lot (once in a blue moon), at least they keep adding new ways for us to kill stuff.  Plus, I am addicted to fashion-framing.  I've dumped more money into this game than is healthy for color palettes, Tennogen skins and syndanas.
In short, this game is fun and worth it (especially since it's free).  The only stuff you can't get by grinding is the Tennogen stuff, and the Prime Access exclusive cosmetics.  But it's not really suited for impatient people unless they're willing to pay money to get stuff faster.
Final note: The one thing that gets on my nerves is that despite my 500+ hours in this game, Lotus still jabbers on during EVERY SINGLE MISSION about what I need to do.  It's ok early on when you've not done very many missions.  Now imagine how I feel as I near my 2000 mission mark, hearing the SAME EXACT MESSAGE from Lotus for the 2000th time, and I just wish I could shut her up.  But there isn't an option to turn her voice off.  The only thing you can turn off is your Cephalon's voice, and he's much less annoying because he doesn't talk nearly as much.

Enjoyed my first year of this game right after the start of the Open Beta (is still going?)...
... then started the self inflicted pain, where i started seeing the humongous possibilities this game had, starting following the devstreams to keep myself informed about the future changes of the game.
Took the game too seriously, missing totally the point of the existance of gaming (from my point of view), which is having fun and distracting myself from the stress of life (like many other) and ending up expecting too much from a game that cannot go further from mediocre.
Now, after pointing out my personal experience, lets go for the details:
Pro :
- Art and Graphic quality : both top notch, from this point of view DE gave its best, even from the technical side, getting better on and on;
- Sound : same;
- 1/3 of the Gameplay : using Warframes is awesome, the agility and the great amount of skillsets at your disposal can make you do exactly what you expect from a Space Warrior/Ninja (well, lets forget the ninja part shall we?);
- Cash Shop : microtransaction here is one of the best i've ever seen, making possible to obtain ANYTHING (except workshop items) the game has to offer, from Warframes & weapons to cosmetics, giving the opportunity to everyone to achieve a great amount of customization even without spending a dime.
Con :
- 2/3 of the Gameplay : using Warframes is awesome right? well, it will be like bringing a granade launcher into a glass house, making you destroy enemies just by looking at them, throwing away that Space Ninja promise out of the window by giving you the impression of being a Space Technomage instead, pushing you to repeat the same maps over and over to have that pathetic chance to get that item you need to complete that weapon/frame/pet/wathever that eventually will not be used 'cause the meta is so strong the game should be called Metaframe;
then the stopping wall appears, making your godlike armorsuits look like small babies in front of to the bulletsponges that all of a sudden will start spawning, making your life miserable forcing you to use specific warframes than can exploit certain situations with their specific mechanics.
They tried to put that "borderland" feeling to a cut&shoot game where numbers shouldn't exist AT ALL, promising many times in the devstreams to remove the modifications on damage to make it possible to use all the weapon aviable (or at least enough of them) if you would like to push yourself in higher levels, but instead enforcing the idea of stats modifications adding more RNG to the table, making you farm more and more with each new patch...
... can't even keep going with a coherent pro-con review because i still remember how many times it was said they were going to reduce the grinding in many devstreams just to double right after the next big patch, turning the game into a grindfest where every item/weapon/frame/wathever you end up making turned up to be just a part of the collection that you would eventually start making, because it is the only thing you do, collect and never use except those few weapons, frames and mods that turn you into an unstoppable sponge killing machine.

I've seen a lot of negative reviews over the last few weeks and felt that I had to submit a review of the game itself, rather than a review of Studio Wildcard.
This game has come a long way from where it was when I first purchased it in early access. As I recall, it was about a week before they added the stone tier. At that time, I was getting about 25 fps with my GTX 770 using medium settings. I point this out as the most common thing I see is that the game lacks optimization. Due to finances, I'm still playing on the same rig but now I get 60+ fps with some setting set to high so it has come a long way. Is there room for improvement? Sure there is, and just about every update includes some improvements.
So on to the review:
This is a highly detailed world and is quite immersive. The first time I played it - and I should point out that I went in cold and had no idea what the game was about other than my adult daughter telling my "it's like Minecraft, only with dinosaurs" - I scared my whole family as I was yelling my head off as I tried to escape from a dilo. I died in less than a minute. Aware of the dangers now, or so I thought, I respawned and, as in Minecraft, I proceeded to punch a tree - after checking for dilos. The tree killed me. After uttering a few choice words and glaring at my daughter who found this to be the funniest thing in the world, I respawned yet again. I lucked out and appeared close to my own dead corpse - which I found just a little creepy, especially when I discovered later that you can harvest your body for meat. Having recovered my wood and thatch, I tried punching a boulder to no effect to get the stone I needed to make a pick. Ignoring the snickers from my growing audience, I decided to try something else and discovered how to harvest bushes. I think it was around the fifth bush when I accidentally picked up some stone. I made a pick and levelled up! Progress. Now armed and presumably dangerous, I set forth to conquer the Ark. I spotted another dilo, or possibly the same dilo as before and stalked it when I heard this strange noise. I never saw what made the noise but have since learned that it is the sound a raptor makes when it kills you. I only knew that it was a raptor since the game was kind enough to tell me what killed me.
That was pretty much the story of my first experience with Ark. The game has a very steep learning curve and can be very frustrating at first. With time and many respawns and not a few rage-quits, I eventually learned that a) bows are wonderful, b) crossbows are even better, c) not all two-legged dinos want to eat me, d) some four legged dinos do want to eat me, e) aim carefully, f) don't shoot if you might hit something else by accident, and g) build more than one bed.
I've only attempted to play on a couple of official servers and I have to admit that what other reviewers have said is true, most long standing servers have "Alpha Tribes" who dominate the servers. Everywhere you go, you find nothing but pillar after pillar preventing resources from respawning outside of areas that aren't under the direct control of the Alpha tribe. PvP play on an official server consists of finding an out of the way nook and building a very modest camp that is generally limited to stone as metal deposits are too well staked out by others  so the tiny amounts harvested from regular stone have to be used for tools. Then they find you and reduce your fort to ruins. Repeat.
Single player was largely ignored until just prior to the official release but has since received a well thought out make over. In fact, until about July, 2017 if I wanted to play single player, I'd actually run my own server rather than play single player in order to tweak the settings to make single player possible. The game was envisioned as a co-operative effort and has been developed with that in mind. This is evidenced by the fact that it is impossible for a single individual to learn all the engrams - there are too many and your level caps out long before you can have enough engram points. Also the bosses are also meant to be fought as a team so they have the health and strength to make that a challenge meaning, of course, that an individual has no chance at all. Some dinos such as the Quetzal - something I've never even come close to killing, let alone capturing or taming - pretty much require at least two people working together to capture. Having said that, single player has been revamped quite a bit and is now playable and enjoyable, although I still have no idea how to get a Quetzal without a partner.
I haven't played on a PvE server as yet, mainly due to my experience with the PvP servers and mainly played on a server I ran myself for a few friends on a casual basis or play single player. Setting up a server is quite easy and one of the best features of the game, although I recommend using a third party tool like the Ark Server Manager.
I am a mod addict - I love being able to add mods to my games and this game has countless community created mods that allow you to make Ark into the game you want it to be. Are you a Brony? There's a mod for that! Want to tone it down a bit so your kids can play it? There are mods for that as well.
All in all, I have to say that this is a game that is well worth the price - the base game itself allows for hundreds of hours of gameplay. With the availability of online play - whether on an official server or an unofficial server you set up for a friends, plus the availability of multiple maps - both official and user created - and the more than 3000 currently available mods, there is really no limit to the possibilities for this game.
Regarding the negative press that Studio Wildcard - developing a game of this scale is a challenge in of itself. Building a game of this scale, making it work on PCs using different versions of Windows, Unix/Linux, Mac, XBox One, AND PS4 - all at the same time? That is a truly Sisyphean task. Most of the complaints I've seen are that they either a) ignore their players, b) refuse to fix bugs in the game, or c) "nerf" everything good. I've found Wildcard to be quite responsive to suggestions and issues. Foe example, I started a topic in the game suggestions forum that tools tips be added to the Host/Local setting sliders that explained what the sliders do and those were included in an update within at most a couple of weeks. This shows that they do indeed pay attention to what we as players are saying. Just about every update usually fixes something or another. Some fixes take longer than others, especially ones that are difficult to replicate. Some fixes did take far too long to get resolved, such as the long wait for a fix in single player for dinos getting stuck on trees, but it did finally get fixed, although at times I actually miss that bug, made hunting sooo easy. The loudest complaint is that Wildcard nerfs everything, pterodon flying speed was probably the biggest complaint I saw and I believe is still being moaned about. This is part of game development, it is known as balancing the game. Pterodons could fly faster than players could track and fire at them making them virtually unstoppable when attacking, especially when used as suicide bombers with C4 strapped to them. The speed reduction was necessary to give players a chance to defend themselves. In other words, it made the game fair - it must be noted that the ones who complained the most were, in my opinion, the ones who used this exact tactic.
As for releasing a paid DLC when the game was still in EA, it didn't effect negatively effect the base game development and likely provided a much needed cash infusion to the company. Programmers and graphic artists don't work for free.

Ark is not a bad game itself but there really isn’t much to it either. This game is a survivor/explorer game with dinosaurs in it, that’s pretty much it. The game does have some features, like temperature, that add a little to the survivor part of the game but nothing we haven’t seen before in other survivor games. This game lacks a lot of things like automatic systems for feeding your dinos and harvesting crops, so you must find/harvest the food for yourself and the dinos constantly. Some dinos have specific functions but again nothing special. Single player gets boring quick unless you have an unbelievable passion for dinos and harvesting berries and extreme patience’s for taming. You can change the settings to accelerate and reduce almost all processes but it adds to the boredom and removes virtually all the challenges of the game.
On multiplayer, there are tons of servers but if you plan on building a base with your buddies be prepared to rebuild and rebuild. Because of glitches, someone can penetrate your base and destroy it while you’re away or it can just get wiped because the game froze on you. I’ve put in a lot of hours in the game because I have owned it for a long time so I have popped in on occasion to see if the game improved but it didn’t.  The game is still very demanding on the pc and has many glitches and is very, very unbalanced. Developers focused on creating new dinos which stream workshop is more than capable of instead of implementing new features and balancing the game. Again, expansions are just new maps with some new dinos and some new resources; a waste of money and nothing a mod from the workshop couldn’t do. Servers are limited to number of players so you will fight off the same players until you get bored and move on which will happen very quickly. Please if there’s a demo try it, you will most likely not like the game.

One of the most important things that any game developer can do is generate hype over their products. Depending on the project, this can be a relatively difficult thing to do. Studio Wildcard’s Ark: Survival Evolved is one of the few examples of a title which generates its own hype based on concept alone: it is a dinosaur themed open-world survival game, built upon the idea of taming one’s own dinosaurs. For many players, this childhood wish fulfillment might be enough of a sell by itself. When you combine this premise with over two years or pre-release early access, the amount of hype and expectations can only grow so much more. Now the questions become focused on how Ark: Survival Evolved meets those lofty hopes and expectations.
In my opinion, there are many ways that the game does meet expectations. One of these ways is the game’s general atmosphere. Wherever you begin your journey on the island map, it is always immediately clear that you really are in an open world. The environment is beautiful, but it also feels huge and daunting. The creatures in ARK appeal in a similar fashion. They are colorful, they fit in with their environment, and many of them really do feel dangerous, especially in the early levels. A player who attacks a Triceratops with nothing more than their torch or stone axe is definitely a dead player.
While surviving alone is importantly very difficult, forming a tribe with online friends and taming dinosaur friends feels equally empowering. Riding into battle against a boss monster or a weaker tribe on the backs of several, high-level Rexes is a gratifying feeling unlike anything any other game in the survival genre can give you. Unfortunately, what ARK gains with its atmosphere, it loses with lack of polish. For a game which spent over two years in early access, the amount of bugs is a little shocking. For example, it is possible for tamed dinosaurs to simply fall through the world and disappear due to pathing and collision issues. While a Spinosaurus might feel powerful while you ride it into battle, it loses so much of that power and awe when you can tame or kill it as a solo player by trapping in a patch of trees which any kind of real thinking, living creature would seem to be able to walk around or break through.
In addition to the bugs, the game mechanics feel a little slow. Gathering resources and taming dinosaurs are always lengthy ordeals. They are compounded by the fact that one’s life and belongings are not safe when they sign off for the day. Warframe is an awesome game in the beginning, but gradually looses its appeal as you get to higher content.
But for the first 50-100 hours, fun and challenging.
What I like:
- Progressing through planets and missions and being locked out till you finish. This can give a little frustration but the reward is great feeling of accomplishment, a very much missed thing in modern games; I love how Warframe makes this bold move in a world on instant gratification gaming.
- Player skill matters, and so does gear .. in a good balance (at least till higher content). It is a great feeling to see you get better at the game as you learn small tricks and gain knowledge.
- Extremely good random map generator. It really feels like maps are handcrafted while they are actually random generated chunks.
- Feels damn good to be a space ninja. It is one of those things you can't explain, the game just clicks gameplay wise.
- Farming for materials to build stuff.. you actually need to earn your gear (disregarding you have no idea what gear you want or need whatsoever as only the wiki gives you clues there)
- There is really no warframe that is better than the other, it is all about how you play it and your upgrades. You could argue there is no p2w as "everything" in theory can be farmed and you can max a (one) warframe to the same degree as a paying player. Pretty fair monetization model, and that is a rare thing these days.
What I dislike:
- It is impossible to play this game without extensive reading about various mechanics on wiki, forums etc. Learning these things by trial and error or otherwise observing in game is not possible, as it is so complicated.
- Many missions and story progression are impossible to figure out on your own. Watching youtube, wiki, forums etc is the ONLY way to solve these complex mysteries, there are no pointers or help in the game or the missions. Some missions require special gear types (that require farming other stuff, that require completing other missions); this is not a problem in itself as it add challenge, the problem is you cannot figure this out ingame, you have to read the wiki.
- When playing most mission types with others, it is just a race to finish.. You will probably find yourself struggling just to keep up with the frontrunners, hardly doing anything useful for the mission.
- The freespace missions/maps are annoying.. nothing more to say, simply not fun.

One of the most important things that any game developer can do is generate hype over their products. Depending on the project, this can be a relatively difficult thing to do. Studio Wildcard’s Ark: Survival Evolved is one of the few examples of a title which generates its own hype based on concept alone: it is a dinosaur themed open-world survival game, built upon the idea of taming one’s own dinosaurs. For many players, this childhood wish fulfillment might be enough of a sell by itself. When you combine this premise with over two years or pre-release early access, the amount of hype and expectations can only grow so much more. Now the questions become focused on how Ark: Survival Evolved meets those lofty hopes and expectations.
In my opinion, there are many ways that the game does meet expectations. One of these ways is the game’s general atmosphere. Wherever you begin your journey on the island map, it is always immediately clear that you really are in an open world. The environment is beautiful, but it also feels huge and daunting. The creatures in ARK appeal in a similar fashion. They are colorful, they fit in with their environment, and many of them really do feel dangerous, especially in the early levels. A player who attacks a Triceratops with nothing more than their torch or stone axe is definitely a dead player.
While surviving alone is importantly very difficult, forming a tribe with online friends and taming dinosaur friends feels equally empowering. Riding into battle against a boss monster or a weaker tribe on the backs of several, high-level Rexes is a gratifying feeling unlike anything any other game in the survival genre can give you. Unfortunately, what ARK gains with its atmosphere, it loses with lack of polish. For a game which spent over two years in early access, the amount of bugs is a little shocking. For example, it is possible for tamed dinosaurs to simply fall through the world and disappear due to pathing and collision issues. While a Spinosaurus might feel powerful while you ride it into battle, it loses so much of that power and awe when you can tame or kill it as a solo player by trapping in a patch of trees which any kind of real thinking, living creature would seem to be able to walk around or break through.
In addition to the bugs, the game mechanics feel a little slow. Gathering resources and taming dinosaurs are always lengthy ordeals. They are compounded by the fact that one’s life and belongings are not safe when they sign off for the day. If a new player must spend hours on their first wooden base, for example, it does not seem like a healthy game feature for this base, and all of the players dinosaurs, to be killed and destroyed overnight.
Overall, Ark still feels like a game that is a little in the rough. The concept is still as appealing as it always was, but it currently feels somewhat unpolished and overfilled. In my opinion, it is still definitely worth checking out.

I'm seeing a lot of negativity in the reviews about this game.
So i figured i'd make my own.
I haven't been playing this game that long, only since like a month or 2 before release, and so far, i love it.
It has both pros and cons as all games does.
But all in all, i find this game to be a must have for everybody who likes the survival and/or dino genre of games.
Pros:
The landscape, it's absolutely incredible. From the snowy mountain tops, to the grassy fields and the coral filled ocean floor, especially on the community created maps.
The variety of dinos, there's so many different dinos out there, many of them with their own unique abilities.
The dungeons, large mazes filled with creepy crawlies and loot. Some has minor "puzzles" to complete, other just have a more straight forward feeling, but with more of a maze feeling. Oh and did i mention loot?
The challenge of surviving, so many things to pay attention to. Food, water, shelter, materials to expand, base defense (counts for both PVE and PVP, otherwise Rex might come chew on your roof) and upgrading when ever you can. Even taming dinosaurs is essential to success.
The ascending, the feeling of "beating the game" and discovering the truth behind the Ark.
Private servers and single player, absolutely awesome because the settings, rules and gameplay can be set exactly how ever you want it. That means the end of alpha tribes, spawn traps and dino sales.
And if i keep listing pros i'll never get to cons.
Cons:
Dino AI IQ, some dinos behave like they have an IQ around 2. A giant Rex chasing you, you run in between 2 tiny palm trees about as thick as your arm and Rex gets stuck in the trees.
The loot drops, so many useless lootdrops. Chasing loot is great yes, but not when you find the same useless wood and thatch items and blueprints that is pointless.
The shotgun, when i put a shotgun in the face of a raptor on close range and pull the trigger, i want to see it's head explode. Not repeat the process 5 more times or die trying. It feels wrong with a shotgun that weak.
Official servers, i just downright hate them. Filled with alpha tribes and stupid settings that makes it near impossible for new players or solo players to make any progress.
Would i recomend this game?
Absolutely.
It's a lot of fun.
Hundreds if not thousands of hours to spend on it.
Always discovering new things when ever you explore.
Yes it has a few minor glitches and bugs, but nothing gamebreaking.
I do see a lot of negativity about the games optimization and FPS issues and people calling it unplayable, personally, i run it with everything set to Epic and have an average of 50-60 fps, so i don't see where all the fps negativity is coming from.
Maybe it's time to update hardware for those people.
However, i would recomend the developers to change the minimum requirements of this game, because running it with those specs, you won't get an fps higher than like 15-20.
They have highly underestimated the minimum requirements for this game.

I never played the Early Access, I bought the game after it was 'fully released' and have been playing exclusively on an unofficial server with friends so take this with a grain of salt.
First off, $60 dollars is steep for lots of people, so I understand why people are angry that it is no longer at its early price point, BUT I would consider that money well spent!
I've had a ton of fun taming dinos (mostly the loser little ones and the herbivores because I'm scared of dying) and especially a ton of fun with building bases across the Ragnarok map!  Mods help, Mods help a lot, like S+ and some of the more decorative mods (since the game is meant for survival not pretty houses).
Flying out and discovering cool loot from the skygods is always exciting, even if you end up with just enough materials for a 1x1 thatch house.  It's gambling without more money, and I appreciate that thrill.  Just exploring, even, with the threat of being eaten by something big and scary (or sometimes SMALL and scary, gosh darn Terror Birds...) is a thrilling experience, with the payoff of finding a beautiful area that you kinda wish you could live in forever, in the real world? Like, that's awesome to me.
I play PvE, because again, low stress, but I imagine PvP is WILD if that's your thing.
The engram tree is chock full of interesting stuff, and it's real neat when you can FINALLY build everything you want to, or craft saddles for that one dino you've been praying for, or hey, wow, a sickle! FINALLY NO MORE HAND PICKING FIBER.  You start out with so little (aka, nothing) and everything is so frightening, and you will die, and suffer, but eventually you will get to a point where, hey, those Dilos that were kicking your rear before? They're food now. They might as well be dodos.  And it keeps advancing like that. Those carnos? Dodos. Rexes? Dodos. There is a great sense of accomplishment.
I would hate to play this solo, I imagine, it gets sorta lonely, but that option is available to you.
All in all, I love this game. I haven't played a ton of hours, but it's been the game I've been exclusively playing for weeks now and I have yet to lose interest.  And hell, when this little base I'm building is done? Like 'done'-done?  Build a new one, in a prettier spot, with prettier dinos.  It goes on!
PROS:
Cute Dinos.
Mods exist to make things prettier, if building is your thing.
Excellent Team Building opportunities.
BEAUTIFUL GAME BEAUTIFUL LANDS BEAUTIFUL TREES BEAUTIFUL WATER GORGEOUS.
You feel your character getting stronger and your dinos getting stronger as you advance.
CONS:
Price point is steep compared to what it used to be.
Updates CONSTANTLY with tiny updates that can sometimes break your server so you have to update that a bunch, too.
Default mapped keys can sometimes confuse you so you end up eating feces instead of actually feeding it to the dung beetle like you're supposed to.
Snap-Points can be confusing (leading you to place a wall in the exact opposite spot you wanted to place it)
Microraptors.
Overall, YES I recommend it.

I only play single player PVE, so I can recommend this game for that purpose only if the settings are adjusted in the options menu. The original settings make the game quite difficult and time consuming. I recommend changing many things that will make your labor burden less, this for me is essential to keeping the game fun and not laborious and repetetive. For example, change the harvest settings to increase yield of resources per action
(swing of an axe, etc.) and change the daylight settings to increase the length of day or speed up the length of night. Another helpful change is increasing the tamed dino carryweight and decreasing the time it takes to tame them. I do not recommend changing many other stats as this can break the challenge of the survival game and destroy the experience.
I also recommend not looking online for answers or where to find resources, play the game like a true survival experience and it will be rewarding.
I don't recommend reading online for answers to the game. It can break the whole point of the game, which is to survive through trial and error testing your own abilities. You really must patiently explore and experiment to learn and dominate.

When I first tried out Warframe I didn't know what to expect. At first glance it didn't seem like much, but after getting into it I realized there's much more to it than I initially thought. I'll list the pros and cons about the game, based on my experience. Don't take this review for granted, its only my opinion after all.
- Plenty of frames to choose and play with:
warframes or frames for short are what you play as in the game. Each frame has its own playstyle and set of unique abilities that you can choose from that you can then further customize based on your needs.
- A variety of game modes to mix up the gameplay:
These are sufficient in quantity and have different objectives. In Defense you protect an artifact from the enemies, in Survival you simply survive for as long as you can, in Spy you must retrieve data from vaults, and so on.
- Huge selection of weapons to use:
There's everything from simple weapons like knives and bows, to assault rifles and grenade launchers, as well as high tech energy weapons. There's enough to choose from to satisfy almost any playstyle.
- Mods:
As you play you find various mods that you can use to improve and model your frames and weapons the way you want. Everything from basic health and damage increasing mods to complex mods that give you certain effects when hitting or killing an enemy in a specific way. There's also mods that give your frames useful passive abilities, as well as mods made specifically for a certain frame.
- Primes: Prime weapons, frames or mods are better versions of their original counterparts. The regular versions function well enough that the power gap isn't too big, so you don't need a prime to be good at the game.
- Freedom of customization:
Want a bow that shoots exploding arrows and causes electricity damage? Ever thought of trying out an assault rifle that shoots freezing bullets? Wondered how a pistol that causes radiation and corrosion is like? The game told me I can do all of that and much more!
- Freedom of playing the way you want:
A friend asked what sets of weapons frames have. He asked if a stealth frame has a bow and a dagger. I responded by taking a squishy little stealth frame into a Defense mission, chopped up the first squad of enemies with a giant two handed sword, killed the 2nd squad with a radiation spewing handgun then blew the remaining squads up with a grenade launcher. And the game was okay with that, you can put any weapon on any frame you want.
- The game is F2P (Free to play):
This of course means that you try it out, play it for a bit and then decide if you like it or not. Almost all of the game's content is free. The devs are also pretty generous, often giving players events where they can acquire upgrading components for weapons/frames, special weapons and sometimes even cosmetics, completely for free.
- Trading:
You can trade some (but not all) of the items you find in Warframe with other players. The game has its own trading chat to help you find what you're looking for, and there are filters to make searching even easier. You can even make platinum (the game's premium currency) by selling items you can get simply by playing the game.
- The community:
Warframe has one of the friendliest communities I ever saw in a video game. Players help each other out, veteran and new alike. New players have no problem getting advice when they need it, and even help in missions they can't complete on their own. Sure you might meet a toxic player every now and then, but every game has a few of those bad apples.
- Clans:
Small to large groups of players that you can also become a part of. There are a huge amount of clans in Warframe, and you can make your own too if you want. Joining a clan gives you access to more weapons and some other useful items, as well as your own dojo where you can hang out in, or trade.
- Cosmetics:
The game offers you a beautiful selection of colors to paint your warframe and your weapons with, as well as various attachments you can use from syandanas, shoulder and legs pads, chest plates and sugatras. Skins are also available. Most of these cost platinum, but that can easily be acquired through trading without having to spend a single penny. For those who wish to support the game and buy platinum, its easily affordable with coupons you can get from daily rewards. The cosmetics themselves aren't that expensive either.
- PvP:
While Warframe is mainly a PVE game, a PvP mode called Conclave is also available where you can fight against other players.
- Very grind heavy: Yes you can get almost all of the game's items for free by playing. No you won't get them all easily and/or quickly unless you're the god of luck. Grinding for resources, weapon/frame parts and mods can take up a lot of your time depending what you want. And that's just the start, because...
- RNG:
Tied directly together with grinding. Only a few items in the game are a guaranteed drop, and for everything else you're at the mercy of a random number generator. You can get your item on the first try, or you can be there for a hundred missions and still have nothing. This applies to resources and mods, as well as parts for weapons and warframes. You'll always get something, but chances are it won't be what you want and/or need.
Sometimes you'll even need to make a key/cypher/some other item to access the mission (for example the recent Razorback event) which costs resources, making it that more frustrating if you can't get the items you want.
- Levels and tilesets:
Don't get me wrong, they're pretty to look at and keep you amused for a good while, but eventually you'll notice you know all of them by memory. That exact same bridge, that same room, that familiar set of stairs you saw in several other different missions. You'll also likely be grinding for your items I mentioned in the exact same level too, over and over again.
- Demands dedication:
Simply put, if you want the best Warframe has to offer you'll have to play it a lot. New content's constantly coming out, and while that's a good thing if you can't really take longer break if you want to keep up. Combined with the grinding and RNG you have to play pretty regularly.
- Time limited special events:
What's that? You couldn't play the game during the unique event that lasted a few days because of real life stuff, or you couldn't play enough to get all the content it had to offer? Well too bad, kiss those rewards and the event away, because they're not gonna come back anytime soon.
- The Prime vault:
New primes come out every once in a while, and when that happens they replace an older set of prime items that are moved into the vault. This basically means you can't farm for them anymore, unless you have relics to access the missions where their parts once dropped, or getting the parts from players who got them before they got vaulted by trading.
- Early game is confusing:
While the game has a tutorial and players are willing to help out new people, the game's amount of content and all the mechanics it has take a while to learn, confusing new players or turning them away from the game. When I started playing I was running around like a headless chicken trying to figure out what to do.
- Late game doesn't have much to do:
So you decided to play a lot, testing yourself just how far the game will take you. You got all the available frames, you have an entire arsenal full of all sorts of weapons. You have acquired the best gear the game has to offer. You are now a master of Warframe, you can solo the hardest missions without breaking a sweat, the toughest enemies fall before you like insects, you're always the best player in your squad, you have a mountain of resources stockpiled from how many missions you've completed.
And then? Then you find you have nothing left to do because you already have everything you need, and you slowly get bored.

There are parts of this game that I love... Or I should say parts that I *did* love for a while. The first few days on a server is great! Learn the terrain, the tribe dynamics are new and unknown and there's learning the crafting and setting up a new base.
Then comes the grind. Oh lordy is this grindy... Prepare to spend many hours gathering materials to feed the materials that will eventually allow you to tame the dinos and build the base that you want. You'll need a dedicated team of friends to spend weeks of work to collect enough to defend your base. You'll need dinos to make this efficient, and a decent base with good defenses to keep them safe from hostile tribes or just from solo trolls or opportunists.
All of this isn't really bad, the grind gives value to your work and there's a sense of accomplishment when you have set up some decent defenses.
The bad part of Ark is that all of this means nothing. There is nothing you can do, no defenses great enough, no number of dinosaurs sufficient enough to protect against a tribe that decides to attack you with a high level quetzal to drain your guns while you're offline. No defense against a tribe that brings in some reinforcements from another server. Its just far too easy to destroy in an hour what took hundreds of hours to create.
The game is heavily weighted towards attacking and attacking in the wee hours while other tribes are offline is just too rewarding.
This feels like a balance problem, and it has never been properly addressed in the while time I played.

Warframe is a coop third-person shooter.
For the most part, it CAN be played solo, but most people prefer to work in groups (either with people that you know or random pubs). Typical combat is in teams of 1-4 players, with basic shooter style levels: defense, escort, and retrieval missions (to name a few). Besides standard combat, there are occasional space levels, with somewhat difficult to learn flight controls with devisive enjoyability.
Outside of the missions, a large portion of in game time is spend in the players Lander, a ship owned by the Tenno that houses all of your equipment: Warframes, followers/companions, weapons, etc.
Item creation and acquisition for the majority of the game can be either purchased using platinum (an in game currency that can either be traded between players or bought with real money), or manufactured by buying and fulfilling blueprints using credits (in game currency that can be obtained in game through playing missions) and various other components found in game. Certain special improved variants of equipment can be obtained by running unique missions, often with specific difficulty improvements over the standard game.
Socially, there are two likely locations for hangouts: in clan Dojos, and in the Tenno Relays. Previously, most planets used to have a relay, but occasional challenging events threaten the relays, which have caused most of them to succumb. The remaining relays are locations where unique items can be purchased from the various political factions (which the player can join, with benefits and detriments to each one) and the bi-weekly appearing void trader, who carries exclusive randomised items with high potential, and numerous cosmetics that cannot be obtained in other ways.
The clan dojo is a fully customizable facility that those with the appropriate permission in a clan can construct. The room orientation, coloring, decor, and accessories of every dojo is unique to its creators, and construction requires careful management of available resources to optimise production while minimizing costs. The dojo labs offer a plethora of clan-tech weapons whose blueprints can only be obtained after getting contributions from clan members, offering those who work together a greater variety of an arsenal.
The quest content and lore is extremely slim. For me, this is one of the biggest things I look for in an MMO, but putting significant lore and quest based material into an online-focused shooter doesn't often turn out the best. A handful of quests are required to obtain certain warframes' blueprints/components, but most of them follow various depressing stories relating to the wide-scale disruption and destruction throughout the solar system.
--------------
Overall, Warframe is a complex game that delivers well in action and player involvement, with active players running almost around the clock and around the year. It uses a ranking system that slightly favors those who put money into the game, but allows players to choose to earn their keep by selling wares obtained in game to other players. The available cosmetics for the equipment and warframes is vast and various enough with plenty of customisation to appease those looking for a unique appearance with their individual characters (fully customisable and can be changed at any time). The biggest thing that I find fault in the game is that their is no way of transfering in-game obtained materials for platinum. The game continues to develop and evolve alongside the player base, and I will continue to work on exploring the game, grinding levels out, and working with other players around the world.

Alright Im chef Tony and I will show you how to make homemade chicken ramen
INGREDIENTS
2 chicken breasts (boneless, skin-on)*
kosher salt and freshly-ground black pepper, to season
1 tbsp unsalted butter
2 tsp sesame or vegetable oil
2 tsp fresh ginger, minced
3 tsp fresh garlic, minced
3 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce
2 tbsp mirin
4 cups rich chicken stock
1 oz dried shitake mushrooms (or 1/2 cup fresh)
1-2 tsp sea salt, to taste
2 large eggs
1/2 cup scallions, sliced
2 (3 oz) packs dried ramen noodles
optional: fresh jalapeño slices, for serving
Cook the chicken*: Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Season the chicken generously with salt and pepper. Melt the butter in a large oven-safe skillet over medium heat. Add the chicken, skin-side down, and cook until the skin is golden brown and releases easily from the pan, about 5-7 minutes. Flip the chicken over and cook for another 4-5 minutes, until golden. Transfer the skillet to the oven and roast for 15-20 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through. Remove from the oven, transfer the chicken to a plate and cover with foil until ready to serve.
Make the ramen broth: Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat, until shimmering. Add the garlic and ginger, and cook for a few minutes until softened. Add the soy sauce and mirin, and stir to combine. Cook for another minute. Add the stock, cover, and bring to boil. Remove the lid, and let simmer uncovered for 5 minutes, then add the dried mushrooms. Simmer gently for another 10 minutes, and season with salt, to taste.
Make the soft-boiled eggs: Fill a pot with enough water to cover the eggs, and bring to a boil. Gently lower the eggs (still cold from the fridge) into the boiling water, and let simmer for 7 minutes (for a slightly-runny yoke) or 8 minutes (for a soft, but set-up yoke).
Meanwhile, fill a large bowl with ice water. When the timer finishes, transfer the eggs to the ice bath to stop the cooking process. Wait at least 5 minutes, or until cool enough to handle, then carefully peel away the shell and slice in half, lengthwise. Set aside until ready to serve.
Assemble the ramen bowls: Meanwhile, chop the scallions and jalapeño (if using). Slice the chicken into thin pieces. Set aside. When the eggs finish cooking, add the ramen noodles to the boiling water. Cook for 2-3 minutes, until soft, then divide the noodles into two large bowls. Add the sliced chicken and the ramen broth. Top with the fresh scallions, jalapeño and the soft boiled egg. Serve immediately And enjoy.
