Being a co-op game doesn't mean that you have to ignore a competent storyline (see Left 4 Dead), but Warframe seems content to establish its universe at a basic level: players are acrobatic robot-suited warriors fighting an alien invasion. Then it simply throws us into a long series of very samey-feeling missions. Whether you're asked to rescue a hostage or retrieve an alien artifact or destroy a reactor, rest assured that your primary goal is to shoot nigh-endless waves of enemies.
It's good, then, that Warframe makes it quite fun to kill things and watch them die. Movement and shooting feels smooth and responsive, targets are plentiful, and there's just enough ragdoll silliness in the enemy death animations to always make me look forward to my next kill. There's a good variety of guns to choose from, including a powerful bow that can pin enemies to walls, and although the sci-fi swordsman archetype might be overplayed lately, the melee combat here is also satisfyingly weighty. Charged attacks that can slice enemies clean in half are their own reward.
Animations in general are fluid and interesting, and although the environments tend toward blandness, they're lit up by a Technicolor explosion of enemy fire and player ability effects. Some tweaking is required (the bloom effects are fairly ridiculous at their default setting), but this is still one of the best-looking free-to-play games to date. Warframe runs on Digital Extreme's proprietary Evolution engine, which does a fine job of both looking great and running smoothly. Dips below 40fps were very rare at 1920x1080 on a system running a Core-i7 920 CPU and a Radeon HD 6950 videocard, even when the screen filled up with a dozen enemies and a full team of four players.
The primary fodder of Warframe are the Grineer, a race of privateer space marines that do a passable job of taking cover and attempting to retreat or advance as the situation demands. However, they'll also regularly send out seeker bots, which are by far the most annoying enemies I've fought lately due to their small hitboxes and extremely rapid movement. Meanwhile the Infested race (read: space zombies) are almost exclusively melee attackers, and I found I could usually reduce them to confused immobility simply by standing on a tall box.
Standing on top of boxes is just one of the abilities of these high-tech super soldiers. Each of the three warframe classes gets a suite of four unique superpowers: Volt relies on electrical attacks, Nyx uses psychic powers to turn enemies against each other, Loki becomes invisible for stealth attacks, and so on. Those abilities are fun to use, but the downside is that you wind up unlocking all of them fairly early on; some advanced superpowers at the upper end of the level curve would've been a nice reward for sticking with a single suit. Also, any of the three warframe classes can use any gun, which is understandable given that you might be paying real money for them, but it makes them feel interchangeable when it comes to shooting.
Wiping the grins off the Grineer.
Speaking of guns, the lack of grenades and other explosive options is a bit odd, but it did at least force me to move forward to engage enemies behind cover rather than bogging things down in protracted long-distance firefights. You can sneak up behind some enemies and perform backstabs to critically wound them, but in the chaos of a four-person mission, I found that stealth usually goes by the wayside fairly quickly.
Most customization comes from an extensive modification system in which you plug in collected upgrades like elemental damage to your weapons and extra shields to your warframe. The interface for this system still needs a fair amount of work, though; I ran into a nasty bug that completely prevented me from switching mods out on one of my warframes, and in fact required a complete game restart every time I attempted to do so. Plus, the random nature of the drops can also be frustrating. If you miss out on the basic shield and health boosters, you might find yourself needing to re-run early missions until you get some lucky drops, as they're almost required to complete later missions.
A job well done.
One of Warframe's significant issues at the moment is its failure to display important information, especially in the mission-select interface. It's a slick piece of work, letting you pick where you want to go in the system in a cool way, but the level ranges of each individual planet aren't shown, making you click around until you find somewhere appropriate to play. Likewise, games in progress are marked, but you have no idea of the relative level of the players involved until you actually join a game in progress. Since there isn't an quickmatch button, I had to go through a fair amount of planet-browsing each time I wanted to hop into a match, and false starts are a drag.
There's always the option to simply hop into a mission by yourself and hope that someone joins you, but some missions aren't well-balanced for solo play. Some require you to carry an item that prevents you from firing your main weapon; others consist of defending critical points from enemies attacking from multiple angles. Running out of ammo is also a concern when you're outnumbered this badly.
Most critically, there's no lag or ping display anywhere. Given Warframe's reliance on peer-to-peer connections, it's frustrating not to know whether you're about to hop into a game hosted by someone who's streaming HD movies from Netflix in the other room. I ran into latency problems that ranged from noticeable to almost unplayable in around a quarter of the games I joined.
Splat.
As with most free-to-play games, Warframe contains a store where you can exchange real-world money for one of the two in-game currencies, platinum. There isn't much in the cash-only store that could be considered mandatory, although some of these items, like the in-game pets that stun and shoot nearby enemies, additional daily revives, and power-boosting items that let you slot in twice as many mods to your frame and weapons could be classed as "very, very handy." Still, the economy feels fair, especially since you're only paying to be able to kill AI enemies more efficiently.
You'll also earn the other currency, credits, as you play, and the market does a reasonable job of ensuring that most items (aside from things like XP boosters and slots for extra warframes) can be purchased with them. There's an extra laborious crafting hurdle for free players, but it's not tedious to the point of frustration. I spent $50 to buy 1,000 platinum, with which I was able to buy a bundle consisting of a new warframe, three new weapons, and a set of boosters which made earning XP and credits much quicker for a few days, with enough platinum left over to purchase another warframe and a weapon or two. For perspective, it would've taken at least a few days of regular play (not counting crafting time, which is often on the order of 12 hours per item) to earn the credits to buy them all.
One other note: Warframe's technically in open beta (again, Digital Extreme gave us the go-ahead to review it now), so this may be a temporary issue, but there are often only a few hundred players on each regional server; when this population is further spread across solo games, private matches, and online play on the 100+ missions, it can be difficult to actually find anyone to play with. But, because it's free and requires only four players for a full game, it's a easy enough to bring three friends along for the ride.
The Verdict
In its current state, Warframe feels like the foundation (or frame, you might say) of a game that might be really interesting at some point in the future. It just needs more of everything: more mission variety, more good enemies, more polish, more environments, more players. Monthly content updates are promised, so hopefully some of this will be arriving soon

I loved this game since I got it.I played it all the time, even added people I met in it. I played on the oldschool duel servers and then used gained skills to help my team in TO.
But recent changes are making the game worse. I used to click on the icon on my desktop, wait through a bit of the logo and get to the game.
Now, I have to wait for the launcher to pop-up, click play, wait for the game to start, wait for at least 3 fixed-lenght animations to finish and then I get dumped into this mess the main menu has become.
Not to mention that if you want to be good, you have to learn how far you have to get from a sword for it to not hit you. I learned that and I became pretty good. But I just played this abizmal new updated version after a few weeks and the hate that's been rising since I picked this game up again after a few months just reached a point, when I can't play this clusterf**k anymore.
The crouch and sprint has a noticeable delay after pressing the key. Hitting a shield midswing doesn't stop enemies to get you with a backswing. You no longer time blocks, you just press the button and hope. Reach on the weapons is stupid and in no way represents their lenght in any logical way. And even if you finally get to someone with a long range weapon, they are less that a foot far from you, you hit them in the middle of their chest, they don't block and that hit just doesn't count...
I adored this game. I was near addicted. It sucked me into those old times better than any game ever. And that's why it's so sad to see it turn this bad.
I will come back to it a few months. Maybe it will become what it used to be. Maybe it will be better. Or maybe it will be the same, because frankly, I can't see it getting any worse. (but I also didn't expect for it to even get worse at all)

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is over all a great game, and well worth the money, especially if it is on sale.
The Graphics are very good. The textures for random objects on the map are very detailed and look very realistic and good. The textures for small, meaningless things aren't blurry or just 1 solid color. Every part of each map is very detailed.
Speaking of maps, the maps are great. i LOVE them. thats one big thing i hate about online games, the maps usually suck. I'm not a big fan of CS:GO maps, Call of duty maps are horrific, Team fortress 2 official maps are bad except for like 3, but in chivalry, all the maps are Outstanding. The maps will very drastically depending on what gamemode you are playing. If you are playing Free for All, you might be in a well made Arena with traps and stadium watchers and everything you would see in the new Hercules movie! If you are playing something like Team objective, you will probably get a Very Large map. I love large maps, thats why i dislike CS:Go maps they are too small. Some games that do tend to have big maps, the textures of the environmental things are dulled down drastically (Ex. dirt, grass, rocks, wood, buildings). In Chivalry, you can be on a big map and still have Great looking dirt, sand, grass, trees, rocks, chairs, and everything else.
The game is very entertaining. I haven't played it for too long, but i can tell it will keep my attention for maybe close to 100+ hours (which is alot for me). I would like to see a few more cool game types though.
Team killing is a big problem i have with the game. In games like CS:GO, you have to literally aim right on them and shoot to hit them. in Chivalry, your sword swing will cover at least everything in your vision, a good 180 degrees around you. So if an enemy is there and a teammate is there also, you might actidentally hit him, especially since they move around alot. But you won't get banned for days for team killing, your respawn time may be increased by like 3 seconds.
Depending on what character they are playing as, its hard to tell if they are on your team or the enemy team. some people have customized looks and some dont have a spec of blue or red. I have seen guys who were white and green? i thought maybe he was on my team and i ignored him, but i payed the price after. I have also killed guys who i thought were enemies.
This game does have minor problems, but makes up for it in big advancements. I recommend this game if your looking for a multiplayer, realistic-style medieval game, and i rate it a 8.5/10

Warframe is a high action, quick paced, highly customisable game.
Its high action comes from the near swarm levels of enemies you fight on a nigh constant level, while it has stealth missions and a suprisingly good detection mechanics, you'll mostly be tearing your way through an array of soon-to-be-giblets enemies. The bad guys range from:
the Warmongering Grineer:
(who use everything explosive, from bullets to rockets and exploding punches.)
The Greedy Corpus:
(A faction of ruthless buisnessmen who find more technological means of murder, including Particle beams and death robots.)
And the infected Horde:
(Your neighbourhood parasitic infestation, using toxins, meat batons for hands, and swarms of what-used-to-be corpus and grineer flesh puppets.)
The quick pace comes from the mission speed, while you can take your time and loot everything that may or may not be nailed down, you can also ignore most of the enemies and charge through to the objective, combining that with the ease in which you can blitz your way through and enemies you encounter (with numbers being the enemies real advantage) and you have a game where mission time depends mainly on your play style. There are exceptions to this, such as survival mode and defence mode where you wait for a timer, but these give you the chance to end the mission every five minutes, with rewards given each time it offers.
The customisation ranges from the statistics on your armor, it's elemental bonuses, it's shielding, your total health, movement speed, ability power, range and efficiency, to the Weapons damage, range, fire rate, elemental effects, special bonuses, ammo capactiy/storage and critical chance/damage. You even get little pets to bring with you, who ALSO get to be heavily customised. Color changes are literally everywhere too, every inch of every weapon, companion, armor and ship can be recolored or reskined. It's really damn difficult to find someone who looks even remotely similar to you.
The story is while quite scarce,intriguingly deep. with twists and turns enlightening you to the vast worlds you find yourself fighting for. Granting powers and equipment as you progress.
In conclusion, Warframe is a great game if you want to tear through an enemy stronghold with some guns and a big stick, or a flamethrower, an organic flem pistol and a chakram. While best played with friends it's still good to play alone, as you shred your way across the system.

When I first tried out Warframe I didn't know what to expect. At first glance it didn't seem like much, but after getting into it I realized there's much more to it than I initially thought. I'll list the pros and cons about the game, based on my experience. Don't take this review for granted, its only my opinion after all.
- Plenty of frames to choose and play with:
warframes or frames for short are what you play as in the game. Each frame has its own playstyle and set of unique abilities that you can choose from that you can then further customize based on your needs.
- A variety of game modes to mix up the gameplay:
These are sufficient in quantity and have different objectives. In Defense you protect an artifact from the enemies, in Survival you simply survive for as long as you can, in Spy you must retrieve data from vaults, and so on.
- Huge selection of weapons to use:
There's everything from simple weapons like knives and bows, to assault rifles and grenade launchers, as well as high tech energy weapons. There's enough to choose from to satisfy almost any playstyle.
- Mods:
As you play you find various mods that you can use to improve and model your frames and weapons the way you want. Everything from basic health and damage increasing mods to complex mods that give you certain effects when hitting or killing an enemy in a specific way. There's also mods that give your frames useful passive abilities, as well as mods made specifically for a certain frame.
- Primes: Prime weapons, frames or mods are better versions of their original counterparts. The regular versions function well enough that the power gap isn't too big, so you don't need a prime to be good at the game.
- Freedom of customization:
Want a bow that shoots exploding arrows and causes electricity damage? Ever thought of trying out an assault rifle that shoots freezing bullets? Wondered how a pistol that causes radiation and corrosion is like? The game told me I can do all of that and much more!
- Freedom of playing the way you want:
A friend asked what sets of weapons frames have. He asked if a stealth frame has a bow and a dagger. I responded by taking a squishy little stealth frame into a Defense mission, chopped up the first squad of enemies with a giant two handed sword, killed the 2nd squad with a radiation spewing handgun then blew the remaining squads up with a grenade launcher. And the game was okay with that, you can put any weapon on any frame you want.
- The game is F2P (Free to play):
This of course means that you try it out, play it for a bit and then decide if you like it or not. Almost all of the game's content is free. The devs are also pretty generous, often giving players events where they can acquire upgrading components for weapons/frames, special weapons and sometimes even cosmetics, completely for free.
- Trading:
You can trade some (but not all) of the items you find in Warframe with other players. The game has its own trading chat to help you find what you're looking for, and there are filters to make searching even easier. You can even make platinum (the game's premium currency) by selling items you can get simply by playing the game.
- The community:
Warframe has one of the friendliest communities I ever saw in a video game. Players help each other out, veteran and new alike. New players have no problem getting advice when they need it, and even help in missions they can't complete on their own. Sure you might meet a toxic player every now and then, but every game has a few of those bad apples.
- Clans:
Small to large groups of players that you can also become a part of. There are a huge amount of clans in Warframe, and you can make your own too if you want. Joining a clan gives you access to more weapons and some other useful items, as well as your own dojo where you can hang out in, or trade.
- Cosmetics:
The game offers you a beautiful selection of colors to paint your warframe and your weapons with, as well as various attachments you can use from syandanas, shoulder and legs pads, chest plates and sugatras. Skins are also available. Most of these cost platinum, but that can easily be acquired through trading without having to spend a single penny. For those who wish to support the game and buy platinum, its easily affordable with coupons you can get from daily rewards. The cosmetics themselves aren't that expensive either.
- PvP:
While Warframe is mainly a PVE game, a PvP mode called Conclave is also available where you can fight against other players.
- Very grind heavy: Yes you can get almost all of the game's items for free by playing. No you won't get them all easily and/or quickly unless you're the god of luck. Grinding for resources, weapon/frame parts and mods can take up a lot of your time depending what you want. And that's just the start, because...
- RNG:
Tied directly together with grinding. Only a few items in the game are a guaranteed drop, and for everything else you're at the mercy of a random number generator. You can get your item on the first try, or you can be there for a hundred missions and still have nothing. This applies to resources and mods, as well as parts for weapons and warframes. You'll always get something, but chances are it won't be what you want and/or need.
Sometimes you'll even need to make a key/cypher/some other item to access the mission (for example the recent Razorback event) which costs resources, making it that more frustrating if you can't get the items you want.
- Levels and tilesets:
Don't get me wrong, they're pretty to look at and keep you amused for a good while, but eventually you'll notice you know all of them by memory. That exact same bridge, that same room, that familiar set of stairs you saw in several other different missions. You'll also likely be grinding for your items I mentioned in the exact same level too, over and over again.
- Demands dedication:
Simply put, if you want the best Warframe has to offer you'll have to play it a lot. New content's constantly coming out, and while that's a good thing if you can't really take longer break if you want to keep up. Combined with the grinding and RNG you have to play pretty regularly.
- Time limited special events:
What's that? You couldn't play the game during the unique event that lasted a few days because of real life stuff, or you couldn't play enough to get all the content it had to offer? Well too bad, kiss those rewards and the event away, because they're not gonna come back anytime soon.
- The Prime vault:
New primes come out every once in a while, and when that happens they replace an older set of prime items that are moved into the vault. This basically means you can't farm for them anymore, unless you have relics to access the missions where their parts once dropped, or getting the parts from players who got them before they got vaulted by trading.
- Early game is confusing:
While the game has a tutorial and players are willing to help out new people, the game's amount of content and all the mechanics it has take a while to learn, confusing new players or turning them away from the game. When I started playing I was running around like a headless chicken trying to figure out what to do.
- Late game doesn't have much to do:
So you decided to play a lot, testing yourself just how far the game will take you. You got all the available frames, you have an entire arsenal full of all sorts of weapons. You have acquired the best gear the game has to offer. You are now a master of Warframe, you can solo the hardest missions without breaking a sweat, the toughest enemies fall before you like insects, you're always the best player in your squad, you have a mountain of resources stockpiled from how many missions you've completed.
And then? Then you find you have nothing left to do because you already have everything you need, and you slowly get bored.

My reveiw is going to be on a serious note, I think this Clicker deserves at least that. The Developer(s) came up with the idea to apply Mathmatics (What every Clicker is) onto the concept of Basic Fantasy Adventure. It's a lot more interesting to engage with than boring "Cookie Clicker". I have played a very striped down version of having an Adventure but more in the imagination because that game was only Buttons, it only had buttons, Kill monsters with only a button and have some text, Level up, and repeat that. That's kind of what Clicker Heroes is, but you have the Clicker/Mathmatics format and visuals of killing monsters and all they drop is mountains of gold! I believe we fight them on platforms because the worlds were mined of all gold material.
Update: Tue, Mar 14, 2017
Honestly, it's the best Clicker Game. It's made by people that know their stuff and being a Nerd that loves Numbers your smarts will help you a lot later in the game when you need to gain Ancient Souls to then make your game much more over-powered. But I do recommend playing this game on the side while playing another game, it's good for passing time. I wouldn't claim there is an offical way to progress through the game even though people have made guides about it. Guides for late game are outdated fast, because the Devs keep the game updated and advanceing. once you understand the game you can figure out how you want to progress and invest time into a, Idle/Active/Hybrid(idle&active), build useing your Ancients.
Building up your own game will take hundreds of hours. Getting to Levels beyond 2,500 will then take thousands of hours. When you decide to invest a lot of time into the game you can advance to epic numbers.
You can call Clicker Game's pointless, but that completely depends on the person. Most people like AAA Title games, again Most people like indie games, some people like games that make them rage and are ment to be an impossible challenge. Clicker Heroes is just relaxing and ment to pass the time, it's a really nice game! Minor features need to be fixed, but it doesn't impact the overall game and make it unplayable. The minor features are just outdated.
The Devs actively update the game and anything major they add are Beta tested like Transcend, thus they know how to balance their game very well.
You can obtain all items in the Shop without paying for a single Ruby, Clicker Heroes PC/Mobile will give you A LOT of Rubys over time for Free. I wouldn't recommend paying for Ruby's.
If you want a game that's only about getting more of what you already have, but it's a massive time sink, mainly walking away form the PC or doing something else for Hours. It's Free anyway!
Other people copy Clicker Heroes for a reason: 10/10 I'll update thousands of hours later.

Review for Deadliest Warrior that I can't review for some reason.
Game is a lot of fun, server browser is broken beyond anything.
Server say 20/20? Prepare to join a server with 1 other person. Happens EVERY single time. EVERY TIME. Imagine playing cs 1.6 and not knowing which servers were full of only bots. It's like that. Half your time is spent trying to find a server with other players.
The game itself is pretty fun, but the balance is screwed up. 1 samurai can take on 2 ninjas easily, but 2 spartans will school 1 samurai. Pirate and ninja takes incredible skill to be able to kill anything 1v1 consistently. Kick is all messed up so all the spartan/viking has to do is spam hit which drains your stamina and that stops you from being able to kick meaning you have to alt swing and run to the left in hopes of getting around the shield, all while blocking. It can be done, but rarely against skilled opponets. The spartan is OP without spears, yet the game gives them 6. If you don't have a shield then you're screwed. 2 spears and you're done, but they have 6. Shield-bash + swing = you're dead. Too fast to block and they have to aim high if you want to crouch out of the slash. Basically if you are fighting a spartan and you aren't Nicholas Cage from Next, then fight them on a staircase and jump all over the place like an idiot. Feint and look-at-the-ground feint before alt-swings and you might land a good hit.
If anything, they should do what War of the Roses did...break the shield if it takes too much damage. That's all it needs.
Vikings are balanced as about as balanced as a spam swing class can be. Ninjas can easily be countered with a polearm or longsword with a wide swing. Feints work really well against ninjas who side-dodge instead of away-dodge. Run from Pirates, they either suck and will just boost your killstreak or they will completely wreck your world. Vikings make a ton of noise when attacking, even before animations begin, so they are easy to block and avoid feints. Samurai are tricky. Alt-swings work pretty well as do look-at-the-ground feints. If you're wondering what a look at the ground feint is, then just look at the ground quickly if you have a spear. Looks like you're going for a jab.
So yeah, server browser is annoying, but I love the game. I have War of the Roses, but this is satisfying in a more annoying way. WotR was easy to get a hang of and wreck everyone, but my stubborness keeps telling me that I can get good at pirate/ninja, so I keep working for it in C: DW even though I do believe balance is REALLY messed up.
Seriously, devs, get to it. Breakable shields after 5-10 hits and it's all good. Increase pirate health to 175% and ninja damage by 125% and you're good to go.
You bet I recommend this game regardless of the terrible broken server browser. The fun to be had when you find a full server is unmatched. Ducking swings and side-stepping jabs is fantastic. Beware of laggers...you sometimes cannot block their attacks and you will watch your weapon go straight through them and do nothing. Still better than any Arma game though, so can't complain too much.

Two things of note before you dive into this review: I purchased ARK: Survival Evolved for $25 when it first hit Early Access (though only played it for roughly 3 hours before damn near release because it frankly ran horribly), and I have played exclusively solo or on a private server with friends and custom settings.
That being said, I don't know if I'd consider this game 'worth it' for $60. The value proposition is up in the air depending on how freely you can spend your money. However, having cranked up settings so that most of the time sink of the game is negligible on my private server, I've still put in 58 hours now. It's fun to explore the worlds of ARK, and they've released 3 quality maps for free if you, like me, don't have an inkling to purchase the expansions.
I have put most of my time, as in roughly 95%, on The Island, the game's default map, only having given some console-command fueled fly-overs of the other two maps to see the sights. In this play time I have built rudimentary wooden shacks, giant dino-sized walls and gates, tamed critters big and small and bred little babies and been killed at least a few dozen times. I've delved into caves and subsequently been spooked out of them only to die slowly of poison as I fell unconscious at the entrance, yet I still respawn and go off somewhere else. I've been taken off of my Pteranadon in mid-flight by a giant cat that jumped definitely way higher than it's supposed to, and I respawned and carried on. This is because I have tweaked the game's settings and implemented a mod that kills off respawn point cooldowns and thus frustrations of sinking time into taming, recovering corpses, gathering, etc. are all moot. I'm making my own fun, and excluding some small things like respawn cooldowns, the game allows me to tweak these settings as I please.
As for performance, I will say that it's bizarre how next to impossible it is to hit the golden 60FPS without reducing the game's graphics to the quality out of last decade by butchering the resolution scale. But I never see the game necessarily chug, either. It sits pretty in the mid-40's and 50 range on just about all graphics settings, low or high, and it honestly makes no sense to me. Running on a GeForce GTX 970 4GB, 3.2GHz Intel i-5 and have 8GB of DDR3 RAM for comparison. The game never performs poorly, but it also never performs greatly. That being said, it does look fantastic a lot of times, though the bloom is horrendously overdone.
I can't speak to the company or any screw-ups they may have made because I just didn't pay attention to this game during its Early Access due to it not performing well at the start. It performs much better now, and I've been having fun with it in my own way. If you think that maybe all the rough-and-tumble PvP isn't for you, and you're worried about griefers, let me say that running a private server with some friends can still be a ball. There's lots of emergent gameplay and, even when there are bugs (which there are plenty), they've always been goofy things like dinosaurs getting partially stuck in the geography or floating corpses or weird physics bugs.
Overall, I'd recommend it, if you have friends who will play it with you. Especially recommend it if they don't mind playing against the 'official' grain.

Being a co-op game doesn't mean that you have to ignore a competent storyline (see Left 4 Dead), but Warframe seems content to establish its universe at a basic level: players are acrobatic robot-suited warriors fighting an alien invasion. Then it simply throws us into a long series of very samey-feeling missions. Whether you're asked to rescue a hostage or retrieve an alien artifact or destroy a reactor, rest assured that your primary goal is to shoot nigh-endless waves of enemies.
It's good, then, that Warframe makes it quite fun to kill things and watch them die. Movement and shooting feels smooth and responsive, targets are plentiful, and there's just enough ragdoll silliness in the enemy death animations to always make me look forward to my next kill. There's a good variety of guns to choose from, including a powerful bow that can pin enemies to walls, and although the sci-fi swordsman archetype might be overplayed lately, the melee combat here is also satisfyingly weighty. Charged attacks that can slice enemies clean in half are their own reward.
Animations in general are fluid and interesting, and although the environments tend toward blandness, they're lit up by a Technicolor explosion of enemy fire and player ability effects. Some tweaking is required (the bloom effects are fairly ridiculous at their default setting), but this is still one of the best-looking free-to-play games to date. Warframe runs on Digital Extreme's proprietary Evolution engine, which does a fine job of both looking great and running smoothly. Dips below 40fps were very rare at 1920x1080 on a system running a Core-i7 920 CPU and a Radeon HD 6950 videocard, even when the screen filled up with a dozen enemies and a full team of four players.
The primary fodder of Warframe are the Grineer, a race of privateer space marines that do a passable job of taking cover and attempting to retreat or advance as the situation demands. However, they'll also regularly send out seeker bots, which are by far the most annoying enemies I've fought lately due to their small hitboxes and extremely rapid movement. Meanwhile the Infested race (read: space zombies) are almost exclusively melee attackers, and I found I could usually reduce them to confused immobility simply by standing on a tall box.
Standing on top of boxes is just one of the abilities of these high-tech super soldiers. Each of the three warframe classes gets a suite of four unique superpowers: Volt relies on electrical attacks, Nyx uses psychic powers to turn enemies against each other, Loki becomes invisible for stealth attacks, and so on. Those abilities are fun to use, but the downside is that you wind up unlocking all of them fairly early on; some advanced superpowers at the upper end of the level curve would've been a nice reward for sticking with a single suit. Also, any of the three warframe classes can use any gun, which is understandable given that you might be paying real money for them, but it makes them feel interchangeable when it comes to shooting.
Wiping the grins off the Grineer.
Speaking of guns, the lack of grenades and other explosive options is a bit odd, but it did at least force me to move forward to engage enemies behind cover rather than bogging things down in protracted long-distance firefights. You can sneak up behind some enemies and perform backstabs to critically wound them, but in the chaos of a four-person mission, I found that stealth usually goes by the wayside fairly quickly.
Most customization comes from an extensive modification system in which you plug in collected upgrades like elemental damage to your weapons and extra shields to your warframe. The interface for this system still needs a fair amount of work, though; I ran into a nasty bug that completely prevented me from switching mods out on one of my warframes, and in fact required a complete game restart every time I attempted to do so. Plus, the random nature of the drops can also be frustrating. If you miss out on the basic shield and health boosters, you might find yourself needing to re-run early missions until you get some lucky drops, as they're almost required to complete later missions.
A job well done.
One of Warframe's significant issues at the moment is its failure to display important information, especially in the mission-select interface. It's a slick piece of work, letting you pick where you want to go in the system in a cool way, but the level ranges of each individual planet aren't shown, making you click around until you find somewhere appropriate to play. Likewise, games in progress are marked, but you have no idea of the relative level of the players involved until you actually join a game in progress. Since there isn't an quickmatch button, I had to go through a fair amount of planet-browsing each time I wanted to hop into a match, and false starts are a drag.
There's always the option to simply hop into a mission by yourself and hope that someone joins you, but some missions aren't well-balanced for solo play. Some require you to carry an item that prevents you from firing your main weapon; others consist of defending critical points from enemies attacking from multiple angles. Running out of ammo is also a concern when you're outnumbered this badly.
Most critically, there's no lag or ping display anywhere. Given Warframe's reliance on peer-to-peer connections, it's frustrating not to know whether you're about to hop into a game hosted by someone who's streaming HD movies from Netflix in the other room. I ran into latency problems that ranged from noticeable to almost unplayable in around a quarter of the games I joined.
Splat.
As with most free-to-play games, Warframe contains a store where you can exchange real-world money for one of the two in-game currencies, platinum. There isn't much in the cash-only store that could be considered mandatory, although some of these items, like the in-game pets that stun and shoot nearby enemies, additional daily revives, and power-boosting items that let you slot in twice as many mods to your frame and weapons could be classed as "very, very handy." Still, the economy feels fair, especially since you're only paying to be able to kill AI enemies more efficiently.
You'll also earn the other currency, credits, as you play, and the market does a reasonable job of ensuring that most items (aside from things like XP boosters and slots for extra warframes) can be purchased with them. There's an extra laborious crafting hurdle for free players, but it's not tedious to the point of frustration. I spent $50 to buy 1,000 platinum, with which I was able to buy a bundle consisting of a new warframe, three new weapons, and a set of boosters which made earning XP and credits much quicker for a few days, with enough platinum left over to purchase another warframe and a weapon or two. For perspective, it would've taken at least a few days of regular play (not counting crafting time, which is often on the order of 12 hours per item) to earn the credits to buy them all.
One other note: Warframe's technically in open beta (again, Digital Extreme gave us the go-ahead to review it now), so this may be a temporary issue, but there are often only a few hundred players on each regional server; when this population is further spread across solo games, private matches, and online play on the 100+ missions, it can be difficult to actually find anyone to play with. But, because it's free and requires only four players for a full game, it's a easy enough to bring three friends along for the ride.
The Verdict
In its current state, Warframe feels like the foundation (or frame, you might say) of a game that might be really interesting at some point in the future. It just needs more of everything: more mission variety, more good enemies, more polish, more environments, more players. Monthly content updates are promised, so hopefully some of this will be arriving soon

After 174 hours of playing from the time I am writing this review I can say that this game is AMAZING. I've had it for a long time now through some of the questionable patches and updates and I would still recommend this game to anyone who enjoys survival games.
There are plenty of mods available for Ark. Even ones that undid some of the patch updates (Like the patch preventing putting lvls into movement speed for flyers). And there are Total conversion Mods that will give you a whole new challenge on surviving.
As far as Graphics go it is a very beautiful game even on medium graphic settings. And if you have the capability to run it on epic settings it is well worth it. The only time I run into any FPS issues is when there are a lot of dinos around or a lot of textures loading in like if I am running through a forest that hasn't loaded in yet.
All in all this is a great game. Would recommend it to any person who is interested in survival style games or getting into them. Yes there are still bugs they are working through with but I personally rarely run into any bugs.
Overall I would give Ark a solid 8/10. Its an amazing game. BUT there have been patches that have caused seasoned players to hate. But there were Mods that came quickly to fix said "patches". The daily updates of late around the lauch have been annoying with keeping a server updated which honestly isn't that hard to do. Excited to see where they are going with the next couple DLCs as the recently annouced DLC looks amazing and terrifying.

Clicker Heroes is an okay idle, run-in-the-background game which is worth checking out if you are really bored.

However, as the game goes on, it gets more repetitive and less enjoyable which I guess is unavoidable due to its endless-ness.
Another thing to be noted is that this game makes it very easy to share saves. As such, you could load up a save which instantly gives you almost all of the achievements. Similarly, you could get a save with a lot of rubies, which is their micro-transaction currency. I like this because it empowers you to play the game however you want, although it does diminish the sense of accomplishment you get from building up your save from scratch.

Assuming you are paying less than $12 for the "Complete Pack", I absolutely DO recommend this incredibly silly game. It's a bit clunky and a bit outdated, but both of those things actually add to the game, in my opinion, because they make it impossible to take too seriously. That is, of course, the great flaw in the FPS world: the taking of things too seriously. How many otherwise solid games does The Serious ruin? More than I could count. There ain't none of that going on round these parts.
There's stuff to unlock, and customization options, and several game types, although you'll probably want to spend most of your time in the Team Objective mode, because that's a hell of lot more fun than overplayed junk game modes like team deathmatch. There's a key for yelling. That's my favorite key. You can yell a lot of stuff, and almost all of it sounds like it was recorded from drunk SCA members. There's a lot of very silly gore: remember the fight with the Black Knight in Monty Python and the Holy Grail? This game is like a 7gb homage to that battle.
Another thing I heartily approve of is the support this game is getting from its devs. Twenty-eight major updates, and countless smaller ones, in less than two years. I'm sure it desperately needed twenty-seven of those. But it got them! Kudos to these goofy people for providing their goofy game with a classy, old school level of post-release love.
Again, just to be clear, do NOT, under any circumstances, pay full retail for this game. $12. Or less. For both the game and the expansion. (The expansion is terrible, and no one seems to play it, but that doesn't matter, because, as every gamer knows, COMPLETIONISM IS ITS OWN REWARD.)

I initially wrote a positive review on this game when I had played about 30 hours on it. But since then I have to change my review to a do not buy. Too expensive for the quality of game you get. Too unforgiving to lower level players. Too difficult for the solo or smaller tribes. Developers seem to not understand balance.
**Skip next 2 paragraphs to get back to review and not soap box speech**
Let me make a point at stating the survival/craft MMO game type is not for everyone, and it should be noted that the learning curve is bruital. But like learning a new FPS, or the introduction of BattleRoyal (for instance) into an already established game type, there will be distractors and people who this game does not fit. The unfortunate thing is it usually takes half a dozen hours to really see if you like the game and by that time people cannot return it. I believe this fuels some of the negative reviews.
The survival/craft MMO is a relatively new concept in main stream video games. Rust (2013) or DayZ (2012) were about the first major undertakings. Yet to this day Rust and DayZ(and countless others) are still considered ALPHA games on steam. But Ark was brave enough to take it out of Alpha and do a full release. Unfortunately they ♥♥♥♥ed up peoples accounts and effectively people lost, not just man hours of in game work, but man YEARS. This made the die hard player base angry and a spike in negative reviews followed. It should be noted that it states on the steam, and developer pages, when a game is in Alpha total wipes and revamps are possible. But being the first real Alpha -> Release game I can really find on steam (outside of AAA studios) the studio should be applauded and not scorned for attempting to make the system work.
Back to the review:
--Negative--
Building structures is an awkward and combersome process. Rust has a much better system in place for this, but ARK truely beats out Rust in the creative and depth you can build.
When a new server opens up, anyone can join. So if you are a newb and want to level, on a new server that openned earlier that day. Good luck, max levels will somehow claim all the good areas, and constantly gank you. How is that a positive experience for everyone except the high levels that transfer.
Taming of Dinos, litterally the most (if not most) important aspect of the game takes way too long for a casual player. I get that top tier Dinos should take a long time, and that the game should not be brought down to the lowest common factor. But if you only have 3 hours a night to play (I know that is a bunch for some people as is) there will just be certain Dinos out of your reach. They will not get done in the entire 3 hours you have to play. So that limits the upward mobility and end game, and in game, aspects a casual can have. Plus the fact that 3 hour dino can be killed in 5 seconds doesn't add to the game play value.
Certain Dinos have no counters in game (air dinos). So you see everyone rush for air dinos because people on the ground are helpless to defend against them. This seems like a gross oversight unless the developer wanted a top tier situation where it is no longer X > Y > Z > X but more of a who can get the most of Z always wins. It makes for boring game play and limited creativity.
Base defense is a joke! There is none. Let me rephrase that, there is none that is reliable, good, effective. If you do a simple google on Ark strats for base defense it comes up with article after article that is as follows, "Get good noob, build this type of base which requires an entire 10 person tribe a week to make, offense is the best defense." Again, this limits how effective and how much fun a new player can have. If you log off every day and come back to a destroyed base (and in turn all your work and hours of play destroyed), you are stuck on the lowest teir of gameplay. And although base raiding should be a part of the game, the ability for someone with a fully stone base (T3 material in game) to be wiped by a dive bombing griffin (air unit balance like I stated above) or a single C4 charge is poor game design and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience for everyone except the people in the high end tribes that just gank low level people.
Optimization is poor, but easily fixed with a YouTube video search. I have a 3 year old computer and the game looks good to me, just the render distance is closer even at max than I would like.
Environment, weather, and animals are all not optimized. Why am I freezing to death in the easy/suggested starting zone as soon as I spawn in. And why am I then 'hot' in that same zone regardless if I jump into the water, get rained on, sit in the shade? How can I be cold sitting virtually in a fire? These type of details are really annoying and detract from the game play, again a spot where Rust does have ARK beat out.
Animal levels seem confusing to a new player. For instance, in a standard MMORPG (WoW etc.) if I run up to a level 150 creature and attack it, I can expect about the same level of difficulty regaurdless if it is a wolf, chicken, demon lord etc. Yet in ARK a level 15 Spider will rip your face off and suck your blood while you pound on it with spears until you break about 5 of them, yet walking up to a level 150 Dodo and 2 hits it is dead. It seems like an awkward and confusing system to new players.
The game could use further, quality of gameplay, improvements. Little things like one way material deposits into safe rooms to test out the effectiveness of new tribe members. Player ran shops of mats, weapons, dinos etc. Little things like that would bring the game a long way.
++Pros++
Much more indepth game on almost every level than every other Survival/Crafting MMO. More structure choices and building options. I believe fewer in number melee weapons than other games but you are in the melee stages for longer so not everyone is running around with AK's after 1 day, or that is how it FEELS it should be.
The game encourages you to be in a tribe and it pays off. So instead of a KOS type game (it does happen) you want to try and group up because it makes things easier and you can level faster.
The environment animals (DINOS!!!) are more than just an after thought to get hids and meat. The game has endgame objectives, I have not experienced this but unlike just running around and raiding there are extream 'boss' dinos to tame, kill and get goodies from.
==Closing==
This has to go into the "So much potential" pile of games. And unlike rust where I can fault the community of being toxic and therefore making the game unplayable. It is the developers who fail to understand the concept of balance, the players who exploit it, and the system of not even trying to fix the problems that are to blame for this game. In the end, Ark exploits an awesome concept of Open world Survival MMO with DINOS (such a cool idea) as their one trick pony, and fails to convert that into an enjoyable game play experience. And definatly not one worth $60.

I initially wrote a positive review on this game when I had played about 30 hours on it. But since then I have to change my review to a do not buy. Too expensive for the quality of game you get. Too unforgiving to lower level players. Too difficult for the solo or smaller tribes. Developers seem to not understand balance.
**Skip next 2 paragraphs to get back to review and not soap box speech**
Let me make a point at stating the survival/craft MMO game type is not for everyone, and it should be noted that the learning curve is bruital. But like learning a new FPS, or the introduction of BattleRoyal (for instance) into an already established game type, there will be distractors and people who this game does not fit. The unfortunate thing is it usually takes half a dozen hours to really see if you like the game and by that time people cannot return it. I believe this fuels some of the negative reviews.
The survival/craft MMO is a relatively new concept in main stream video games. Rust (2013) or DayZ (2012) were about the first major undertakings. Yet to this day Rust and DayZ(and countless others) are still considered ALPHA games on steam. But Ark was brave enough to take it out of Alpha and do a full release. Unfortunately they ♥♥♥♥ed up peoples accounts and effectively people lost, not just man hours of in game work, but man YEARS. This made the die hard player base angry and a spike in negative reviews followed. It should be noted that it states on the steam, and developer pages, when a game is in Alpha total wipes and revamps are possible. But being the first real Alpha -> Release game I can really find on steam (outside of AAA studios) the studio should be applauded and not scorned for attempting to make the system work.
Back to the review:
--Negative--
Building structures is an awkward and combersome process. Rust has a much better system in place for this, but ARK truely beats out Rust in the creative and depth you can build.
When a new server opens up, anyone can join. So if you are a newb and want to level, on a new server that openned earlier that day. Good luck, max levels will somehow claim all the good areas, and constantly gank you. How is that a positive experience for everyone except the high levels that transfer.
Taming of Dinos, litterally the most (if not most) important aspect of the game takes way too long for a casual player. I get that top tier Dinos should take a long time, and that the game should not be brought down to the lowest common factor. But if you only have 3 hours a night to play (I know that is a bunch for some people as is) there will just be certain Dinos out of your reach. They will not get done in the entire 3 hours you have to play. So that limits the upward mobility and end game, and in game, aspects a casual can have. Plus the fact that 3 hour dino can be killed in 5 seconds doesn't add to the game play value.
Certain Dinos have no counters in game (air dinos). So you see everyone rush for air dinos because people on the ground are helpless to defend against them. This seems like a gross oversight unless the developer wanted a top tier situation where it is no longer X > Y > Z > X but more of a who can get the most of Z always wins. It makes for boring game play and limited creativity.
Base defense is a joke! There is none. Let me rephrase that, there is none that is reliable, good, effective. If you do a simple google on Ark strats for base defense it comes up with article after article that is as follows, "Get good noob, build this type of base which requires an entire 10 person tribe a week to make, offense is the best defense." Again, this limits how effective and how much fun a new player can have. If you log off every day and come back to a destroyed base (and in turn all your work and hours of play destroyed), you are stuck on the lowest teir of gameplay. And although base raiding should be a part of the game, the ability for someone with a fully stone base (T3 material in game) to be wiped by a dive bombing griffin (air unit balance like I stated above) or a single C4 charge is poor game design and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience for everyone except the people in the high end tribes that just gank low level people.
Optimization is poor, but easily fixed with a YouTube video search. I have a 3 year old computer and the game looks good to me, just the render distance is closer even at max than I would like.
Environment, weather, and animals are all not optimized. Why am I freezing to death in the easy/suggested starting zone as soon as I spawn in. And why am I then 'hot' in that same zone regardless if I jump into the water, get rained on, sit in the shade? How can I be cold sitting virtually in a fire? These type of details are really annoying and detract from the game play, again a spot where Rust does have ARK beat out.
Animal levels seem confusing to a new player. For instance, in a standard MMORPG (WoW etc.) if I run up to a level 150 creature and attack it, I can expect about the same level of difficulty regaurdless if it is a wolf, chicken, demon lord etc. Yet in ARK a level 15 Spider will rip your face off and suck your blood while you pound on it with spears until you break about 5 of them, yet walking up to a level 150 Dodo and 2 hits it is dead. It seems like an awkward and confusing system to new players.
The game could use further, quality of gameplay, improvements. Little things like one way material deposits into safe rooms to test out the effectiveness of new tribe members. Player ran shops of mats, weapons, dinos etc. Little things like that would bring the game a long way.
++Pros++
Much more indepth game on almost every level than every other Survival/Crafting MMO. More structure choices and building options. I believe fewer in number melee weapons than other games but you are in the melee stages for longer so not everyone is running around with AK's after 1 day, or that is how it FEELS it should be.
The game encourages you to be in a tribe and it pays off. So instead of a KOS type game (it does happen) you want to try and group up because it makes things easier and you can level faster.
The environment animals (DINOS!!!) are more than just an after thought to get hids and meat. You tame them and each species has a strong and weak points (although the T-rex doesn't seem to weak anywhere and flying units seem to have no real counter). The game makes Dinos required to really get into the mid/late game of building and crafting. Although you can in theory do without them.
The game has endgame objectives, I have not experienced this but unlike just running around and raiding there are extream 'boss' dinos to tame, kill and get goodies from.
==Closing==
This has to go into the "So much potential" pile of games. And unlike rust where I can fault the community of being toxic and therefore making the game unplayable. It is the developers who fail to understand the concept of balance, the players who exploit it, and the system of not even trying to fix the problems that are to blame for this game. In the end, Ark exploits an awesome concept of Open world Survival MMO with DINOS (such a cool idea) as their one trick pony, and fails to convert that into an enjoyable game play experience. And definatly not one worth $60.

When I first tried out Warframe I didn't know what to expect. At first glance it didn't seem like much, but after getting into it I realized there's much more to it than I initially thought. I'll list the pros and cons about the game, based on my experience. Don't take this review for granted, its only my opinion after all.
- Plenty of frames to choose and play with:
warframes or frames for short are what you play as in the game. Each frame has its own playstyle and set of unique abilities that you can choose from that you can then further customize based on your needs.
- A variety of game modes to mix up the gameplay:
These are sufficient in quantity and have different objectives. In Defense you protect an artifact from the enemies, in Survival you simply survive for as long as you can, in Spy you must retrieve data from vaults, and so on.
- Huge selection of weapons to use:
There's everything from simple weapons like knives and bows, to assault rifles and grenade launchers, as well as high tech energy weapons. There's enough to choose from to satisfy almost any playstyle.
- Mods:
As you play you find various mods that you can use to improve and model your frames and weapons the way you want. Everything from basic health and damage increasing mods to complex mods that give you certain effects when hitting or killing an enemy in a specific way. There's also mods that give your frames useful passive abilities, as well as mods made specifically for a certain frame.
- Primes: Prime weapons, frames or mods are better versions of their original counterparts. The regular versions function well enough that the power gap isn't too big, so you don't need a prime to be good at the game.
- Freedom of customization:
Want a bow that shoots exploding arrows and causes electricity damage? Ever thought of trying out an assault rifle that shoots freezing bullets? Wondered how a pistol that causes radiation and corrosion is like? The game told me I can do all of that and much more!
- Freedom of playing the way you want:
A friend asked what sets of weapons frames have. He asked if a stealth frame has a bow and a dagger. I responded by taking a squishy little stealth frame into a Defense mission, chopped up the first squad of enemies with a giant two handed sword, killed the 2nd squad with a radiation spewing handgun then blew the remaining squads up with a grenade launcher. And the game was okay with that, you can put any weapon on any frame you want.
- The game is F2P (Free to play):
This of course means that you try it out, play it for a bit and then decide if you like it or not. Almost all of the game's content is free. The devs are also pretty generous, often giving players events where they can acquire upgrading components for weapons/frames, special weapons and sometimes even cosmetics, completely for free.
- Trading:
You can trade some (but not all) of the items you find in Warframe with other players. The game has its own trading chat to help you find what you're looking for, and there are filters to make searching even easier. You can even make platinum (the game's premium currency) by selling items you can get simply by playing the game.
- The community:
Warframe has one of the friendliest communities I ever saw in a video game. Players help each other out, veteran and new alike. New players have no problem getting advice when they need it, and even help in missions they can't complete on their own. Sure you might meet a toxic player every now and then, but every game has a few of those bad apples.
- Clans:
Small to large groups of players that you can also become a part of. There are a huge amount of clans in Warframe, and you can make your own too if you want. Joining a clan gives you access to more weapons and some other useful items, as well as your own dojo where you can hang out in, or trade.
- Cosmetics:
The game offers you a beautiful selection of colors to paint your warframe and your weapons with, as well as various attachments you can use from syandanas, shoulder and legs pads, chest plates and sugatras. Skins are also available. Most of these cost platinum, but that can easily be acquired through trading without having to spend a single penny. For those who wish to support the game and buy platinum, its easily affordable with coupons you can get from daily rewards. The cosmetics themselves aren't that expensive either.
- PvP:
While Warframe is mainly a PVE game, a PvP mode called Conclave is also available where you can fight against other players.
- Very grind heavy: Yes you can get almost all of the game's items for free by playing. No you won't get them all easily and/or quickly unless you're the god of luck. Grinding for resources, weapon/frame parts and mods can take up a lot of your time depending what you want. And that's just the start, because...
- RNG:
Tied directly together with grinding. Only a few items in the game are a guaranteed drop, and for everything else you're at the mercy of a random number generator. You can get your item on the first try, or you can be there for a hundred missions and still have nothing. This applies to resources and mods, as well as parts for weapons and warframes. You'll always get something, but chances are it won't be what you want and/or need.
Sometimes you'll even need to make a key/cypher/some other item to access the mission (for example the recent Razorback event) which costs resources, making it that more frustrating if you can't get the items you want.
- Levels and tilesets:
Don't get me wrong, they're pretty to look at and keep you amused for a good while, but eventually you'll notice you know all of them by memory. That exact same bridge, that same room, that familiar set of stairs you saw in several other different missions. You'll also likely be grinding for your items I mentioned in the exact same level too, over and over again.
- Demands dedication:
Simply put, if you want the best Warframe has to offer you'll have to play it a lot. New content's constantly coming out, and while that's a good thing if you can't really take longer break if you want to keep up. Combined with the grinding and RNG you have to play pretty regularly.
- Time limited special events:
What's that? You couldn't play the game during the unique event that lasted a few days because of real life stuff, or you couldn't play enough to get all the content it had to offer? Well too bad, kiss those rewards and the event away, because they're not gonna come back anytime soon.
- The Prime vault:
New primes come out every once in a while, and when that happens they replace an older set of prime items that are moved into the vault. This basically means you can't farm for them anymore, unless you have relics to access the missions where their parts once dropped, or getting the parts from players who got them before they got vaulted by trading.
- Early game is confusing:
While the game has a tutorial and players are willing to help out new people, the game's amount of content and all the mechanics it has take a while to learn, confusing new players or turning them away from the game. When I started playing I was running around like a headless chicken trying to figure out what to do.
- Late game doesn't have much to do:
So you decided to play a lot, testing yourself just how far the game will take you. You got all the available frames, you have an entire arsenal full of all sorts of weapons. You have acquired the best gear the game has to offer. You are now a master of Warframe, you can solo the hardest missions without breaking a sweat, the toughest enemies fall before you like insects, you're always the best player in your squad, you have a mountain of resources stockpiled from how many missions you've completed.
And then? Then you find you have nothing left to do because you already have everything you need, and you slowly get bored.
Amazing, even with bugs you still getmore fun then anything of its genre.

Fan of Cookie Clicker? Well, this game is like that but so much better. For one, this game has levels, there this is more goals than to just get the next upgrade/hero/factory for more dps. For the most part, this game is basically the same with cookie clicker AT THE BEGINNING. Towards the mid/late game, it differs.
There's something called hero souls. Each hero soul gives you a 10% bonus damage increase. You can get hero souls from two main ways.
You can:
- Every 2000 hero levels (total), not to be confused with the game stage, gives you 1 hero soul.
- After zone/game stage 100, there is a 25% chance for the first boss of every 5 levels to give you hero souls. The hero soul amount that these (what is called a) primal bosses give you increases as the zone level increases.
You claim your hero souls by doing an ascension, which resets your game, but gives you the hero souls that you've accumilated throughout your run.
Hero souls aren't just for dps, although that is what it IS mainly for . . . You can buy "ancients" for hero souls. There are something around 22 ancients in the game, which all have different effects. You buy and level ancients with hero souls.
Ancients have there synergys, you might imagine. For example, there are ancients which favor idle gameplay, and ancients which favor active gameplay (clicking).
This is the most in-depth clicker game that I've come accross.
My final thoughts? Play this game if you are bored. Play this game if you want something to do while in queue for a game. Play this game while browsing reddit. It's just an afk game (please just don't do the active build) that gives something somewhat-entertaining to do while waiting or browsing videos etc.

3/4 pound ground beef
1 medium onion, diced
3 garlic cloves, minced
2 cans (one 28 ounces, one 15 ounces) crushed tomatoes
2 cans (6 ounces each) tomato paste
2/3 cup water
2 to 3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons plus 1/4 cup minced fresh parsley, divided
2 teaspoons dried basil
3/4 teaspoon fennel seed
3/4 teaspoon salt, divided
1/4 teaspoon coarsely ground pepper
1 large egg, lightly beaten
1 carton (15 ounces) ricotta cheese
4 cups shredded part-skim mozzarella cheese
3/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese
Directions
Cook noodles according to package directions; drain. Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, cook sausage, beef and onion over medium heat 8-10 minutes or until meat is no longer pink, breaking up meat into crumbles. Add garlic; cook 1 minute. Drain.
Stir in tomatoes, tomato paste, water, sugar, 3 tablespoons parsley, basil, fennel, 1/2 teaspoon salt and pepper; bring to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
In a small bowl, mix egg, ricotta cheese, and remaining parsley and salt.
Preheat oven to 375°. Spread 2 cups meat sauce into an ungreased 13x9-in. baking dish. Layer with three noodles and a third of the ricotta mixture. Sprinkle with 1 cup mozzarella cheese and 2 tablespoons Parmesan cheese. Repeat layers twice. Top with remaining meat sauce and cheeses (dish will be full).
Bake, covered, 25 minutes. Bake, uncovered, 25 minutes longer or until bubbly. Let stand 15 minutes before serving. Yield: 12 servings

I've been playing ARK for... a long time and I have to say that as far as survival/crafting games go, it's pretty good. It's more or less functional (crafting, building, weather, temperature, hydration, food, ecosystem, breeding, etc.). You have a sense of progression (tiers of structures, leveling up and improving stats, etc.), and challenging environments. Sometimes the balance in starting areas is a little iffy and up to chance if you'll get your face eaten off the moment you spawn, but at that point you have nothing to lose and can just spawn again. The graphics are very nice and once you're on your feet, there's a lot of fun and scary things to explore. Sometimes the graphics glitch, but I find that fairly rare aside from clipping. Recently the sky turned to the bright, burning white of staring into a fluorescent lamp, but that seems to have been fixed.
Pros:
+ well-developed crafting
+ good world simulation (weather, ecosystem, etc.)
+ beautiful graphics
+ functional breeding mechanics
+ fun world design
+ awesome mod support and great modding community
+ you can play by yourself and tweak settings to your needs/wants
+ dinosaurs to rip your face off
Cons:
+ price (I bought the game a long time ago for... around $30, I think), as fun as the game is, I wouldn't recommend ever spending more than $30 on even a complete game
+ starting sometimes is a bit of roll of the dice (accidentally spawning in a pack of raptors/during a heatwave)
+ long load screens
+ balance for most systems (such as crafting materials or timing) needs tweaking
+ it can take forever to get set up (shelter, tools, etc.) so progress can be a bit slow
Minor complaint: Truth be told, I'm not sure what bugs and poor optimization people are talking about in the reviews and in the forums. I've been playing single-player on a high-end computer, which is an outlier in terms of specs and should not be counted as normal. The most buggy thing I've experienced has been clipping or minor things that haven't actually been implemented such as being unable to repair tents or catcus sap doesn't rehydrate the player. Tiny things. I wouldn't call the game 'broken,' but that's my opinion.

I have 244 hours in this game, I will base this review on those 244 hours and not base it on the opinions of other people nor the developers (unless something I mention is a direct cause of their attention (or lack thereof)).
My experience is a rather limited one despite having 244 hours. Partly due to the fact I have no patience that can match this game and it's demands of time, or because of simple restrictions imposed by the games design and the people who use the games design.
So to get a few things out of the way:
So what happened? Well, me and my friends started off by finding eachother with spawn points that aren't exactly precise to everyone as you are actually spawned in multiple different areas within the spawn regions you select. (I personally liked this as it prevented immediate zerg rushing on a single individual with no consequence.) After we all found eachother we began to run around and see what was possible for us at the time - which was absolutely nothing! Shocked, we all decide to go around and level up to level 15 (so we could get wooden building materials) after we achieved level 15 it was time to get the resources to build the base.
First we decided to start small, 3x3x2 would be fine to start with as it would allow us to expand upon it quite easily. Upon first getting the engrams needed, we would need a lot of wood more than the trees around us would give. After dying around 20 times between the 6-7 of us, we finally have our crowded 3x3x2 wooden house and we went to sleep.
Upon waking up and getting on the ARK server, there was a giant hole in our base along with everyone but me dead. "Fair enough" I thought to myself, I've dealt with this before in other survival games, its just how people can safely play. With that being said, I was very VERY angry about what just happened, as all of the time we spent (about 40 min-1hr) was just invalidated.
We got to level 25-30 amoung the group, and prepared to make a stone hut instead. After spending what felt like an hour and a half of pressing E we finally got a 3x3x2 stone hut prepared, went to sleep after doing some taming, and woke up to an even bigger hole in the wall.
lmao taming
Taming takes forever, we tried taming a level 32 trike only for it to take well over an hour of waiting and spamming narco berries to have a mediocre dinosaur whos intended purpose (gathering berries) is far outshined by any other herbivore that comes after it with barely any more effort put in to taming them.
Now when you're taming higher level creatures? Thats where it
be fun to tame. Taming titanosaurs have completely different mechanics - you need cannonballs or rockets to hit their head to get them to be knocked out. But when you tame things like Giganotosaurus'? it's just flat out painful and tedious, you have to get well over 200 narcotics worth of tranq darts, and keep the shots up quickly because its torpidity drains extremely fast! The worst part is that if it knows its gonna go down soon it'll get a speed and damage boost on top of its already extremely high speed and damage!
Now the AI itself can only be described as a "dumpsterfire fueled with gasoline soaked pinecones that's about to fall into a pit of lava, de-stabilizing the volcano and causing an erruption"-esque catastrophe, it's that bad. Tamed dino's are EXTREMELY stupid and don't do what you intend them to do with the commands you're given. Wild dino's are EXTREMELY stupid and get themselves stuck because they dont ever jump over obstacles that causes the problems.
After we tamed many creatures on land, we decided to tame a few water mounts, this is where things got real fun;
Optimization in this game is terrible, and if you go deep enough into the ocean you'll see why I say that.
If you move - you freeze for a second - if you dont move - you freeze for a second - if you do anything - you freeze for a second. There's no winning strategy here, the game has no compression of files, no optimization of graphic detail, and the folder size in your hard drive is 92.5gb. (to be fair, that is with scorched earth) Downloading even basic patches will take forever due to their size (once again - lack of compression) yet this is not the worst of its optimization.
If you thought the FPS lagging behind was a problem, what if I told you that ARK can let you DoS yourself? I have a 150 mb/s connection, and my modem/router combo can handle up to a gigabit per second of data if set up for it. (set for 450 mb/s at the time this happened) Do you know what happened? I refreshed the server browser, and my entire internet crashed, LAN, WAN, you name it - it crashed and stayed down for a good 5-10 minutes.
, and i can barely muster a consistent 60 FPS at even medium settings and will occasionally struggle to go above 30 fps at high settings.
BOY HERE WE GO
Combat in ARK survival evolve is done with many different weapons that range from spears and swords to rocket launchers and laser helmets on dinosaurs, providing a very diverse set of options for combat.
Well thats what Wildcard and the community would have you believe. Actual combat goes one of two ways:
OR
Gunfighting is a laughable statement, as it never actually happens because guns are too weak to deal with the dinosaurs/creatures because the damage to them is pitiful, or someone dies in one shot because longnecks deal incredible damage (a longneck headshot deals over 170 damage on a person with full chitin armor) and all other guns are useless except for maybe the fabricated pistol.
Combat with dinosaurs is just a statcheck between the two combatants, theres no actual strategy or thought put into the fights just a ton of mindless LMB spamming and maybe the occasional RMB tap if your dino has a different function.
The biggest thing you will notice in ARK is the power difference of a level 15 character and a level 80 character, and I am not talking about stats. The options available to the two characters are on a difference by an order of magnitude; level 80s can have plesiosaur and giganoto saddles, guns of all kinds, c4, pikes, swords, metal shields and turrets while level 15s can get screwed with only a trike or parasaur saddle, spears and bows.
Theres more I'd want to talk about, but I'm at the word limit.
Thumbs down, not full release worthy at all.
