Don't let the short amount of hours into my playtime fool you. I originally picked up this game the minute it went into Game Preview on Xbox One and sunk many, many, many hours into this game where, in truth I was caught hook, line and sinker for the sheer scale of everything the game had to offer. I won't dwell too much on what most people have already covered, and the fellow reviewers are 95% in sync with my view on the game. On the Xbox One we played PvPvE on EU Server 16 and became one of 3 Alpha tribes who had good alliances with the other two. We managed until the day we all just stopped playing to avoid being raided and managed to do mass raids (online only - we were very proud of that) with other tribes to help establish order back on the server. We had a weekly purge to help keep the server running as a PvP server by raising the bar on character levels to encourage tribes to work hard or to band together with well established tribes who could give them jobs to level up quicker and avoid the cull. We had spies, we had our own trading relationships for those who had a stake in land where certain resources were in great supply and we had outposts scattered across the island to help with resource collections. Sadly, after over 1700hrs where I had a lot of time off work due to personal reasons, I had to return to the real world and this is where my time with Ark sadly came to an end.
A few pros and cons:
Pros:
Great learning curve. Unforgiving in your first few hours and unless you are the Bear Grylls of Ark: Survival Evolved, you'll want to play this game with friends or at least people you trust enough to take care of each other.
You feel a real sense of achievement when the whole team rallies together to collect resources and each have designated roles to achieve the greater goal.
You have virtually total control on how you want to develop your tribe, your character and what type of base, dinos etc you want to keep.
You get a real sense of community in the game when you make new friends
The skill tree is diverse and gives you a lot of progression and goals to work to
You can have a lot of fun once you get past the frustration of dying, a lot.
Cons:
Well established tribes will show no mercy in taking you out for the sheer lulz (sorry for the use of slang) because they are high level and you are nothing
The hours you have to sink into this in order to keep things running. If you don't have people who live in different time zones in your tribe or establish a shift pattern you run the risk of losing everything with people who will offline raide you unless you have insane building skills and enough resources such as bullets or species X plants to take care and hold them at bay until you log in.
The grind is real. The first 50-60 hours of this game has you dying a lot if you wish to explore. If you have no plans exploring and want to just stay close to home you do limit your ability to grow and expand. Sure you can level up by chopping trees and hitting stones until the raptors come home but it will take a long time to level up. You have to be willing to lose everything and make sure you have back ups to go out and do it again or willing to grind again to get the same gear back.
Prior to official release the game had no end-game or real purpose other than just building, taming and fighting so after a while things became stagnant and that's when you start doing silly things
You will find yourself talking in your sleep, hallucinating and even air punching to keep dinos at bay (at the risk of hitting your better half while she's sleeping. This isn't a joke. There is video evidence of me doing this on the internet somewhere. After 15-20 hour long sessions you do start to go a bit crazy.
And that basically leaves me with this to say. It's not worth it. It isn't a game when you play it like that, it becomes a way of life. The game itself has tonnes of flaws and bugs and exploits that seasoned players have accepted it as the norm. Want to take out an alpha rex? Glitch it into a rock and just pepper it with ammo. Want to be able to shoot rockets down at a base while your Argie takes all the species X damage but it just tickles them? Sure, just have a max health and stamina bird and hang your buddy from your legs who can avoid getting hit. Hell, send the tortoises in to take all the bullet damage and you'll be fine. They're tanks for crying out loud and so easy to tame.
Alpha tribes can also be the end of a server. It sucks to admit it but eventually when there was no competition there wasn't anything to have to do on the server and we would log in less and less and eventually not at all. The tribe I was in, for the most part was a neutral Alpha. We didn't attack unless provoked, be that in the chat or by someone trying to destroy our base or tames and would protect the smaller tribes from bullies after gathering the right intel. But there are some tribes, who get so big so well that the only way to make them crumble is by getting them from the inside. Having a spy turn off the turrets, or destroying a wall so you can sneak in. Those were fun times but they are so few and far between now that the game it once was is no more because it spent so long in early access, and to some degree still is.
To finish off, buy it if you want a game that will kick you repeatedly for the first 100 hours and then leave before it gets worse. Don't buy it if you are looking for a finished product. Because it's not finished. Every time I log into steam there is an update for Ark and I can't for the life of me think what is being done because when I launch it, nothing seems that different.

I've been playing ARK for about six months now. From early access to official launch now. I have to say, I really love this game, despite some of the glitches and frustrations encountered from time-to-time. I have seen many things improve in that time, while other things have stayed the same. (Rafts, I'm looking at you!)
It is a fantastic game with a healthy amount of content and breadth of play, however there are a few major issues that would make me hesitate to recommend it to others.
The first, is an (apparent) lack of support. I've only ever had to file a couple of tickets, the first one they flat-out refused to restore a major capital dino that was destroyed by a game crash. Disappointing sure, but it was early access... so I forged ahead. The second time, another game crash caused my main character's stats to be utterly gimped. I waited weeks for a response, receiving none... and then they decided to launch full release and threw my ticket out! They also decided that the "legacy" servers would receive no more support, choosing (somewhat understandably) to focus on the new official servers for the full retail launch. It was hard to start over again from the beginning on a new official server, but I thought I would give it a shot. Since then, there have been days I can't play because it's full and there is no queue to join. Now, the server I play on is crashing repeatedly 30+ times now, and has been going down like that for hours. ZERO response or feedback from support.
I guess if you choose to invest in a truly fun game, you have to be prepared to tough it out on your own. Support cannot be counted on. Do they do anything? Who knows!? (Please, tell me!)
I do love the game, and will continue to play.. despite these frustrations, lost progress and some days of being unable to play... but Wildcard really needs to look at how their support department is operating because from this player's perspective, they certainly aren't. Expect to wait for weeks for a canned copy & paste auto-reply and possibly no help at all.

I have been playing Chivalry for about a little over a year now and have come to the point where I am able to rate it. The game has many strengths, but also its weaknesses. Starting with the strengths, the gameplay is fun and incredibly satisfying. As well, each class in the game has their own purpose and is unique.
The knight tanks and can do massive damage, however is slow leaving him prey to archers. Archers are about hitting targets long range and attacking quickly with a small weapon, but is easy to kill by other classes. Vanguards push the team and are the main fighting force using long ranged melee attacks that are very powerful. Men at Arms are agile and can combo easily while dodging attacks.
Furthermore, the duel mode and team objective maps are fun and what you'll likely play the most. In addition, the maps are well made and allow many ways to tackle any situation. This allows for tense gameplay where often games are down to the wire. However, there are problems that have yet to be fixed and exploits which can ruin the game.
The blocking mechanic is completely destroyed by spammers due to the fact that they can keep hitting you while you can only block before it's broken. This is because the game works on a system of stamina where by blocking, it is drained. However, if you hit a person blocking, your stamina does not go down, so you can keep hitting until they die. As well, many textures are awful and lighting could be improved.
So should you buy chivalry? Well, if you want a fun game that involves decapitating men and mowing down peasants, some laughs, and a sometimes frustrating blocking system, this game is for you. I have a love/hate relationship with this game and I think I may have problems. Either way, game's fun, pick it up on a sale some time.

Tl;dr: If you generally dislike grinding, this isn't the game for you. If you don't mind ALOT of it, you'll barely manage to stay sane for the first few hours. If you plan to go past just a few hours... Whatever sanity remained, it will slowly be disintegrated as you continue to play, but at least you'll be having a load of fun by then ^^
I like to generalize the Warframe experience in 3 phases; The new player, The general player, The masochi- I mean, The true space ninja
The New Player: Most who just started the game would feel very overwhelmed after completing the first few intial missions, as there is literially no more given help or tips on what to do next. But to make up for the lack of assisstance, most of the community would be willing to help you out if you just ask. Hell even sometimes give you free stuff to start off.
The General Player: This is where the majority of both new and old players either get loads burnouts or just straight up quit the game. As all they see is 'grind, grind, grind, and more grind'. Yes that is basically the entire game, but that means they're missing the 'hidden' message of the game (not really, just wanted to make it sound cool)
To put it simply in my own words.. Because it's fun. You're probably thinking "How the hell can endless hours of constant grinding be fun" or something along those lines. Well that's the exact same mindset for those new and old players who did quit the game, which leads to the final phase.
The True Space Ninja: As repetitive any gamemode may be in Warframe, the amount of frames and weapons to choose from make the grind not just bearable, but legitimately fun. Even the worst kinds of weapons can be surprisngly effective or do the most hilarious things you would not see in any other game. The joy of bringing the wrong set up to a mission, then finding out by the end it worked better than expected.
To avoid making this review anymore lenghty, I would say to truly enjoy Warframe; Change your usual set-up for certain mission types, challenge yourself with small but fun objectives while in mission, helping other players can be either fustrating to funny experiences or a nice break from the constant grinding.

ARK has gone through a lot of ups and downs. made good decisions as well as some bad ones. sometimes the animations can be a little janky (especial on the female character).
What it did right:
It certainly succeeds in one area, even though it's just a game you feel like you worked hard and achieved something. the time it took to build a sick♥♥♥♥♥castle or raise a baby wyvern actually feels like it reflects how much effort you put it, which can be a lot. it takes time but has that way of keeping your attention. In my opinion ARK feels far more like a survival game against monsters and the elements than other survival games like minecraft (i love minecraft by the way, but its more of a world builder to me than a game). the difficulty is what makes it fun, and makes it that much more satisfying when you actually achieve something.
What they should fix:
They certainly need to clean up a lot of their bugs and sometimes unconvincing animations like the slow motion encumbered walk just being the normal animation slowed down, or the opposite being way too fast (like olod timey fast farward too fast). or how the sound of you running, the 1st person animation of you running, and the 3rd person animation all being completely out of sync with one another.
I do wish there were more in-between crafting options (like between the crossbow and the long neck rifle, maybe a musket) or that that a single bullet from an assault rifle or fabricated pistol did much more than primitive weapons. but at the same time they already have tons of options and i shouldn't complain.
To summerize I would say that ark is a great way to spend way too much time and realize that youve been playing for 6 hours straight and that you should take a break, because its actually challenging and rewarding. but they just need to fix a few logical question marks as well as several bugs with gameplay and animation.

A very fun, satisfying game. If your into the Medieval genre, then this is the game for you (hence the title!).
Realistic maps including forests, ramparts, castles, bridges etc.
Interactable items such as; boulders that can be pushed down hills.
Couldrons of oil that can be tipped onto enemies
Catapults that can be projected towards soldiers, or castle walls.
& Much more!
Ranged infantry can be very satisfying when getting fluke shots from long distances, heavy infantry (vanguard) are powerful, but like all other classes, has its weaknesses. Knights are a well-balanced class, can have a two handed sword, or a one handed weapon with a shield, customization is great. Warframe has come a long way from when i first started playing, but i can honestly say the majority of it was great! Let me start by describing what warframe is. Its an over the shoulder third-person shooter where you play the role of a ninja warrior in space. The solar system is in chaos, and it's up to you to maintain the balance. With many weapon types to choose from, and different frames to use to suit your playstyle, the possibilities are endless. However there are certain strategies in higher level missions that even veteran players will tell you work. It's pretty much an MMO at this point, so certain "classes" of warframes work better at farming resources on certain missions. The developers also release new content as operations to introduce the new features, for example, the newest addition was corpus dropships that drop squads of enemies into battle. It was introduced as Operation: Ambulas Reborn, which featured a reworked boss that dropped in from the ship with a squad of regular enemies. There were a few bugs at first, but the incredibly awesome support team was very quick to respond to reports and get back within 24-48 hours. All in all, this has become one of the best free to play games i have ever played, and the graphics do an excellent job of immersing you in a living, breathing world that is constantly changing. I have to say that there are certain aspects of the game which require you to pay for features. Such as certain weapons, cosmetic packs, etc. Other than that, if you work hard and spend a decent amount of time on it, everything important is attainable without paying money for it. I do encourage you to support the developers by buying things that you may like, but only at your own discretion. Speaking of which, there is also a thriving market for the ingame currency, platinum, where you can spend platinum to buy parts, weapon mods, and other hard to obtain aspects from other players, as well as selling your own parts and mods to other players to obtain platinum. The prices will indeed vary on the rarity of what you are trying to get, but there is also sites and a wiki for any questions you may have about said things. All in all i have had a great experience with this game, rather than reading my long-winded review about the game, why not try it yourself? It's free! Also feel free to add me ingame and i will do my best to be as helpful as possible, my name is Mix_Masterson. See you on the battlefield, and have fun!

Okay so before I begin, let me just acknowledge that I am aware of the fact that I don't have much playtime compared to many of the other reviewers, but I think I've played the game enough to know how the game goes.
Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a first-person game, mainly revolving around close-quarters melee fighting. There is a lot of skill involved in these battles, so if you're just swinging non-stop to try knocking a few heads off, you will be swiftly dealt with. An important factor of this game to consider, is that 'friendly fire' is always on, meaning you're going to have to be very careful where you swing your weapons, or else you could be aiding the wrong team. Another key factor is Parrying. Parrying is something not only possible, but highly used here too. Unless you have a shield on you, due to the fact parries only last about a second long, you're going to need to precisely time them if you wish to counter the enemy's onslaught. Fail to do so, and there ends up being a small window of opportunity that leaves you wide open to attack if you blocked too soon. Not to mention there is also the ability to feint your attacks mid-swing, to trick your opponent into needlessly blocking before you take advantage of this to unleash a real attack while they regret their mistake.  There is also a stamina bar which gets used up for just about anything you can do (funnily enough, one of the exceptions being sprinting), so you need to make every move count. Fights quickly become mind games due to these techniques, and the first one to slip up is usually the one that falls. Speaking of falls, ragdolls in this game are fantastic, and very reminiscent of the Fallout series. It's extremely satisfying to take an enemy's arm or leg off in the final hit of a bout.
The game itself incorporates a health bar as opposed to 'regenerating health' seen in a lot of FPS games these days. The health bar itself however, can actually regenerate health back if you haven't been attacked for some time, but be warned... get hit too many times, and the amount it regenerates begins to decay until you lose this magical ability to self-heal until your next respawn.
That is a perfect mechanic for a game like this, and it ensures you that no-one in the match can be permanently invincible, yet gives players a second chance to go back out there and fight the good fight. Speaking of which, time to dive deeper into some gameplay.
There are four distinct classes to choose from, each bringing a different quality to the battlefield. You have the fast-paced "Man at Arms" class, which besides being able to hit the fastest of the bunch, has the ability to dodge attacks by sidestepping or backstepping (you can also use it to perform a quick dash at an opponent and hit them before they have a chance to know what's happening if you master it). The downside of course is that he can't take much of a hit before being decapitated. Next up, is the Vanguard class. This class has a bit more bulk on him than the Man at Arms, and also has a longer range to jab at enemies from a distance. This in itself is very useful, because if you keep far away enough while lunging, your opponent won't be able to reach you at all with their puny weapon. Another bonus of the Vanguard is that he has the ability to perform a sprint attack. After running for a certain amount of time, you will notice the weapon in your hand slightly changes position or movement tempo at which point, if you were to attack, you'd dash forward and perform a powerful move based on your weapon of choice (a lunge attack if you have a spear-style weapon, or a full-on swing attack if you have a sword etc.). It may not sound like much from the description of it, but if you were to try it out, you would realise how useful of a tool this skill can be. Then there's the Knight Class, effectively the 'tank' of the game. All of the Knights primary offenses are extremely powerful weapons that can murder just about anybody in one or two swings. Being the tank, it goes without saying that he also has the most armor and can take the most hits while dishing out everything thrown at him... and then some. As powerful and armored as he is, the Knight is the slowest class in terms of how quick he moves and how nimble his attacks are, making it easier for other players to dodge or parry his moves. The final class is simply known as the "Archer".
The Archer is exactly what you'd expect it to be... an archer capable of ranged attacks. There's the options to use a simplistic Bow and Arrow, the slightly more advanced Crossbow, throwing weapons such as javelins, and even a sling which you can use to bombard the enemy with rocks. Most of these weapons can't be used in rapid succession as they need to be reloaded or redrawn, meaning the Archer is frequently left open to attack in those positions.  In my opinion however, the archer class really should not exist. Even though they have pros and cons like every other class, they are a major annoyance when you consider the fact they are guarded well behind a wall of their melee-loving teammates from the other three classes. It's very common to be fighting an enemy up-close and personal, only for an archer on their team to shoot you in the back from 40 feet away, ultimately leading you to your death. Even if you don't consider their teammates being around, because they are able to be so far away, they are capable of getting 2-4 shots off before you're close enough to strike them, thus giving them a huge advantage over everyone else. You're only safe bet is to hope the person behind the screen isn't all too great at aiming. Sadly, they are just one of the multiple nuisances I've come across in my time playing this game, but I will leave the other mentions until the end of my review.
Moving onto one of this game's finest features: Map Diversity. You can tell that a lot of the stock maps in this game have been built around the gameplay itself. There are open spaces galore for the most part, allowing you to swing your weapon of choice freely without worrying too much about hitting a wall and getting a rebound like in games such as Dark Souls. That doesn't mean to say there aren't any narrower hallways at all, because there are a few of them around as well, yet the distribution on these maps between open space and narrow hallway is what I believe to be a perfect balance between the two. I know I blasted archers a bit earlier on, but I'd also like to point out that there's also a good amount of key vantage points for archers to sit in on and scoop out enemies from higher ground. From a map-design perspective, it's great that the developers managed to pull off all that they did, and I'd even go as far as to say that out of all online-games I've played, Chivalry: Medieval Warfare has the highest like-dislike ratio for the maps it includes. There are quite a few games out there that I've played which have maps that I loathe, and despise when a server switches over to it. Here however, I find myself being excited for each and every map that comes up. These maps are only enhanced further in the Team Objective gamemode due to them being expanded once an objective is completed. I wish I could talk more about the gamemodes, but I don't have much space left in this review, so you're going to have to see them for yourselves.
Now all that is said and done, let me address this games flaws as quickly as I can, as to not emphasise on them: The game has crashed for me multiple times on my high-end PC, matches glitch from time to time and never end until everyone is dead or until the timer runs out, the players I've played with tend to votespam a lot, which makes a box appear on the side of the screen and gets in the way. Archers. All these things let the game down for me, and I feel like you need to have a high tolerance level to be able to stick with it for too long.
Would I recommend this game though? Absolutely.

I can't think of a review, so here's a cinnamon roll recipe:
Ingredients
For the Dough:
1 cup whole milk
one 1/4-ounce packet active dry yeast (2 1/2 teaspoons)
1/4 cup plus 1/4 teaspoon granulated sugar
4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted, plus more for the bowl
1 large egg yolk
1 1/2 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 3/4 cups all-purpose flour, plus more if needed
3/4 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon freshly grated nutmeg
For the Filling:
All-purpose flour, for dusting
12 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus more for the pan
1/2 cup granulated sugar
3 tablespoons ground cinnamon
For the Glaze:
2 cups confectioners' sugar
1/3 cup heavy cream
4 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted
Directions
Make the dough: Warm the milk in a medium saucepan over low heat until it reaches about 100. Remove from the heat and sprinkle in the yeast and 1/4 teaspoon sugar (don't stir). Set aside until foamy, 5 minutes. Whisk in the melted butter, egg yolk and vanilla.
Whisk the flour, the remaining 1/4 cup sugar, the salt and nutmeg in the bowl of a stand mixer. Make a well in the center and pour in the yeast mixture. Mix on low speed with the dough hook until thick and slightly sticky. Knead on medium speed until the dough gathers around the hook, 6 minutes. (Add up to 2 more tablespoons flour if necessary.)
Remove the dough and shape into a ball. Butter the mixer bowl and return the dough to the bowl, turning to coat with butter. Cover with plastic wrap and let rise until doubled, 1 hour 15 minutes.
Roll out the dough, fill and cut into buns (see instructions below). Butter a 9-by-13-inch baking pan; place the buns cut-side down in the pan, leaving space between each. Cover with plastic wrap and let rise until doubled, 40 minutes. Preheat the oven to 325.
Bake the buns until golden brown, about 35 minutes. Cool in the pan 15 minutes. Meanwhile, make the glaze: Sift the confectioners' sugar into a bowl, then whisk in the cream and melted butter. Transfer the buns to a rack and spoon the glaze on top while still warm.
How to Form Cinnamon Buns
1. On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough into a 12-by-14-inch rectangle with the longer side facing you.
2. Spread with the softened butter, leaving a 1/2-inch border on the far long edge. Mix the sugar and cinnamon; sprinkle over the butter.
3. Brush the unbuttered far edge with water. Roll the dough away from you into a tight cylinder and press on the long edge to seal.
4. Cut the cylinder with a sharp knife to make 6 equal-size buns.
